#6422. Crystals reveal what pushed seven very different volcanoes to erupt

Crystals from seven Andean volcanoes share one chemical fingerprint, tying each volcano eruption trigger to a pulse of hot magma from below.

A volcano that erupts once and goes quiet forever seems like a different animal from one that has blown up again and again.

A study of seven Andean volcanoes suggests that, despite their different histories, their eruptions shared a trigger.

The last crystals to grow before each eruption carry the same chemical fingerprint, and it points to a pulse of hotter magma pushing up from below.

Daniela Parra-Encalada, a doctoral student in the School of the Environment at the University of Queensland, read that fingerprint out of plagioclase.

That’s the common white mineral that makes up most of the crystals in volcanic rock.

Parra-Encalada worked with senior author Teresa Ubide and colleagues from Australia, the Universidad de Chile, Spain and Argentina.

Together they collected lava and ash from seven volcanoes along 143 miles (230 kilometers) of the Central Andes.

The work rests on 28 rock samples. Whether the same signal could ever help forecast an eruption is a question the team has only begun to test.

“Plagioclase grows in magma only a few kilometers below the surface, reacting to changes in temperature, water content and magma composition,” Parra-Encalada said.

One of those reactions is a swap of calcium for sodium, so each crystal keeps a record of the melt it grew from.

Two kinds of crystal turned up in every rock the team cut open. Large ones, up to about a twelfth of an inch (2 millimeters) long, grew slowly while the magma was stored underground.

Tiny ones, shorter than about a hundredth of an inch (300 micrometers), grew during the final rise to the surface.

The tiny crystals are the only ones that formed entirely from the magma that erupted.

Across all seven volcanoes, they held nearly the same calcium-to-sodium balance, and the outer rims of the large crystals matched them.

The team named that narrow band the plagioclase eruptibility field. The volcanoes couldn’t have been much more different.

Lascar, the most active volcano in the region, has neighbors that erupted only once, some as long as 3 million years ago.

Some lie on the main volcanic arc and others far behind it, where the crust is half as thick.

In an interview with Earth.com, Parra-Encalada was asked what surprised her most about the match.

“What surprised us most was discovering that this similarity was related to the textures and shapes of plagioclase crystals,” she said.

The cores of the large crystals told a different story. About half of all the plagioclase in these rocks didn’t grow from the erupted magma at all.

Its chemistry points to a silica-rich melt that cooled and crystallized for a long time a few miles down. Along the way it soaked up material from the surrounding crust.

Volcanologists call that kind of sluggish, crystal-packed body a mush.

In the Andean rocks, pieces of it arrived as clusters of interlocking crystals and as chunks of fully solidified rock, pulled loose and carried up when the eruption came.

The trapped crystals share their chemistry with crystals in the region’s ancient super-eruption deposits, which Parra-Encalada told Earth.com was one of the two findings that excited her most.

The same stalled magma systems may also matter for how copper and gold collect underground, she said.

The team is now comparing Andean crystals with those from large ore deposits.

To work out what the fingerprint means, the researchers ran computer simulations of magma cooling and crystallizing at different depths.

The trapped crystals formed at about 1,380°F to 1,560°F (750°C to 850°C), within 7 miles (11 kilometers) of the surface.

The eruptibility-field crystals formed hotter, at roughly 1,650°F to 1,790°F (900°C to 975°C). Their magma had just been reheated by a fresh injection from deeper down.

The fresh injection also carried more dissolved water. As the mixture rose, the water began bubbling out and building pressure in the shallow magma chamber.

Strontium isotopes told the same story: crystal cores carried the signature of melt that had digested old crust, while the rims matched the fresh carrier magma.

The team’s reading is that a volcano on this arc needs a shove from below to erupt, and the shove is what the newest crystals record.

Parra-Encalada then pulled plagioclase data from a public geochemistry database covering 26 volcanic arcs.

The average crystal composition worldwide fell inside the Andean eruptibility field. So did the averages for the Cascades and for Kamchatka.

“And this was not just in the Andes!” she said.

In the Aleutians and in Indonesia, the crust changes from continental to oceanic. There too, the crystal rims fell in the field while the cores scattered.

The result also speaks to an old puzzle. Lavas with intermediate silica levels commonly erupt along these arcs, yet the silica-rich and silica-poor magmas that mix to produce them rarely reach the surface on their own.

The crystals suggest the crust works as a filter: the thick, silica-rich mush and the dense, iron-rich mush both stay trapped, and only the reheated blend in between gets out.

Two of the samples came from an ancient deposit beneath Lascar. It was left by one of the caldera-forming explosive eruptions that buried the region about 4 million years ago.

Those crystals showed almost none of the reheating signature. In a chemical map of an entire rock slice, 97% of the crystals had grown steadily without disturbance.

So the shove that sets off an ordinary Andean eruption may not be what sets off the giant ones.

The authors suggest those huge silica-rich reservoirs can destabilize and empty on their own once enough magma has piled in.

Using crystal chemistry to identify volcanoes more likely to erupt remains an untested idea.

The idea, Parra-Encalada said, is that a volcano whose large crystals also fall near the eruptibility field may hold magma already close to erupting conditions.

Some crystal interiors at Lascar do. Lascar last erupted in the year 2022, two weeks after the team finished fieldwork there.

“If we observe a similar pattern in other polygenetic volcanoes, where most plagioclase crystals have compositions within the eruptibility field, it could indicate a volcanic system that deserves closer attention,” Parra-Encalada noted.

Polygenetic means a volcano that erupts more than once.

Nothing in this study links the fingerprint to how often a volcano erupts or how soon, and the team’s next paper takes up that question.

The samples also come from one slice of one continental arc. The global comparison relies on other researchers’ data, most of it without the crystal-by-crystal sorting this study depended on.

The team is expanding its work to Tonga to test whether the pattern also holds in an oceanic setting.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6419. Teen messaging and well-being: Who is on the other end matters

A study of Swedish teens links messaging with offline friends to higher well-being and contact with online-only friends to lower scores.

The usual question about a teenager’s phone is how many hours. A survey of 3,034 Swedish 15-year-olds asked a different one: who is on the other end?

Teens who messaged close friends or their wider circle several times a day or more scored higher on a well-being test than teens who rarely did.

Teens who kept up with friends they had only ever met online, even just weekly, scored lower.

Viviane Straatmann of Stockholm University is the study’s senior author.

She conducted the study with first author Madeleine Björnsdotter Orfanidou, also at Stockholm, and Kenisha Russell Jonsson of the University of Gothenburg.

The survey was taken at one moment in each teen’s life, so it can show a pattern and not a cause.

In an interview with Earth.com, Straatmann said parents should take an interest not only in how much time teens spend messaging but in whom they message.

“Online communication can be a valuable way to maintain and strengthen friendships with people adolescents know offline,” she said.

The teens came from two rounds of the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, a long-running study of young people’s health across many countries.

One round ran in the 2017 to 2018 school year, the other in 2021 to 2022, and the team pooled them.

Each teen was asked how often they sent and received texts, emojis, photos, videos or voice messages, or made video calls, with three kinds of people.

One was a close friend. One was a larger group of friends. The third was friends they had met through the internet and never in person.

The answers were sorted into three levels: rarely, weekly to daily, and several times a day up to almost all the time. Two-thirds of the teens were in that top band with their close friends.

Well-being was measured using seven questions about the past two weeks, including feeling optimistic, useful, relaxed and close to other people. Higher scores mean better well-being.

Teens who messaged a close friend several times a day scored about 1.6 points higher than teens who rarely did.

Once the team accounted for gender, family finances, family situation and survey year, that gap shrank to about one point and was no longer statistically significant.

Frequent messaging with a larger friend group remained associated with higher well-being after the same adjustments, with a gap of nearly one point.

Straatmann called that an important finding, because it means online communication was not uniformly negative.

Digital contact, she said, can be a positive tool when it complements a teen’s everyday offline relationships.

The pattern reversed for friends a teen knew only online. Teens who messaged such friends weekly to daily scored about 0.9 points lower than teens who rarely did.

Teens who did so several times a day scored about 0.7 points lower. Both gaps survived the adjustments.

The split is not new. The authors wrote that studies in the United Kingdom and Finland found the same thing.

Teens in touch online with friends they knew offline reported higher well-being, and teens communicating mostly with online-only friends reported lower.

Those are small differences on the scale. For comparison, girls scored almost three points lower than boys.

Teens from families they described as well off scored almost three points higher than teens who said their family was not.

The association with online-only contact remained after adjustment, but the differences by gender and family finances were larger.

“This does not mean that all online-only friendships are harmful, but it underlines the importance of open conversations, age-appropriate guidance, and a safe digital environment,” Straatmann told Earth.com.

Girls were more likely than boys to message a close friend several times a day or more: 77% compared with 65%.

Teens from the most affluent families were far more likely to do so than teens from the least, 82% to 62%.

Boys were slightly more likely than girls to be in frequent contact with online-only friends, though the gap was not clearly beyond chance.

The team adjusted for those differences. But the authors wrote that their models did not test whether the link between online-only friends and well-being differs for girls or for lower-income teens.

The study could not establish which way the relationship runs.

“As this was a cross-sectional study, we cannot say whether these online relationships contribute to poorer well-being, whether adolescents with lower well-being are more likely to seek such relationships, or whether both processes are involved,” Straatmann said.

The study also measured only Swedish 15-year-olds, couldn’t apply the survey’s population weights, and didn’t ask about cyberbullying or how good the friendships were.

Teens surveyed in the 2021–2022 round scored almost two points lower than those in the earlier round, and the design can’t separate the pandemic from everything else that changed between the rounds.

Sweden’s public health agency recently issued its first screen guidance for teenagers, built around a daily limit of two to three hours for ages 13 to 18.

The authors wrote that the nature of online contact, not only its length, might belong in future updates of that advice.

Straatmann said the next step is following the same teens over time, to watch how messaging and well-being shape each other.

She also wants to know whether the pattern holds for neurodivergent teens, including those with ADHD or autism, for whom online contact may offer an unusually important route to connection.

The full study was published in the journal Child and Adolescent Mental Health.

#6417. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

#6416. People with early-onset Alzheimer’s often face depression and dizziness before their diagnosis, but not high blood pressure

Before early-onset Alzheimer's was diagnosed, depression, dizziness and brain injuries became more common, but high blood pressure did not.

High blood pressure and high cholesterol are two of the best-known risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease in older people.

In people diagnosed at 65 or younger, researchers in Finland found these two were no more common than in people of the same age without the disease.

What did rise was a scattered set of other problems.

In the five years before diagnosis, people who went on to develop early-onset Alzheimer’s were more often diagnosed with dizziness, depression, headaches, delirium, epilepsy, and brain injuries.

“Our findings support the view that early-onset Alzheimer’s disease is not simply a younger-age version of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease,” said Johanna Krüger, an adjunct professor at the University of Oulu and the study’s lead investigator.

“Rather than the familiar cardiovascular risk factors, we observed a range of other health problems becoming more common as diagnosis approached.”

Early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for up to 10% of all Alzheimer’s cases. It tends to move faster than the late-onset kind, and it more often starts in unusual ways.

The early-onset disease is also slower to diagnose.

Earlier studies cited by the team put the average time to diagnosis at about 42 months, compared to about 31 months for the late-onset disease.

Diagnosis is often delayed by several years after the first symptoms appear.

The researchers wanted to know whether the years before diagnosis leave a trail in medical records.

The team came from the University of Oulu and the University of Eastern Finland. It started with every patient sent to the memory clinics at Oulu and Kuopio university hospitals from 2010 to 2021.

In Finland, suspected early-onset cases in those regions are sent to those two hospitals.

The team re-checked each record against standard criteria for Alzheimer’s. That left 407 people diagnosed at age 65 or younger, with an average age at diagnosis of about 61.

For comparison, a national agency randomly picked 4,035 people matched to the patients by age, sex, and region. None had a neurodegenerative disease.

Next, the team pulled every diagnosis for both groups from Finland’s national health records. Finnish doctors must record a diagnosis code after every visit, public or private.

The team compared the groups at three stretches of time before diagnosis: one to five years, six to 10, and 11 to 15.

Eleven to 15 years before diagnosis, none of the conditions the team examined differed between the groups. Six to 10 years out, one did.

Tinnitus and hearing loss were recorded in 4.7% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

The bigger change came in the last five years. Dizziness was recorded in 5.9% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

Depression appeared in 5.7% compared to 2.3%, and headache in 4.9% compared to 1.6%.

Brain injuries, strokes, epilepsy, thyroid disorders, alcohol-related disorders, and delirium were all more common too.

Delirium is a sudden state of confusion, and it was recorded in 1.5% of future patients compared to 0.1% of the others.

Each of these conditions was still uncommon, recorded in no more than about 6% of future patients.

High blood pressure or high cholesterol was recorded in 10.6% of future patients in the last five years, compared to 9.3% of the comparison group.

That gap was too small to rule out chance, and the two groups were close at every earlier stretch as well.

In late-onset Alzheimer’s, those heart and blood vessel risks have been linked to the disease in earlier research.

The authors wrote that only one earlier, smaller study had reported a similar result for the early-onset disease. They suggested that the causes of the two forms may differ, at least in part.

Health care visits rose only near the end. In the year before diagnosis, future patients had an average of 3.3 recorded care episodes, compared to 1.9 for the comparison group.

In the year of diagnosis it was 6.3 compared to 2.0. Two or more years out, the groups did not differ.

“Of course, no single disease or symptom predicts Alzheimer’s disease,” said Laura Leppänen, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oulu and the study’s first author.

“Our results suggest that, in the years before diagnosis, patients may accumulate a variety of seemingly unrelated symptoms and healthcare encounters. Recognizing this overall pattern could help raise suspicion of a neurodegenerative disease earlier than is currently the case.”

The study compares records, so it can’t say whether any of these conditions helps cause the disease.

Depression, delirium, or alcohol-related disorders may be early signs of brain changes already under way, and the authors wrote that the design cannot tell those possibilities apart.

The registers held no information on social and economic background, lifestyle, or genes, and diagnoses in them could not be checked independently.

Only people who lived through each stretch were counted. People in the comparison group could also have had early brain changes that had not been diagnosed.

Early onset was defined by age at diagnosis, not at first symptoms, which may have left out people whose symptoms began just before 65.

The results come from one country’s health system, and the authors wrote that they need to be checked in other datasets.

Researchers at the same universities have reported that early-onset dementia is more common than earlier international studies suggested.

Other teams are working on blood tests that might flag the disease years before symptoms.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia.

#6415. You Could Hire a Magician to Find Your Lost Stuff 400 Years Ago. The Real Danger Was If They Failed.

Service magicians known as “cunning folk” tracked down stolen goods with sieves and shears—until a spell went wrong.

Christabel Robyns was only trying to find some spoons and a pewter jug. In 1629, there were no smartphones or microchips to track lost items and no hidden cameras to play back video of how they vanished. Instead, Robyns, a widow, is thought to have turned to a more unusual way of getting her belongings back: magic. Word apparently got around, because she soon found herself accused of witchcraft and facing possible death by hanging.

Hers was hardly the only case of someone, especially a woman, being suspected of dabbling in the dark arts. In an age without modern technology, people with problems often turned to “cunning folk,” also known as service magicians, who used their own forms of magic to help. Some were healers or diviners. Others had a knack for finding lost or stolen objects. Whether Robyns was one of these cunning folk is unclear, but she must have either hired one or used magic herself, because she ended up before Ignatius Jurdain, a magistrate known for his rigid religious views. By then, courts across most of England had become skeptical of witchcraft accusations and were lenient toward the accused. Exeter retained its anti-witchcraft fanaticism.

That is where historian Mark Stoyle of the University of Southampton comes in. Stoyle was born and raised in Exeter and has long been fascinated by centuries-old accusations of the occult. His research shows that Robyns was saved when the chief justice of the Court of King’s Bench stepped in and sent her case to a higher court outside Exeter. She escaped with her life, but many others prosecuted on little more than hearsay weren’t as lucky. In Exeter, even service magicians, who were usually seen as harmless, were at risk, especially when their magic failed. That’s what happened to John Blachett in 1666, when a client hired him to find a lost hood. Blachett insisted the hood was in a neighbor’s house, but a search turned up nothing, and the client reported him. He was tried for “certain devilish and hateful arts” but, fortunately for him, wasn’t convicted.

“The city of Exeter possesses the grim distinction of being the last place in England in which people are known to have been executed for the crime of witchcraft,” Stoyle wrote in a study published in History: The Journal of the Historical Association. He also recently published the second edition of his book Witchcraft in Exeter, 1558–1666.

Executions for witchcraft in Exeter are traditionally said to have ended in 1685 with the hanging of Alice Molland. However, no record of her execution has been found, and Stoyle has argued that a court clerk may have misspelled her name, writing “Alicia” instead of “Avicia,” or Avis. Local archives record an Avis Molland who died in 1693, eight years after “Alice” was supposedly hanged. If Stoyle is right, England’s last executions for witchcraft took place three years earlier, in 1682. That year, Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards and Mary Trembles, known as the “Bideford Witches,” were hanged at Heavitree, then a parish on the outskirts of Exeter. Sometimes simply being near a person considered suspicious was enough to seal someone’s fate. Long before germ theory, people who fell ill and died soon after meeting such a person were often thought to have been bewitched.

Society’s outcasts were frequent targets, too. Edwards, Lloyd, and Trembles were poor, living on parish relief and whatever scraps they could find. Each was also unmarried, widowed or abandoned, and a woman living alone was already viewed with suspicion. If someone fell ill with smallpox after meeting or even passing such a woman, she could end up in a prison cell awaiting a trial that might end in a death sentence. Female cunning folk faced particular danger in Exeter, because their work was easily mistaken for witchcraft. In 1642, a client hired Anne King, a weaver’s wife, to find out who had stolen a purse. King balanced a sieve on a pair of shears and recited suspects’ names, and the sieve turned when she said the name Marie Matthews. King herself was then reported and arrested for witchcraft, but she was released on bail and survived.

In most of England, cunning folk went about their business while the authorities looked the other way. Stoyle’s research in the archives, however, shows that they often met a hostile reception in Exeter, where the outcomes for accused witches were sometimes recorded in court documents. A conviction was marked “culpabilis,” meaning “guilty,” followed by “susp.,” short for the Latin “suspensus,” meaning “hanged.” Burial records sometimes confirm these executions. One such case was Thomasin Short, whose name appears with several different spellings. She had been arrested again and again as a “scold,” an unruly woman who constantly criticized others and picked fights. Short is said to have shouted a dark threat at a family that then suffered several deaths. She was found guilty of witchcraft, and her court record is marked “susp.”

“The particular sets of circumstances which resulted in Shorte…being hanged when a number of other supposed Exeter witches managed to escape that fate can only be guessed at,” said Stoyle. He suspects that an outburst of “popular rage,” combined with what seemed to be unimpeachable evidence, “...eventually persuaded the judges to hand down a death sentence.”

Today, finding a lost spoon takes nothing more than a look under the couch cushions, but in 17th-century Exeter, searching the wrong way could cost a woman her life.

#6414. Adding limestone to farmland is helping to store more carbon dioxide than it releases

Agricultural liming in the Mississippi Basin removed more carbon dioxide than it released, after accounting for acid from fertilizer and pollution.

Limestone is rock made partly of carbon, so spreading it on farm fields sounds like a way to put carbon dioxide into the air. Climate accounting rules treat it that way.

However, a new study finds that, over the past century in the Mississippi River Basin, the limestone that farmers spread has removed more carbon dioxide than it released.

The old math leaves out the acid. Fertilizer and air pollution add acid to soil and water. That acid releases carbon dioxide, whether or not anyone spreads lime.

Measured against a basin with the same acid and no limestone, the lime has worked as a carbon sink.

Geochemist Tim Jesper Suhrhoff of the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture led the work with colleagues at Georgia Tech and elsewhere.

The team paired a computer model of soil chemistry with a century of river records from one giant watershed.

In an interview with Earth.com, Suhrhoff said the result adds to what farmers already gain from lime.

“Liming may provide a public climate benefit on top of the benefits farmers already get from healthier soils and better yields,” he said.

Many farm soils slowly turn acidic, and crops grown in acidic soil tend to yield less. Farmers fix that by spreading finely ground limestone or a similar rock called dolomite, a practice known as agricultural liming.

Between 1935 and 1950, lime use in the U.S. rose from about 1.1 million tons (1 million metric tons) a year to about 22 million tons (20 million metric tons).

Most of it went to the Mississippi River Basin, the land drained by the Mississippi and its tributaries. It holds about 65 percent of the cropland in the contiguous U.S.

When limestone dissolves in acidic soil, it gives off carbon dioxide. So the default method from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) treats all the carbon in applied lime as emitted.

The U.S. national inventory assumes about half of it escapes.

When nitrogen fertilizer and manure break down in soil, they produce acid. Burning coal and oil sends sulfur and nitrogen pollution into the sky, and it comes back down as acid.

Rivers carry carbon dissolved in a form called bicarbonate. When acid reaches that water, it turns some of the bicarbonate back into carbon dioxide, which escapes into the air.

Across the basin, acid from farming and pollution far outpaced the lime. By 2015, about half of all the acid added since 1900 hadn’t been offset by lime, mostly on land that sees little liming.

In parts of the Corn Belt, though, decades of liming matched or exceeded the acid.

In 1980, the team’s model estimated, acid alone would have released about 22 million tons (20 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide.

Adding lime cut that to about 17 million tons (15 million metric tons). The IPCC and U.S. methods came in lower, at roughly 8 million and 4 million tons (7 million and 3.5 million metric tons) respectively.

So the standard methods assign the emissions to the lime and miss most of what the acid does.

“I was also struck by how much excess acidity has been added to the system over the last century, implying that agricultural CO₂ emissions from acidification may have been substantially larger than we usually account for,” Suhrhoff told Earth.com.

To check the model, researchers pulled more than seven decades of water chemistry from five U.S. Geological Survey stations between Vicksburg, Mississippi, and Belle Chasse, Louisiana. Samples from the early 1900s filled in the start.

The team compared the bicarbonate that the river carried once liming took off with what it carried before. They traced the extra to about 440 million tons (400 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide. This was removed between 1900 and 2015.

That’s roughly 90 percent of what the lime could have removed if all of it had reacted in the ideal way.

The soil model, built up from conditions across the basin, estimated about 240 million to 410 million tons (220 million to 370 million metric tons). Two different methods reached nearly the same answer.

“I was surprised by how well the bottom-up modeling and top-down river data converged, and that we could actually see these trends at the scale of the entire Mississippi River Basin,” Suhrhoff said.

When liming first ramped up in the late 1930s, the model shows a brief burst of carbon dioxide before removal began. Calcium from dissolved lime attaches to soil particles and releases acid stored there.

That stored acid has to be neutralized before much of the lime’s effect reaches the river.

In the river records, carbon left the basin decades after the limestone went down. The authors warn that carbon removal programs that credit lime as soon as it’s spread could overstate the near-term benefit.

Liming is a close relative of enhanced weathering, which means spreading crushed rock on fields to draw carbon dioxide out of the air.

“This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to trace more than 120 years of historical records that can tell us whether enhanced weathering works,” said Noah Planavsky, a corresponding author at Yale University.

“I would caution against assuming that the Mississippi result translates directly everywhere,” Suhrhoff said.

The early emissions, the delay and the amount of carbon removed all vary, he added. They depend on how much lime is used, the local soils and how water moves.

Where acidic soils hold back harvests and farmers can’t afford lime, he said, subsidies or pay-for-practice programs could widen access. Three of the authors advise CREW Carbon, a company that adds lime in wastewater treatment plants rather than on farm fields.

For most of the Mississippi’s own tributaries, the records aren’t long or continuous enough to separate lime’s effect from everything else.

The authors call for more regional studies wherever long, detailed records exist. Spreading more lime than the basin’s farmers did would need its own look at local soils, water and that early burst of emissions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6412. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6411. A fossil pygmy sperm whale discovered in Peru might hold the record for the most uneven, lopsided face of any mammal ever recorded

A 6-million-year-old pygmy sperm whale from Peru had both nostrils on the left, a snout angled 31 degrees down and a face unlike any other whale.

In 2015, Aldo Benites-Palomino was working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima, Peru, when he examined a fossil sperm whale skull that looked twisted.

The skull had been found in the mid-1990s in the Pisco Formation of southern Peru. It stayed unnamed until this month.

Benites-Palomino and 10 colleagues have now described it as Scaphokogia huachafo, a pygmy sperm whale about 9 feet (2.7 meters) long.

According to the University of Zurich, it shows the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any cetacean and possibly in any mammal, though that claim rests on a single skull.

The holotype, the specimen that defines a species, carries the catalog number MUSM 972. It came from Aguada de Lomas in the Sacaco basin of Arequipa, from rock laid down between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago.

Toothed whales already have uneven skulls, because the fatty organs they use to make sound sit in the forehead. In this animal, both bony nostrils lie left of the midline and the left one is much larger than the right.

The right premaxilla, a bone of the upper face, grew thick and heavy, while the two sides around the eyes differ in shape and reach.

Benites-Palomino, who studied the fossil for his doctorate at the University of Zurich and now teaches at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, gave the university a blunt summary. “The skull looks completely crooked,” he said.

The first worry was damage. Sediment can flatten or twist a skull over millions of years, so the team checked the bones for signs of it.

The sutures were fully closed, and the paper reports no deformation elsewhere on the skull. Benites-Palomino called the shape “genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The drawing of the fossil in the paper also marks shark bite marks along the snout. Sharks left similar traces on other Pisco fossils, and a separate study found that megalodons went after the fatty noses of sperm whales in the same formation.

The team placed 37 points on the facial bones of 3D skull models with a program called MorphoDig, then ran the statistics in R.

The sample held 31 taxa, among them 11 sperm whales, 4 early toothed whales and 16 members of the group that includes modern dolphins.

Francesco Nobile produced the 3D scans of MUSM 171, according to the acknowledgements, which describe the paper as the end of nearly a decade of work on Peruvian fossil sperm whales.

S. huachafo sat at the extreme of the pygmy sperm whales in the first whole-face analysis and again in a second one that corrected for family relationships.

Other strange skulls sat near the edges too, including the walrus-like dolphin Odobenocetops, also known from Peru. The analysis placed Pebanista, the giant freshwater dolphin from the Peruvian Amazon described by Zurich paleontologists, close to some sperm whales.

The authors listed flatfish, with both eyes on one side, and owls, with offset ears, as the better-known cases of uneven heads in vertebrates.

The species name comes from a term that Peruvians use for something flashy, bizarre or tacky. Benites-Palomino said the proportions of the whale “broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans.”

“Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it,” he said.

The snout of S. huachafo tilted 31 degrees below the main axis of the skull. Its relatives had less of a bend, with about 16 to 21 degrees in S. cochlearis and 27 degrees in S. totajpe.

Dense bone and ossified cartilage filled out the snout, which would have moved the center of gravity forward. Heavy bone often goes with bottom feeding in sea mammals, as in sea cows and walruses, and the dense skeleton of Perucetus colossus is another Peruvian example of a whale built with extra bone.

A second skull, MUSM 171, kept the atlas, the first bone of the neck. With the neck raised as far as it could go, the snout still pointed 22 degrees downward. With the neck lowered fully, the angle reached 55 degrees.

Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, a co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich, said the whole arrangement served one purpose. “The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” he said.

Living sperm whales hunt squid in deep ocean water, the university said. The paper describes S. huachafo as a bottom feeder in the shallow coastal seas of the late Miocene.

Most bottom-feeding marine mammals find food by sight or with specialized structures around the mouth, the authors wrote. Scaphokogia appears to lack those structures, and they proposed that it used echolocation to find prey in soft sediment.

Eight large tooth sockets mark the underside of the upper jaw, and spongy bone had filled them in. The authors suggested that the animal may have had teeth earlier in life and lost them.

The paper states that the size of the nasal organs in Scaphokogia cannot be assessed, because soft tissue rarely fossilizes. The authors based the sonar idea on the attachment sites those organs left on the bone.

MUSM 171 is identified only as Scaphokogia sp., and it is the one specimen of the genus with an atlas. The range of motion given for S. huachafo is therefore a reconstruction from a related animal.

When the team compared only the left and right premaxillae, the most extreme animal was S. totajpe, a species Benites-Palomino helped name in 2020, and not S. huachafo.

That test ranked Scaphokogia as the most asymmetric whale genus in the sample. A separate comparison between groups gave a p-value of 0.076, which the authors called marginal.

The university said this way of feeding disappeared as ocean conditions changed at the end of the Miocene. Surface scans of the skull are public through Morphomuseum. The catalog number MUSM 972 still ties the original to the Lima museum where Benites-Palomino first saw it in 2015.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

#6410. Amazon’s New Kindle Paperwhite Is Here. Here’s What’s Different From the Last Version.

From slimmer designs to updated displays and charging features, here's what's changed with Amazon's latest e-readers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon has refreshed its Kindle lineup for 2026, introducing new versions of the popular Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition. Both e-readers have notable design updates, but if you already own a previous model, you might wonder whether it's worth upgrading.

The short answer? It depends on which Kindle you're using. Compared to the 2024 models, the latest Paperwhites offer a sleeker design, updated display technology, and some welcome improvements to everyday usability. The Signature Edition, in particular, gets a few extras that make it feel more like a premium device. Here's what's changed and what's stayed the same.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition

The most noticeable upgrade is the design and appearance. Amazon has made the standard Paperwhite thinner and slightly lighter, reducing its thickness from 7.8 millimeters to 6.8 millimeters. It also weighs approximately 204 grams, compared to the previous model's 211 grams. That might not sound like much, but a slimmer e-reader is always welcome when you're holding it for hours or slipping it into a bag.

The redesigned display construction also creates a more seamless, edge-to-edge look. Amazon uses a new display stack with an oxide thin-film transistor backplane, designed to deliver excellent contrast, deeper blacks, and crisp text. The screen is still 7 inches with a 300-ppi resolution, so don't expect a dramatic jump in sharpness over the 2024 model.

Another small but genuinely useful change is the power button's placement. Instead of sitting along the bottom edge, where it was easy to press accidentally, it's now positioned on the upper-right side.

And if battery life is your biggest concern, there's good news: Amazon still promises up to 12 weeks on a single charge, just like the previous generation. The new model also maintains its IPX8 waterproof rating and adjustable warm lighting.

The Signature Edition receives the same thinner design and updated screen construction, but Amazon has made a few additional changes to distinguish it from the standard Paperwhite.

For starters, it now has an aluminum back instead of the previous model's plastic construction, giving it a more premium look and feel. That upgrade comes with a trade-off, though: At approximately 229 grams, the new Signature Edition is actually a little heavier than its 214-gram predecessor.

The new model also introduces pogo-pin connectors for charging and accessories. These let the Kindle connect to Amazon's new charging stand and a magnetic Page-Turn Cover with physical buttons, which could appeal to readers who miss the page-turn buttons on older e-readers.

One important difference is that the 2024 Signature Edition supported conventional Qi wireless charging, while the 2026 model switches to the new contact-based pogo-pin system.

Amazon also highlights a double-tap feature that lets you advance pages by tapping the side or back of the device, making one-handed reading a little easier.

Otherwise, you'll still get 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. Both generations are waterproof, too.

If you're shopping for a new Kindle rather than replacing an older one, the decision mostly comes down to whether the Signature Edition's premium features are worth an additional $50.

The standard Paperwhite starts at $199.99 and includes 16GB of storage, adjustable warm lighting, and a 7-inch glare-free display.

For $249.99, the Signature Edition doubles the storage to 32GB, adds an aluminum back and automatic brightness adjustment, and supports the new pogo-pin charging accessories. It's also available in Seaglass Green, whereas the regular Paperwhite comes in Graphite.

Both deliver essentially the same core reading experience, so casual readers probably won't miss much by sticking with the less expensive version.

If you already own a 2024 Kindle Paperwhite or Signature Edition and it's working perfectly fine, you probably don't need to replace it. You're still getting the same screen size and resolution, excellent battery life, waterproofing, and access to Amazon's massive Kindle library.

However, if you're upgrading from an older 2021 Paperwhite—or you're shopping for your first e-reader—the 2026 models are worth considering. The thinner design, improved screen construction, and updated controls make the latest lineup more appealing.

For most readers, the regular Paperwhite will be more than enough. But if you read every day, want the premium aluminum design, or like the idea of a case with physical page-turn buttons, the Signature Edition is a worthwhile step up.
