#6409. A new genetic discovery points to how sloths manage to survive while using so little energy

Scientists mapped the two-toed sloth genome and found a record number of extra gene copies. These unique energy-linked genes may explain how sloths survive on so little daily energy.

Hanging motionless in trees, sloths are doing something no other mammal on record does. They can run their entire bodies on less than half the energy expected for animals their size, and biologists still can’t explain how.

A new genome of the two-toed sloth points to one possible part of the answer. The sloth carries dozens of extra gene copies that it shares only with other sloths, and many of them are tied to how cells make and manage energy.

The researchers think those copies may be part of what lets a sloth live on so little, though that idea hasn’t been tested in living cells yet.

“Evolution has already run billions of experiments,” said Marcela Uliano-Silva, a bioinformatician at the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Cambridge, England, who co-led the work. “By studying unusual animals like sloths, we sometimes uncover biological solutions that humans never evolved.”

The sequenced sloth was Lama Su, a two-toed sloth from Tierpark Berlin. When zoo veterinarians euthanized the animal for reasons unrelated to the study, the team collected its spleen, blood, brain, lung and liver and froze them at once.

DNA from the spleen became the finished genome, about 3.2 billion letters long, with almost every letter placed on a chromosome.

A southern anteater named Anton, from the same zoo, supplied a second new genome. Sloths, anteaters and armadillos make up Xenarthra, the only major branch of placental mammals that arose in South America.

The team compared the two new genomes with three published ones, from a maned sloth, a second species of two-toed sloth and the nine-banded armadillo. A catalog of mammal genomes, 41 species in all, from mice to people, supplied the wider comparison.

A big share of any mammal’s genome is DNA that can copy itself and insert the copy somewhere else. Biologists call them jumping genes, and in people most of them are old and no longer active.

The machinery a jumping gene uses to copy itself doesn’t only copy the jumping gene. Sometimes it copies the message a cell has just read off an ordinary gene and writes that message back into the DNA as a new copy of the gene.

The copy lands without the switches that turn a gene on, so some geneticists have classed these copies as genes that don’t work.

The two-toed sloth’s genome has 15,898 of them, nearly twice as many as a human genome, which has around 8,000. Other mammals typically carry between 2,000 and 8,000 such copies. No mammal, and no other animal, has been reported with more.

The other four xenarthrans all had more than 10,000. And in the two-toed sloth, some single genes had been copied more than 100 times each.

About a third of the two-toed sloth’s copies, 32%, also exist in at least one of the other two sloths and in no other animal the team checked.

That puts their origin on the branch leading to the ancestor of all living sloths, roughly 30 million years ago, after sloths had split from anteaters and armadillos.

The copying didn’t stop there. Of the copies found in the two-toed sloth and nowhere else, nearly 16% are so close to their parent gene that they were made recently or are still being made.

The jumping genes that do the copying are themselves switched on in the sloth’s tissues, especially in blood.

The anteater and the armadillo show neither sign. Their jumping genes are old, and their gene copies show no sign of recent copying.

To find copies that might be doing a job, the team started with the 5,123 copies the two-toed sloth shares only with other sloths and kept narrowing.

A copy had to be switched on in at least one of the five tissues sampled, and 2,347 were. It had to keep at least 70% of the instructions for its parent protein, and 525 did.

The third test looked at the DNA itself. Mutations that change the protein had to be less than half as common as mutations that don’t, which is the mark of a gene that natural selection is protecting. That left 123.

The team then checked each one by hand and kept only copies with sequencing reads that could have come from the copy alone, not from its parent gene. Thirty-eight remained.

Many of the 38 are copies of genes that work in mitochondria, the parts of a cell that produce its energy. Others come from genes that handle fats or help a cell respond to stress. The energy-related copies are most active in blood, brain or liver, and the stress-response copies in blood.

Why a sloth would keep spare copies of energy genes is the question the team raises next. Some of the same researchers have early, unpublished results on the DNA inside sloth mitochondria.

Those results suggest that mitochondrial DNA in sloths is under less pressure than usual to stay intact, possibly because so little energy is demanded of it.

If that’s right, the extra copies might be compensating for mitochondria that have picked up more mutations than they otherwise would.

“Our findings suggest that sloths might have evolved genetic ‘backup systems’ that help compensate for their ‘relaxed mitochondria’ and support their unique lifestyle,” said Camila Mazzoni, who co-led the study at the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research in Berlin.

The researchers describe the link between the 38 copies and a sloth’s metabolism as a hypothesis, not a result. They haven’t yet tested what any of these copies does inside a living cell, and the mitochondrial finding behind the idea isn’t published yet.

The team also had only one anteater and one armadillo to compare against, out of 11 anteater species and 25 armadillo species alive today.

More genomes will be needed to tell whether what the team saw in those two animals holds across their whole groups.

Uliano-Silva’s team plans to grow sloth cells in the lab next and test what the copies do there.

For now, the 38 copies are candidates. Whether any of them helps a sloth live on so little energy is the question those cell experiments are meant to answer.

The full study was published in the journal BMC Biology.

#6408. Scientists found two tiny new fish species deep in the Red Sea, but they have completely disappeared from the wild since the discovery

Two gobies under an inch long, netted at 98 feet off Saudi Arabia in May 2023, remain the only known specimens of Trimma charon.

On May 15, 2023, Viktor Nunes Peinemann and Matthew Tietbohl Talas of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) collected fish during a scuba dive outside a Red Sea cave off Walih Island, Saudi Arabia. The depth was roughly 98 feet (30 meters).

The team nabbed two small gobies at the bottom of the cave entrance, where the fish had been moving over dead carbonate rock.

A paper from September 2026 names them Trimma charon. Other surveys done after 2023 found no other specimens, and the authors can think of only two possible explanations: a truly rare fish, or it has a home on deeper reefs.

The methods section lists clove oil, a fish anesthetic, and hand nets as the only collecting gear.

The site sits in the northern Red Sea at 27.7897°N, 35.1630°E. The reef there is a steep slope that drops past 328 feet (100 meters).

The authors described the bottom as hard carbonate with little structure and few living or recently dead corals, which they called unusual for the Red Sea. The region’s corals are better known for recovering from heat stress that bleaches reefs farther south.

Peinemann photographed the paratype fresh from the water in an upright photo tank, using a Nikon Z7 body, a 105 mm macro lens and a Godox flash. Almost all the body color faded later in preservative, the paper says, and only the eye kept a faint trace of its pattern.

Both fish went to the ichthyology collection of the Royal Ontario Museum, under catalog numbers ROMI118236 and ROMI118237. The larger one, 0.66 inch (16.8 millimeters) long without its tail fin, is the holotype, the specimen that formally defines the species. The second, the paratype, measures 0.48 inch (12.1 millimeters).

The paper also thanks the captain and crew of the research vessel R/V Al-Azizi for support during field operations.

In life the goby is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe running from the eye to the base of the tail. Three narrow pale bars interrupt the stripe, and each iris is split into four uneven sectors of white and orange.

The tail carries the feature that gave the fish its name. Peinemann described the golden spots in a statement from the publisher Pensoft. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins,” he said.

Charon is the ferryman of Greek mythology, who carried the souls of the dead across the river Styx in exchange for coins. The acknowledgements credit Jesse Cochran with suggesting the name.

Peinemann also connected the name to the reefs below the dive limit, saying those dark, deeper and unexplored reefs could be seen as a kind of underworld.

Before this description, scientists recognized 10 species of Trimma in the Red Sea. The new fish raises that count to 11, and at least nine appear to live only in that region.

That makes Trimma the most species-rich goby genus in the Red Sea, the authors wrote, though Gobiodon, Eviota and Hetereleotris are close behind. Peinemann and his colleagues also built an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, with photographs of each.

Three other members of the group have been named since 2015. One is Trimma berumeni, a yellow goby known from large caves in the Farasan Banks, also collected near 98 feet (30 meters).

KAUST scientists also described the grumpy dwarfgoby on Red Sea reefs, and small bottom-dwelling species of this kind supply nearly 60 percent of the food eaten by other reef fish.

The closest look-alike is Trimma anaima, a pygmygoby recorded from the Comoros to Fiji but never from the Red Sea. The two share the orange-red stripe, but T. charon has 14 rays in each pectoral fin, while T. anaima usually has 16.

The genetic comparison used COI, a mitochondrial gene often used as a barcode for animal species. Among 93 described Trimma species with available sequences, T. anaima came closest, at 85 to 86 percent identity.

The authors used that gap for a rough calculation. Modern reefs have existed in the Red Sea for only about 5.5 million years, so a split inside that window would need at least about 3 percent COI change per million years.

That pace falls within rates estimated for other small reef gobies. The authors noted that it would still imply a long presence in the Red Sea, and that the fish could instead be more widespread or related to an unsampled lineage.

The size of the record is the main limit of the study. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” Peinemann said in the Pensoft statement.

The team surveyed comparable habitats at similar depths on other Red Sea reefs and found no more. The fish also never appeared in the rotenone sampling stations of two earlier reef studies, or in a survey that identified fish larvae by their DNA.

Depth complicates that absence. The authors’ surveys ran mostly between the surface and 98 feet (30 meters), along the Saudi coast from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Farasan Banks, and 98 feet was the deepest the team dived for science, according to Pensoft.

The steep wall at Walih Island continues far below that line. The paper raises the possibility that 98 feet is only the shallow edge of the species’ range, with more of the fish on mesophotic reefs, the dim coral zone below normal diving depth.

The paper offers no deep-reef collections to test that idea. Deep work elsewhere has turned up a new reef fish about 400 feet down off Brazil, and the authors called the Red Sea and wider Indian Ocean particularly undersampled at these depths.

The catalog entry for both specimens still gives one locality and one date, outside a cave off Walih Island on May 15, 2023.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Vilar, B., & McNaughton, P. A. (2026). TRPM8 and TRPM2 ion channels determine sex differences in thermal preference in mice. The Journal of Physiology. https://doi.org/10.1113/jp288076

Zunnash Khan is a mechatronics engineer and a science journalist from Pakistan. She has written for Science, The Scientist and Brainfacts.org, among other outlets.

#6405. Two teeth found in a Thai coal mine reveal a giant ancient rodent that weighed almost seventy pounds

Two teeth from a Thai coal mine point to a new giant rodent of about 66 pounds that lived some 34 million years ago, long before South America's giants.

Two teeth lay in a clay band inside the main coal seam of the Krabi lignite mine in southern Thailand. A Thai-French expedition between Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources and French research institutions collected them, and they belong to a giant rodent weighing about 66 pounds (30 kilograms).

Researchers from Thailand, France and Canada have now named the animal Yakamys sirindhornae. A molar and an incisor are all they have, so that weight is a loose summary, not a measurement.

The molar and the incisor turned up close together in the same fossil-bearing layer. The team links them provisionally to one animal because both are exceptionally large and come from the same horizon.

The clay band sits at Bang Mark Pit, part of the Krabi lignite mine, which the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand manages and where it gave permission to work.

The Department of Mineral Resources holds them in Bangkok as TF 2942 and TF 2943. Mammal fossils from the pit and a magnetic reversal in the rock, Chron 13r, date the layer to the late Eocene. That means 35.1 to 33.7 million years ago.

Yaowalak Chaimanee of CNRS and the University of Poitiers is first author of the paper. Five co-authors from Poitiers, Montpellier, McGill and Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources worked with her. They chose the molar as the holotype, the specimen that anchors the species name.

The tooth is 0.46 inch (11.56 millimeters) long and 0.44 inch (11.27 millimeters) wide. Its crown stands 0.31 inch (7.85 millimeters) high. Contact marks on two sides show that it had erupted and touched its neighbors.

R. Lebrun of the Montpellier evolution institute ISEM scanned it on an EasyTom 150 micro-CT machine, at 9.03 micrometers.

The model is headed to MorphoMuseuM, an open 3D archive. A lone tooth from the Hudson Bay region did similar work for woolly mammoths in Canada, moving their range farther east.

Hulgana had been considered the largest Asian member of the family. Its molars are less than half as long and wide. The nearest match is Manitsha tanka, an Oligocene rodent from South Dakota, with a molar of about 0.32 by 0.35 inch (8.2 by 8.9 millimeters).

The second tooth is a fragmentary left lower incisor, 0.44 inch (11.23 millimeters) across. The lab set it in epoxy, cut it lengthwise, polished it, etched the surface with phosphoric acid for 30 seconds and then coated it in palladium.

A Hitachi S-4000 scanning electron microscope then showed enamel about 235 micrometers thick, under 0.01 inch. Hunter-Schreger bands, sheets of enamel rods that cross each other, were up to five rods wide. Ischyromyidae, an extinct family of very early rodents, have that pattern.

Yak means giant in Thai, and mys means mouse or rat in Greek. Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn receives the species name for backing science and paleontology in Thailand.

Seven published equations based on living rodents gave the mass. Virginie Millien of McGill University, a co-author here, wrote the incisor equations with a colleague in 2010. Molar equations came from a 2024 paper by Boivin and colleagues.

Results ran from 47 to 104 pounds (21.4 to 47.3 kilograms). The mean was 70 pounds (31.6 kilograms), the median 63 pounds (28.6 kilograms).

The authors took the midpoint and rounded it to 66 pounds, a value they wrote “should not be interpreted as a precise point estimate.”

Adding each equation’s error widens the spread to about 24 to 152 pounds (10.8 to 69.0 kilograms).

Later giants in South America weighed far more, though their numbers have also been revised, with Josephoartigasia monesi first put above 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms) and then cut to about 770 pounds (350 kilograms).

Phoberomys pattersoni fell from as much as 1,634 pounds (741 kilograms) to about 617 pounds (280 kilograms) at most.

Age is the other half of the argument. The authors say an early rodent line had grown exceptionally large by the late Eocene. South America’s giant caviomorphs, the group of the capybara, the largest rodent alive, diversified well after that.

Teeth from South China suggest that mammals grew larger before their teeth specialized. A tooth from Chile put a capybara relative in the Atacama 8.8 million years ago.

Most ischyromyids known from Asia were small and came from China and India, so Krabi adds Southeast Asia to the map.

The team also holds a very large unpublished rodent incisor from the Pondaung Formation of Myanmar, from the late middle Eocene. Nobody has identified it yet.

One molar and one incisor were too little for a formal family-tree analysis. The authors could not test whether similarities with the genus Hartenbergeromys reflect kinship or convergence.

Lake clay surrounded the teeth, but the sediment alone “does not demonstrate a semi-aquatic lifestyle,” the paper says. A lakeside life like a capybara’s stays only a possibility.

Size on islands, a common route to rodent gigantism, does not fit either, since nothing suggests Krabi was an island then.

More complete skull and limb material would be needed to test those ideas. Until it turns up, the species consists of one molar and a fragmentary incisor.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6404. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6403. TCL A400U Designer Series TV Review: An Art TV That Puts Movie Night First

TCL's slim art TV gives you deep blacks and bright HDR, but its art mode isn’t quite as mesmerizing.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Frame TVs are built to look good when you’re not watching them. They’re designed to look like a painting, rather than a TV, with thin designs, wood frames, and a rotating set of digital art that lets it fade into the background of your home, unlike home theaters that often dominate the living room.

While appealing conceptually, most of these TVs do not provide the same performance as an equally expensive conventional TV. Specifically, very few of the models we’ve seen or tested have a feature called full-array local dimming, which allows the TV to brighten or darken different parts of the screen to optimize color and contrast. Without it, the whole backlight stays lit, so dark scenes look more gray than true black.

TCL's A400U Designer Series doesn't have that problem. Its QD-Mini LED panel has 836 local dimming zones, making the dark scenes actually look dark and moody instead of a faded gray. It also hits a claimed 2,500 nits at peak brightness, so HDR highlights, like explosions, really pop. And it still has that art TV look and feel: The body is just 1.57 inches thick, so it sits flush against the wall like a picture frame. Those are far better core specs than most Frame TVs, and at $1,600 for a 75-inch set, it costs far less than Samsung's Frame Pro ($2,800 for a 75-inch), the best-known art TV with a Mini-LED backlight.

While the A400U has the power to deliver a better picture when you’re watching, it also isn’t exactly an “art TV” as we’ve come to understand it. In fact, it’s missing a couple of the hallmarks. First of all, it doesn’t actually have a physical frame: It opts for a stylishly thin bezel that one might describe as artful. And the screen features a semi-glossy, low-reflection coating instead of the matte anti-reflection coating that has become a signature across most of the best art TVs, including Samsung’s Frame and Frame Pro, the Amazon Ember Artline, and the Hisense S7SG. Even TCL’s own A300L, a lesser version of this TV, has it. The matte coating is the X factor for art TVs: It makes digital art (especially paintings) look real at a glance. Without it, the A400U falls from possibly the perfect art TV to one that offers a different type of compromise: It’s a great set for folks who want the Frame aesthetic for an attainable price without compromising on TV image quality, at the expense of that “Frame TV” magic.

The A400U’s QD-mini-LED display panel combines two technologies that are fairly common in conventional TVs, quantum dots (that’s the “QD”) and mini-LED, which is a form of LED backlighting that puts thousands of tiny LEDs behind every inch of the screen. Since the TV supports local dimming, those lights are broken up into 836 groups or “zones,” which the TV can independently control, making them brighter or dimmer to more precisely produce whatever’s on screen. You’ll notice the difference most in dark scenes: Local dimming can accurately produce the lighting of a darkly candle-lit room, or even show what it’s like to see in the dark.

I watched Zach Cregger's Resident Evil, which is set entirely at night, and you can see right away how the Mini-LED’s local dimming zones come in clutch. When Bryan is driving through the snowy mountain roads, the night sky and surrounding forest stay black while the headlights and snow stay bright, so you only see what his headlights catch, which is exactly how a horror movie should look. When I watched the same scene on the Ember Artline, which does not have the tech, the whole backlight stayed lit, and the night sky turned a dull gray.

Quantum dots, which you may know best from “QLED” TVs that introduced them, enhance the screen’s color. There’s a layer of tiny nanoparticles in the display that glow a specific color when light hits them. When the backlight passes through the dots, the blue LED light turns into red and green. This allows the TV to produce deeper reds and greens than a standard LED TV, such as the red of Darth Vader's lightsaber or the green of the Hulk in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. TCL says the A400U covers 93 percent of the DCI-P3 color gamut, the color space where most movies and shows are mastered. That’s a respectable figure, though a step behind top-tier TVs. Top OLEDs like LG’s C6 cover 99 percent or more. Still, the colors on the A400U look rich and vibrant.

While the A400U’s display performance is impressive among Frame TVs, its performance does not compare to an elite mini-LED TV. I’ve praised the A400U for having 836 zones, but there are more than 2,000 in the 75-inch TCL QM8K, for example. With fewer, larger zones, excess light from bright spots on the screen can cloud the darker ones around them. (It’s no different from resolution or frame rate, really: Having more dimming zones creates a smoother gradient for the TV’s lighting.) That glow, called blooming, is pretty easy to spot around white subtitles on a black background, but it's a much smaller problem than the gray haze you get on a TV without full-array local dimming.

TCL claims the A400U hits 2,500 nits at peak brightness. That’s much, much better than the roughly 680 nits we measured on Hisense's S7SG. Most streaming content maxes out at 1,000 nits, so the A400U can show HDR highlights, like the flash of an explosion, at full intensity instead of dimming them.

The A400U has the build of an art TV. It comes with a flush wall mount that holds its incredibly slim body right up against the wall. The mount is fixed, though, so you can't tilt the screen down or swivel it toward a different seat. It also leaves no room behind the TV to reach the ports, so plugging in a new HDMI cable is a hassle. The A400U also has a center pedestal stand for setting it on a media console, but given its size, it looks much better on the wall.

But, as I mentioned at the outset, this TV doesn’t have a physical frame. Instead, the edge is a flat edge of black metal, which is closer to a minimalist frame than a chunky TV bezel. I like the look, and it suits the modern vibe TCL is going for, but it doesn’t quite give you that framed picture look. TK. Removing the frame is a strange omission: TCL makes a more affordable version of this TV, the A300L, which comes with a light-wood magnetic frame that snaps onto the edges of the screen.

In the same vein, TCL omits the ultra-matte anti-reflection coating found on most frame TVs, in favor of what the brand refers to as an “ultra-low-reflection coating.” The matte coating is the secret sauce for art TVs: It scatters light that hits the screen instead of bouncing it straight back at you, which cuts out any glare. In most cases, it does a pretty amazing job of making digital images look like a physical piece of art hanging on a wall. The A400U's finish is somewhere between glossy and matte, but closer to glossy. Combined with the bright backlight, that gives paintings a sheen and a glow that a print on the wall wouldn't have.

I put the A400U in the brightest room in my house, on the west wall. There's a small window right next to it and a huge window on the north wall, plus a door with a big glass pane directly across from the TV. The vaulted ceiling goes up about two stories and has more windows along the top. It's the worst spot in the house for a TV, but also the only space that could accommodate its size, which made it a good test.

The low-reflection coating and high brightness kept most of that light from washing out the picture, and glare was rarely bad enough to make me close the blinds. It can't block every reflection, though. When the screen is mostly dark, there isn't much light coming from the picture to cover up reflections, so the windows around the room show up more. During the day, that makes a movie like Resident Evil harder to enjoy. Brighter shows and movies look fine, and dark ones look much better after sunset or with the blinds closed.

When you aren't watching anything, the A400U can show pieces from TCL's Art Library, artificial intelligence–generated art, or your own photos uploaded through the TCL Home app, and none of it requires a subscription. Samsung's Frame TVs give you 30 free artworks a month and charge $5 a month for the full Art Store. TCL’s TV also has an Ambient Mode that plays moving scenes, similar to the looping landscape videos on the Ember Artline.

An ambient light sensor adjusts the screen's brightness to match the room, so a painting doesn't glow too brightly after dark. Unlike the Ember Artline, the A400U doesn't have a motion sensor, so it won't wake up and switch to art when you walk into the room. I usually turn art mode on whenever I'm done watching something, and I set it up to stay on for a few hours before shutting off.

The A400U runs at a native 144Hz and supports variable refresh rate (VRR) and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro. VRR matches the TV's refresh rate to the frames a console or gaming PC is putting out, which prevents tearing when a game's frame rate dips. I played Control Resonant and Marvel's Wolverine on my PS5. The detailed worlds in Control Resonant looked incredible, with sharp textures on the warped buildings and bright effects. In Wolverine, the fast action stayed smooth and clear, without the blur or stutter you'd see on a slower 60Hz screen.

Only HDMI 1 and 2 support 4K at 144Hz, while HDMI 3 and 4 top out at 4K at 60Hz. HDMI 1 is also the eARC port, which you need to send full-quality Dolby Atmos audio to a soundbar. If you plug a soundbar in there without passthrough, you’ll be left with one fast port, so a second console or a gaming PC would run at 60Hz. Since the flush mount makes swapping cables a pain, it’s worth figuring out which device goes in which port before you hang the TV.

The A400U runs Google TV and supports both Chromecast and AirPlay 2, so you can stream video from an Android phone or an iPhone. Google has added more ads over the years, but it's still faster than the Fire TV software on the Ember Artline, which lagged while scrolling through menus.

The built-in speakers are a pair of 10-watt drivers tuned by Onkyo, with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X processing that simulates surround and height effects. When I fired up Top Gun: Maverick, I was impressed by how clear and detailed they sound for TV speakers. Dialogue was easy to follow without raising the volume, and the rumble of the jets filled the room. In other words, I wouldn't rush out to buy a soundbar.

With the A400U, TCL kind of wants to have its cake and eat it too. Its performance, design, and overall vibe are clearly meant to appeal to the art TV crowd, but it doesn’t have a frame or the matte coating, which are arguably the two defining qualities of the category. That isn’t necessarily a problem, though: It just makes this set a niche choice. This is a TV for people who want the aesthetics of art TV, but care enough about how movies and video games look that the standard Frame and other models like it may not live up to their expectations.

Ultimately, the Samsung Frame Pro still comes closer to letting you have it all—great performance and the true, matte-coated “frame” experience. It also has a Mini-LED backlight, along with the matte screen and a frame-style bezel that make art look like it’s actually hanging on your wall. But it costs $2,800 for a 75-inch model on Samsung’s site, compared with $1,600 for the 74-inch A400U.

If the Frame Pro’s price tag is a little too high, there are plenty of affordable alternatives with matte screens and magnetic wood frames that come much closer to looking like real paintings, including TCL’s own A300L and the Amazon Ember Artline. If you want an art TV you’ll also use every night for movies and games, the A400U gets you that for less than the Frame Pro, as long as you can live with art mode looking more like a TV.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. #6402. Simple fungi can recognize shapes, like circles and crosses, when looking for wood to eat

Daily Wonder, Pink Oyster Mushroom A fungus has no brain, no eyes, and no nerves. Yet a wood-rotting fungus, given a cross of wood blocks to grow on,…

A fungus has no brain, no eyes, and no nerves. Yet a wood-rotting fungus, given a cross of wood blocks to grow on, attached more of its threads to the outer blocks than to the inner ones.

Given a circle to grow on, it showed no such pattern and left the center bare. The researchers suggested the difference may be a form of pattern recognition.

Yu Fukasawa of Tohoku University in Japan led the 2024 study with colleagues at Tohoku and at Nagaoka College.

The fungus they used lives on forest floors and builds its networks by sending thick strands of thread, called cords, from one piece of dead wood to the next.

Its name is Phanerochaete velutina, and Fukasawa’s team had earlier found that it remembers the direction to a piece of wood.

“You’d be surprised at just how much fungi are capable of,” Fukasawa said. “They have memories, they learn, and they can make decisions. Quite frankly, the differences in how they solve problems compared to humans is mind-blowing.”

Even so, the team phrased its own conclusion as a question, not a verdict.

The mushroom in the video above is a pink oyster, not the fungus in this study. Pink oysters, named for their salmon-pink caps, grow on dead hardwood and are farmed on straw as food.

The study’s fungus grows as a thin crust on wood, with no cap or stem. Both break down dead wood with a network of threads.

Fukasawa’s team cut beech wood into cubes less than half an inch (1 cm) on a side, weighed them, and let the fungus grow into them for six weeks.

The team then set nine cubes on each tray of damp soil, in a circle or in a cross, with 2 inches (5 cm) between neighboring blocks. Each tray was about 9.5 inches (24 cm) square, and there were ten of each shape.

Everything but the shape was the same from tray to tray. The trays stayed in the dark at 68°F (20°C) for 116 days, nearly four months.

Once a week the team misted them with sterile water and moved them around the incubator. A camera 18 inches (46 cm) above the trays photographed each one monthly.

At the end, the researchers counted the cords attached to each block, then dried and weighed the blocks again to see how much wood the fungus had broken down.

After 116 days, cords ran from block to block across every tray, though a few blocks ended up with no cord attached at all.

In the cross, the four blocks at the ends of the arms had more cords than the four middle blocks and the one at the center. The count ran from zero cords on some blocks to nine on others.

In the circle, no position in the ring had reliably more cords than another. The cross result was the opposite of what the team had predicted.

They had expected the center block, the one with four neighbors, to be the most connected, and instead the blocks at the ends of the arms were.

The team suggested the outer blocks may have worked as outposts, where the fungus absorbed water and nutrients from the soil. The inner blocks, with fewer cords, may have become little more than a path for cords passing through.

The more cords a block had, the more of its wood the fungus had broken down. Blocks in the circle lost between 18% and 65.5% of their dry weight, and blocks in the cross lost between 16.7% and 62.7%. Overall, the cross blocks lost a little less than the circle blocks did.

The researchers also reran the analysis without the extreme blocks, the ones with no cords or with nine. Without them, the difference between the two shapes faded, while the link between cords and decay remained.

The fungus also spread roughly the same amount of thread over the soil in both shapes. So the cross blocks didn’t decay less because the fungus grew less. The network was built differently, and the wood decayed differently.

The recognition argument rests on that difference. In a human brain, different images activate different groups of neurons, and that contrast in activity is what lets the brain recognize an image.

A network of fungal threads that builds itself one way for a cross and another for a circle may be doing something similar, Fukasawa’s team wrote.

Every block started the same way, with threads growing outward in all directions. Then the fronts from neighboring blocks met and fused into one body.

In the circle trays, the merged fungus kept growing outward, and by day 34 a large bare patch had formed at the center.

Fukasawa’s team compared this to fairy rings, the circles of mushrooms that widen year after year because the fungus beneath them grows outward from its edge. Why the fused network left the center empty is something the team can’t yet explain.

One possibility they raised is crowding: fungal growth is known to stop once the threads get dense enough, and the threads inside the ring may have reached that point.

Whether the fungus is conscious is irrelevant, the team wrote, because cognition can run without consciousness even in a brain.

Slime molds, which also have no brain, have already solved a maze and linked food sources with networks about as efficient as a real railway.

The team raised one possible explanation, and it involves rhythm. The amount of calcium at each growing tip rises and falls in a cycle, and so do the flow of material and the electrical activity through the fungus.

When separate colonies fuse, those rhythms tend to synchronize, and synchronized rhythms may be how the network carries information about where things are.

The rhythm idea is a hypothesis, and this experiment didn’t measure it. The team also can’t yet say whether the tray lids affected the empty center of the ring.

The lids were loose and came off every week, so the researchers doubt the middle ran short of oxygen. The way to settle it is a tray with no lid, and that’s the experiment they said would be worth running.

The full study was published in the journal Fungal Ecology.

#6401. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

Tina Hesman Saey is the senior staff writer and reports on molecular biology. She has a Ph.D. in molecular genetics from Washington University in St. Louis and a master’s degree in science journalism from Boston University.

#6400. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6399. The Grand Canyon’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to over six miles of hidden caves

Researchers mapped over six miles of caves beneath the Grand Canyon, revealing how groundwater flows and why its drinking water faces pollution risks.

For decades, the twelve different water spigots used by visitors in Grand Canyon National Park have drawn their water from Roaring Springs, a cave-fed spring on the North Rim.

In an August 2025 study, researchers at Northern Arizona University (NAU) described over 6 miles (10 kilometers) of cave passages behind the spring. They mapped them with a handheld lidar scanner.

The 3D maps reveal the passages that carry water through the limestone below the North Rim. That system is fast and vulnerable to contamination from the surface.

The park’s water supply has served more than 6 million visitors a year from that single cave spring. Its water is almost entirely snowmelt from the Kaibab Plateau.

Built starting in 1965, the 12½-mile (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline carried that water toward the South Rim and its 800-plus historic buildings.

The aging pipe had at least 85 major breaks between 2010 and mid-2026, according to the National Park Service. A single break often tops $25,000 to repair.

A replacement project shifts the South Rim intake to Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch. On August 29, 2026, a flash flood destroyed a water intake pump and other infrastructure.

The Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs intake areas “sustained significant damage,” the park reported in a September 2026 update. Roughly 40 percent of the old pipeline between Phantom Ranch and the North Rim was also damaged.

The South Rim has been under Stage 4 water restrictions while the park arranged to truck in about 200,000 gallons (757,000 liters) a day. Pumping from Bright Angel Creek to a new treatment plant could begin by November 16.

Blase LaSala, a Ph.D. student in ecoinformatics at NAU’s School of Informatics, Computing, and Cyber Systems, led the mapping. He worked with NAU professor Temuulen “Teki” Sankey, a remote sensing expert.

With park staff and volunteers, the team scanned Roaring Springs Cave, Muav West Cave and Redwall East Cave. The handheld scanner uses near-infrared laser light and records up to 300,000 points per second.

The crews documented more than 6.3 miles (10.2 kilometers) of passages in 25 days. The caves extend beyond 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) from their entrances and 1,300 feet (400 meters) below them.

In Muav West Cave, the lidar maps agreed 98 percent with a traditional survey, which covered about half the distance in the same time.

“I had no idea how large and long these caves are,” Sankey said. “Grand Canyon’s caves have never been mapped in 3D like this.”

Karst forms where water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone, opening caves, conduits and sinkholes.

The caves lie in the Redwall and Muav limestones, karst layers some 2,300 feet (700 meters) beneath the plateau surface. Water travels through these limestone layers via steep fractures and underground conduits.

Abe Springer, an NAU professor and co-author, also worked with the park on dye tracing tests. Dye dropped into surface sinkholes reached springs about 12 miles (20 kilometers) away in as little as a week.

From the 3D models, the authors conclude that today’s groundwater follows near-vertical cracks and the tilt of the rock layers. They link those patterns to regional faulting and uplift.

In Redwall East Cave, bubble trails and other features sit above the stream passage. They suggest that today’s flow may reuse pathways carved by an older aquifer.

“It’s like looking at a black box,” LaSala explained. “You see what comes in and what comes out, but it’s very hard to quantify what’s going on in there.”

The researchers describe karst aquifers like this one as both vulnerable to contamination and challenging to model.

Runoff from burned areas or E. coli bacteria entering sinkholes linked to Roaring Springs Cave could force the park to halt its pumps, NAU warns.

The Dragon Bravo Fire, which started on July 4, 2025, burned 149,399 acres (60,460 hectares), including 71,129 acres (28,785 hectares) of the park.

The park’s burned area emergency response listed protection of the drinking water system among its treatments.

The fire also changed conditions on the Kaibab Plateau, where the snowmelt that feeds the spring begins. The NAU team now has to account for those effects.

“It’s a new twist to our study,” Sankey noted.

A new grant from Grand Canyon National Park will expand the mapping across the park. The university scheduled that work to start in early 2026.

LaSala and Sankey plan to use airborne lidar and decades of satellite data to map sinkholes on both sides of the canyon. They will also track how snowmelt has accumulated over the last 40 years.

“Understanding where the water sinks is critical for the infrastructure, the animals, the plants and the rest of the ecosystems that rely on these springs,” LaSala said. “They’re like oases.”

The study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6398. The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W Power Bank Is a Travel-Ready Charging Beast

This laptop charger has everything you could want in a travel power backup solution and only costs $120.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

ReelCharge, a relative newcomer to the portable battery pack market, has caught our eye this year with a few interesting options. Most notable among them is the ReelPro 200W, a compact but massively powerful laptop charger that can keep up with your travel charging needs better than any pack we’ve tested. It features an ample 27,000 milliampere-hour (mAh) battery capacity—about as much as you can get while staying under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour limit—and a maximum power output of 200 watts (W), including up to 140-watt charging on a single device. That beats most laptop wall chargers on speed. Best of all, it costs only $120, substantially undercutting flagship battery packs from legacy brands such as Anker and EcoFlow.

Throw in some premium features and a three-year warranty, and you have a power bank that truly feels like it's setting a new gold standard for high-end power banks that the competition will need to meet.

The ReelPro 200W looks like a bougie battery pack. It has a sleek housing with a matte finish, a glossy front panel, and a color LED display. A display is definitely a must for a high-capacity battery pack in the mid-2020s. It shows the battery’s remaining charge and the wattage going into each outlet, plus status checks on temperature and health. It’s neatly integrated into the pack’s glossy front panel, so it fades into it when turned off, giving it a pleasantly minimalist look.

The ReelPro can charge up to three devices—more than a little, but not the most we’ve seen. It has an integrated, retractable USB-C cable, which can loop around to become a wrist strap. There are also USB-C and USB-A ports for when you want to charge up multiple devices (and to charge the pack itself). Personally, I prefer a battery pack with an external cable to one with a retractable cord because this leaves more interior space for battery cells and allows for a larger capacity.

Having plenty of ports means little if the pack can’t power them properly, and that’s where the ReelPro 200 watts really impresses. As the name suggests, it has a total power output of 200W and can charge a single device at up to 140 watts. That’s as much as we’ve ever seen in a battery pack, and more than you’ll get out of premium wall chargers for laptops and other devices. Case in point: the official charger for the 16-inch MacBook Pro delivers the same amount of power.

Having that extra 60 watts of output means that when you plug in multiple devices, you’re less likely to see a slowdown in charging. I was able to charge my MacBook Pro and an iPhone 18 Pro Max at the same time at full speed. If you were to plug in three large devices (like laptops) at the same time, there would be a substantial drop-off in power going to the first device, but it can handle most common travel setups without that happening.

The result is a backup power solution that works just as well as plugging your devices into the wall, even when you need to charge multiple devices. On a recent weekend trip, I used it to charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro faster than its included 70-watt adapter, without exceeding 140 watts. It’s the kind of performance we all wish we could get from a battery pack, but never actually do.

That’s a lot of protection for any piece of tech, and far longer than most competitors: Anker, for example, backs battery packs with an 18-month warranty, which is better than average. Standing by its products for so long shows the brand has strong faith in them.

If you are a frequent traveler, or a mobile worker who lives and dies by having constant access to a laptop, this is the best high-capacity battery pack I’ve tested to date. It’s definitely too big to fit in your pocket, so it’s overkill if you just need to top up a phone or tablet occasionally, but this is the ReelPro 200W, a big battery backup that you can depend on, and it costs far less than the Anker Prime, our previous laptop charger of choice.

A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A geological reorganization near Japan may have led to the formation of one of North America's most recognizable features.

The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.

The findings will help researchers understand more about plate boundaries, which is where most of the strongest earthquakes on the planet originate.

"It's more than a regional curiosity," study co-author Thorsten Becker, a geophysicist at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), told Live Science. "It's a reminder of the global connectedness of mantle convection and plate tectonics."

The Gulf of California is an example of a rift zone, a place where continental crust pulls apart and creates a spot so low that it can be filled by ocean water. There are many rift zones around the world; a currently active one is the Red Sea. But rifting can slow down, speed up or peter out entirely. In the Gulf of California, rifting not only persisted, but sped up. Rifting took about 6 million to 13 million years ‪—‬ much quicker than the typical speed of 30 million to 80 million years.

Study co-author Guido Gianni, a geophysicist at the Czech Academy of Sciences, wondered why that was. No previous research fully explained the rapid rifting, which changed the face of North America in many ways. Not only did the rifting transfer Baja California to the Pacific Plate, but it provided an outlet for the developing Colorado River, which subsequently carved the Grand Canyon on its way to sea level.

Gianni and Becker's doctoral student at UT Austin, Xiang He, used a global model of plate tectonics, run on supercomputers at the Texas Advanced Computing Center on campus, to find out if far-flung forces might provide an explanation. Around the same time the Gulf of California was pulling apart, Japan was undergoing its own geological changes. Off the coast of Japan, the Pacific Plate subducts, or pushes under, the Eurasian Plate. About 10 million to 12 million years ago, a single subduction zone near Japan transitioned into two separate subduction zones.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A double subduction zone off Japan (left inset) accelerated the growth of the Gulf of California (right inset).

This transition at the western end of the Pacific Plate influenced the tectonic forces on the other side of the plate, He, Gianni, Becker and their colleagues found.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

The Gulf of California was already rifting regardless of the situation across the Pacific. The initial rift was caused by the subduction of a tectonic plate called the Farallon Plate, located under the West Coast of North America. The Farallon slab stretched and thinned the continental crust of the North American plate as it moved. But such rifting might have ended with nothing more than the formation of a little valley or low spot if Japan's influence had not kicked in to give the rifting some extra oomph.

The findings have a direct effect on scientists' understanding of how plate boundaries form, Becker said. And this isn't just academic. The findings could have implications for understanding earthquake-generating faults such as the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, Becker said. Cascadia is what's known as a "megathrust" boundary, capable of triggering quakes of more than magnitude 9.

"If I'm asking what is the mantle doing underneath Cascadia so I get our megathrust correct," Becker said, "I need to include these effects."

Gianni, G. M., He, X., Becker, T. W., & Faccenna, C. (2026). Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting. Science, 394(6823), 515–519. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef5187

#6396. A rare giant moa egg is returning to New Zealand after spending sixty years in an American collection

Colossal Biosciences announced plans to return a rare giant moa egg, discovered in New Zealand in 1966.

A giant moa egg found in New Zealand on January 14, 1966, spent about six decades in a private American collection. On June 12, 2026, it resurfaced at a public auction run by Artemis Gallery in Louisville, Colorado.

Colossal Biosciences, a Dallas-based biotechnology company whose de-extinction projects include the moa, bought the egg. On October 20, 2026, it announced plans to return it to Aotearoa, the Māori name for New Zealand.

Fewer than 40 sufficiently complete moa eggs are known in public collections worldwide. Only eight keep at least 90 percent of their shell.

The egg measures about 8.7 by 6.7 inches (22 by 17 centimeters). That is roughly 1.5 times the length of an ostrich egg and nearly double its volume.

It has been reconstructed from many fragments, and more pieces still need to be reattached.

The egg may have come from a human burial site from the Moa Hunter period, around AD 1300. Further research is needed to confirm that origin.

Colossal made the announcement at the opening of the 11th International Meeting of the Society of Avian Palaeontology and Evolution. The meeting ran from October 19 to 23 at the Christchurch Town Hall and opened with a pōwhiri, a Māori welcome.

Sir Peter Jackson, the filmmaker and a partner in Colossal’s moa program, contacted the company on learning the egg was being sold abroad. Colossal offered to rescue it at its own expense and fly it home privately.

“Every New Zealander grows up knowing the moa and feeling its loss,” Jackson said in a statement.

Once restored, the egg “will very likely become only the ninth known nearly intact moa egg,” Jackson noted.

Colossal plans a repatriation ceremony in December. The egg will be handed to Professor Te Maire Tau, a Māori historian and tribal leader in the Canterbury region.

“When we launched the moa program we made a clear commitment that indigenous leadership would guide the science and every decision surrounding the project,” explained Ben Lamm, the CEO and co-founder of Colossal.

“We are honored to help return it home,” Lamm stated.

The remaining fragments will be reattached under the guidance of Ngāi Tahu researchers.

Non-destructive imaging, or sampling for DNA and isotopes, could confirm the egg’s species and origin. Ngāi Tahu will decide whether and when to do this, following tikanga, or Māori customary practice.

Kyle Davis is a Ngāi Tahu archaeologist and an expert in cultural heritage.

“To see an egg of this rarity return to Te Waipounamu is extraordinary. It carries information about the moa species that birthed it, the landscape it came from and potentially the people connected to it,” Davis said.

Te Waipounamu is the Māori name for New Zealand’s South Island, where the egg is headed.

The moa de-extinction program behind the purchase began in 2025 as a joint initiative of Colossal, the Ngāi Tahu Research Centre, Jackson and Canterbury Museum.

Fossil eggshell preserves ancient DNA from extinct moa, elephant birds and emus, a study of fossil eggshell by Murdoch University researchers showed in 2010. Moa shell carried roughly 125 times less bacterial DNA than moa bone.

A team led by Leon Huynen recovered DNA from the inner and outer surfaces of moa eggs. Sequences from 69 eggshells matched seven moa species.

Several thin-shelled eggs belonged to the heaviest moa, in the genera Dinornis, Euryapteryx and Emeus. They were the most fragile bird eggs measured to date, the team reported in a 2010 study of moa eggs.

Sex-specific DNA on the outer surfaces of Dinornis and Euryapteryx eggs suggests that the lighter males incubated them. Even so, breakage would have been common if they sat on the eggs in the usual way.

The same DNA revealed two distinct lineages within Euryapteryx, whose eggs differed in shell thickness.

Each moa egg “holds information we can get nowhere else,” pointed out Beth Shapiro, Ph.D., Colossal’s chief science officer.

The Canterbury Museum lists nine described moa species, in six genera and three families. In the coastal moa, females could reach 4.9 feet (1.5 meters) tall, while males were about the size of a turkey.

People reached New Zealand more than 600 years ago, and moa disappeared within 100 to 300 years of their arrival.

Frequent hunting of the birds and their eggs drove those losses, a 2025 modeling study by Curtin University and University of Adelaide researchers suggests.

Moa could only have survived alongside people if no-take harvest zones had covered more than half of New Zealand’s land.

Dr. Paul Scofield, senior curator of natural history at Canterbury Museum, is a collaborating scientist on Colossal’s moa work.

“Moa are central to the natural and cultural history of Aotearoa, and this egg has far greater scientific and cultural value here than it could ever have in a private collection overseas,” Scofield remarked.

The information was obtained from Colossal Biosciences.
