#6395. I’m a Tape Measure Guy. But This Laser Measuring Tool is Testing My Loyalty.

Measuring long walls, gauging ceiling heights, and handling the awkward math are where the Mileseey S50C shines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Look, I’m a tape measure guy. Always have been. Always will be. That red Milwaukee 25-footer rides on my hip like Wyatt Earp’s six-shooter, ready to draw when I need fast dimensions across a 2x4 or sheet of plywood. I ask a lot of it, and it always delivers. That is, until I ask it to stretch across a long wall and maintain its rigidity.

But I got my hands on Mileseey’s S50C Laser Measure and it has me reconsidering how often I reach for my trusty tape—especially when my foe is notably larger than normal and physically out of my league. No one ever said I had to fight fair, so lately I find myself reaching for a more technologically advanced weapon of choice. And in that moment before I grab, I always have the same thought: Why am I working so hard?

What’s won me over about the S50C is how easily it takes over the measurements I least enjoy making with a tape. Long distances. Wall-to-wall dimensions. Floor-to-ceiling heights. The sort of thing that usually has me looking around for another person to whom I need to say “Hey, could you hold this for a second?” Aim, press the button, read the measurement. Nobody has to put down what they’re doing and walk over.

The S50C has been impressively accurate and simple to operate. It’s also handy as heck, which matters to me more than a long list of functions. A tool can have enough computing power to figure out a Mars landing, but if taking basic measurements becomes a small administrative project, I’m going straight back to the tape. With this one, I’ve found myself grabbing it as soon as a measurement starts feeling like it’s going to give me a fight, which is exactly how any new tool tends to earn a home in my usual routine.

The S50C also goes way beyond telling you how far away the opposite wall is. You can easily toggle through its measurement modes on the touch screen display to select area, volume, and wall area calculations, along with more specialized functions for awkward dimensions. For something like a basement renovation, that means you can gather room dimensions and calculate floor area without balancing a notebook on your knee or pulling up the calculator app on your phone. For painting, wall-area calculations give you a useful starting point for estimating coverage. You still have to account for multiple coats, product coverage, and waste—I mean, this device isn’t going to manage your entire renovation. But it can take a welcome chunk of arithmetic off your plate.

The trick is choosing the proper mode and taking the measurements it requests. It isn’t one magical button that automatically understands your basement. You supply the dimensions by placing the green laser dot on the opposing wall or ceiling, press the button, and record the measurement. The S50C handles the rest of the calculations.

The S50C has a built-in camera with up to 8x zoom—but it’s for helping you aim at distant targets. A 2.4-inch AMOLED touch screen displays the targeting view, measurements, and menus. That gives the camera a practical reason to exist. Finding a little laser dot at a distance—especially outdoors measuring distances for a fence installation—can become its own project and a huge source of frustration. The camera is there to help you see where you’re aiming, which is great for me and my ever-flagging eyesight.

Mileseey lists a maximum measuring range of 670 feet. I’ve yet to verify that distance without putting the laser on my neighbor’s home five houses away from me, but it does give you some semblance of the work this device is designed to accommodate. It also charges through USB-C and carries an IP65 dust- and water-resistance rating.

There are plenty of measurements for which I’ll keep pulling my tape. Most, come to think of it. Marking a board for a miter saw cut, checking a short dimension, laying something out directly on a workpiece. That familiar steel blade is like an extension of my hand most times.

But the S50C is worth grabbing when distance, access, or a shortage of available hands suddenly turns that tape measure into a nuisance. Its more advanced functions expand the possibilities, I suppose, but its quick convenience is what brings me back in those moments of need. On that note, if you think your measuring needs are more basic in nature, Mileseey’s S50 PrecisionX model is an ideal alternative to all of those extra features of the S50C.

I really didn’t expect to become attached to a laser measure, let alone one with so many bells and whistles. But then my tape buckled halfway across my ceiling, and the S50C gadget was sitting right there waiting.

#6394. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6393. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. #6392. Researchers designed a stiff new solid that keeps heat from escaping better than soft foams and aerogels

A solid crystal film with organic layers blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics, a record for dense solids.

The best heat blockers are mostly made of air. Inside foam, it sits trapped in tiny pockets, which is why foam insulates so well and also why it squashes so easily. Now, engineers and chemists have made a solid crystal film that is stiff and has no air pockets at all.

It blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics.

According to the team, no fully dense solid had ever been measured blocking heat this well at room temperature. The result suggests stiffness and insulation don’t have to be traded against each other.

Jun Liu, an engineer at North Carolina State University, led the work with physicist Dali Sun. Chemists at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and colleagues in China also took part.

So far the stiff crystal film exists only in the lab. It is a layer far thinner than a human hair on silicon wafers, and it contains lead.

In most materials, stiffness and heat flow rise together. Strong bonds hold diamond together, and it is extremely rigid, and it carries heat very well. Plastics are made of loosely stuck chains, which makes them softer and poorer at passing heat along.

“Because, in general, stiff materials are good at conducting heat, and materials that are not stiff are good at insulating against heat,” Sun said.

That’s why most insulation is soft. Foams and aerogels get close to air by being mostly air. However, they give up almost all their stiffness to do it.

Better insulation is one way to save energy in buildings, but a coating that has to hold its shape on a circuit or a solar panel can’t be that fragile.

The stiff film belongs to a family of layered crystals called inorganic-organic perovskites that stack thin sheets of lead and iodine between layers of organic, carbon-based molecules.

In earlier work, Liu’s group found that swapping some of the carbon-carbon chains in the organic layers with benzene rings – stiff, six-sided rings of carbon atoms – made the crystals both stiffer and worse at carrying heat.

This time the team used molecules carrying two rings joined by a double bond. The rings make the layer rigid. They also vibrate mostly at high frequencies, which barely overlap with the vibrations of the lead-iodide sheets, so heat has trouble crossing from one layer to the next.

The longer molecules also jumble the way the sheets stack. That disorder slows the passage of heat even more.

The team compared four versions. The one with a plain carbon chain carried about five times the heat as the best version, which used a molecule called azobenzene ethyl ammonium.

To test the films, the researchers coated each one with a thin layer of metal. A short laser pulse heated the surface, and a second beam tracked how fast that heat drained away into the film below.

At room temperature, the best film carried heat only about 60 percent better than still air. That’s less than half as well as typical plastics, and one spot on one sample came in lower still.

The team got its best results from films about 6 millionths of an inch (150 nanometers) thick. Thinner and thicker films did worse, and only films in a narrow band of thicknesses stayed near the record.

Measurements at several spots on several samples gave consistent results, so the team doesn’t think it was a fluke of one sample.

For the second test, the team pressed a tiny vibrating probe against the film to measure how much it resisted bending. The azobenzene film came out stiffer than most plastics and far stiffer than foams and aerogels.

The films are made by spinning a liquid onto a surface and then heating it. The authors wrote that the method can be adapted to coat large or flexible surfaces cheaply. This is in contrast to earlier, ultralow-heat films that needed a high-vacuum chamber.

In an interview with Earth.com, Liu picked out two early targets for this technology. “Electronics and spacecraft would be the first series of applications, for the near-room-temperature thermal insulation in the form of thin film coating,” he said.

The team also sees it as a coating for use near room temperature, based on how it held up when heated.

The researchers see other possible roles too, such as shielding parts in fuel cells and solar collectors, or slowing the heat that spreads when a battery fails. None of those uses has been tested.

Like the materials in many experimental perovskite solar cells, the film is built around lead.

“Yes, the current formula has lead in it and there needs to be environmental considerations if the exact composition will be used,” Liu told Earth.com.

He called the tested film an example of a design idea, and he pointed to related crystals made without lead as the route to practical use. Handling lead safely is already a question for perovskite solar recycling.

The team also spelled out limits of the design idea. A near-twin molecule, with the two rings joined by carbon atoms instead of nitrogen, didn’t jumble the layers nearly as much and missed the record.

The team’s model accounts for that gap only loosely, and it can’t yet predict which molecule will work before someone makes it.

Nobody has shown whether a lead-free crystal keeps the same trick. By the team’s own estimate, a molecule whose rings twist more easily could push the film’s heat flow close to that of air itself. Making one is the next test.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

Waters, M. N., Wooten, S. L., Abrook, A. M., Brenner, M., Curtis, J. H., Langdon, P. G., Medina-Gonzalez, R. M., Paradeisis-Stathis, S., & Vachula, R. S. (2026). Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya. Science Advances, 12(45), eaeh3280. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3280

#6390. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#6389. A whale buried for 9.5 million years had unexpected company

Scientists discovered ancient brittle star fossils beside whale bones, revealing how marine animals gathered around carcasses millions ago.

Brittle stars gather around dead whales on today’s seafloor, sometimes at much higher densities than on the surrounding seabed. Yet no fossil had ever placed them at a whale carcass.

Studies of fossil whale carcasses have mostly reported clams, snails, and animals that eat bone.

Now fossils from beside a beaked whale skeleton in Denmark suggest that brittle stars joined these gatherings 9.5 million years ago.

If that reading holds, it’s the first fossil record of a brittle star tied to a whale fall. That’s the term scientists use for a sunken whale carcass and the community of life it feeds.

The clues are tiny skeletal plates from a species new to science, now named Ophiura huebnerjenseni. The fossils are loose pieces rather than whole animals, so they can’t show what the brittle stars ate.

Ben Thuy, curator of paleontology at Luxembourg’s National Museum of Natural History, led the study.

Thuy worked with Mette Elstrup and Trine Sørensen of Museum Sønderjylland in Denmark. The fourth author, Lea Numberger-Thuy, works at the Luxembourg museum and at a dinosaur park in Germany.

The Gram Clay Pit in southern Denmark exposes about 23 to 25 feet (7 to 7.5 meters) of clay that built up on the floor of an ancient North Sea. Geologists call these layers the Gram Formation.

The pit is famous for its fossil clams, snails, and animals with backbones, including whale skeletons and giant megalodon vertebrae. Sea urchins, sea stars, and their relatives have been far scarcer there.

Scientists call that group of spiny-skinned animals the echinoderms. Before this study, only one echinoderm species had been reported from the Gram Formation.

Brittle stars are echinoderms too, with long, thin, flexible arms built from many small skeletal pieces.

The North Sea has plenty of them today, yet none had been found in these old clays. Thuy and Numberger-Thuy had already searched for them in clays of a similar age at Groß Pampau in northern Germany, without success.

The new fossils came from sediment collected in 2018, during the excavation of a beaked whale‘s lower jaw and four vertebrae from its backbone.

The bones were found about 21 feet (6.5 meters) below the top of the exposed clay. That level dates to roughly 9.5 million years ago.

Five sediment samples came from around the skeleton. The team dried each one, soaked it in water, and washed it through screens, then washed the leftovers a second time with a detergent-like chemical.

Under a microscope, the researchers picked out the smallest fossils one by one. The best brittle-star pieces were then photographed with a scanning electron microscope.

For comparison, they also processed a sample packed with tiny fossils. It came from 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) below a fossil log that was dug up in 2023.

“Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” Thuy said.

The three samples held 33 skeletal pieces in all. Most were plates from the sides of the arms, along with one piece of an arm’s inner backbone and one plate from the central disc of the body.

The arm plate chosen as the reference specimen for the species came from a sample taken 2 to 8 inches (5 to 20 centimeters) from the whale’s jawbones. Its shape placed the animal in the genus Ophiura, which still lives in the North Sea.

The closest living match there is Ophiura albida. The fossil plates differ from it in two ways: they have a slanted upper edge, and they lack the faint spurs that O. albida plates carry.

A cluster of fossils beside a skeleton doesn’t automatically mean the animals lived there, so the team considered other explanations.

“We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them,” Thuy added.

“However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass.”

Scientists divide a whale fall’s life into stages. In the early stage, the carcass enriches the seabed around it and feeds animals that take advantage of any sudden meal.

In the deep sea, later stages can follow. One of them supports life that runs on sulfur compounds released as the bones decay.

Fossils around the Gram whale included clams that filter food from the water and meat-eating snails, some of them scavengers.

The team found no clams of the kind that live off chemical energy with help from bacteria. The bones had no animals cemented to their surfaces and showed no signs of burrowing.

“We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls,” Elstrup said.

“The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed.”

Ophiura huebnerjenseni honors Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, who founded the heavy metal festival Wacken Open Air. It joins a long line of species named after musicians, but this one comes with a geological link.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-year-old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” Numberger-Thuy said.

Brittle stars have been found before beside the carcasses of ichthyosaurs, ancient sea reptiles, in rocks from the Early Jurassic. A fossil whale fall had never produced one.

The researchers can’t yet say whether this species lived only at whale carcasses.

They favor the idea that it lived on the surrounding seabed and gathered at the carcass in numbers large enough to leave a fossil trace.

Living brittle stars at shallow whale falls also come from the nearby seafloor. Finding plates of this species in ordinary Gram mud, far from any bones, would support that idea.

For now, the only place Ophiura huebnerjenseni has been found is the mud right beside one whale.

The full study was published in the journal Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen.

#6388. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#6387. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6386. Bees make a natural plastic that starts breaking down in soil within months

Solitary bees make natural plastic that breaks down in soil, offering clues for designing less persistent synthetic materials.

A plastic wrapper may be useful for a few minutes, then stay in the environment for centuries. But a small bee makes a plastic-like material that starts breaking down in soil within months.

The bee, Colletes inaequalis, uses it to cover the inside of its underground nest. The material helps protect the young bee growing inside.

Researchers studied these nests in Tennessee. In fresh nests, plastic made up 73% of the lining’s weight, but four months later, that share had fallen to 40%.

Now the team wants to learn how the bee makes a material that is tough but still breaks down. The answer could help scientists make better plastics for everyday use.

Jonathan Coote, an assistant professor at Virginia Tech, led the study.

Laura Russo, who studies bees at the University of Tennessee, first told him about the material while he was a doctoral student there.

Coote kept studying it during his later research at the University of Minnesota. After joining Virginia Tech in 2025, he made it his main research focus.

Scientists identified the chemical makeup of the bee’s plastic more than 45 years ago. But for years afterward, few people studied it further.

Most bees live alone rather than in hives. This species, common in the eastern United States, digs tunnels in the ground and builds small rooms for its young.

The female covers each room with a thin, clear layer, which gives these insects the name cellophane bees. She adds pollen and nectar, lays one egg, and closes the room.

The young bee spends more than 90% of its life inside. The lining likely protects it and its food from water and fungus.

The lining contains silk and a natural plastic made by the female.

A gland connected to her stinger releases tiny, ring-shaped molecules, which join into long chains as she spreads them over the walls.

The bee’s material resembles polyethylene, a plastic widely used in packaging.

Polyethylene contains long chains of carbon atoms held together by strong bonds that are hard to break, even in industrial compost.

Only about 9% of the world’s plastic was recycled in 2022. Nearly a third is poorly managed and ends up in the environment, where it can break into tiny pieces called microplastics.

Scientists have tried making similar plastics with weaker links in their chains. Water or enzymes, natural substances that help chemical reactions happen, can break these links.

These materials are called polyesters, and the bee’s plastic belongs to this group. “This is a polyester that mimics polyethylene,” Coote said.

Even with weaker links, most lab-made versions barely break down.

Their chains pack closely together and keep water out, making the weaker links hard to reach.

The best-studied version lost only 18% of its weight after 280 days in industrial compost. It did not break down at all under milder conditions.

The bee’s nests offered a clue that its material was different. More than 10,000 nests can share one site, and bees may return to the same ground for decades.

Yet the old plastic linings do not seem to pile up. Something appears to break them down.

The team first tried to dissolve the bee’s plastic to study its chains. After two days in a solvent heated to 302°F (150°C), the material still held its shape and size.

This suggested that the chains were linked together like a net.

About 60% of the plastic also formed tightly packed areas called crystals, arranged like those in polyethylene.

Usually, these tightly packed areas make plastic harder to break down. So the bee’s material seemed to have the same features that cause trouble in lab-made plastics.

The researchers collected fresh nests in March 2023 in Hamblen County, eastern Tennessee.

They returned in July and October 2023 and February 2024, digging seven to 12 inches (17 to 30 centimeters) down to find them.

After four months, the linings could still bend and hold their shape. By about seven months, when the young bees had become adults, cracks had appeared.

By 11 months, the linings crumbled when handled roughly. They had not vanished, but they were falling apart.

At first, the lining was about 73% plastic and 27% silk by weight. After four months, plastic made up only 40% of the remaining lining.

Silk usually breaks down fairly quickly, so the team was surprised to find the plastic breaking down even faster.

Later, the balance changed less, suggesting both materials were then breaking down at roughly the same pace.

Tightly packed regions accounted for about 60% of the plastic initially and nearly 100% of the remaining plastic after four months. By 11 months, their share had fallen to 39%.

This suggests the looser parts broke down first. The tightly packed parts appear to have broken down later.

The answer may lie in the plastic’s tiny building blocks. Most are rings with 18 carbon atoms, while some have 20 or 22.

Mixing these sizes may spread the weaker links unevenly along the chains. That could leave more links where water and enzymes can reach them.

The tightly packed areas are also small and less orderly, which could help. Microbes in the nest may also play a part.

Another idea involves an enzyme in the bee’s saliva. It might help build the plastic, then help break it down later.

The researchers rinsed the linings three times and collected the liquid. They added a chemical that this kind of enzyme can break apart.

Liquid from both a new lining and a four-month-old lining broke down the chemical. This suggests enzymes could keep working in the nest for months.

But the test used only one new nest and one older nest. More tests are needed to find out what those enzymes actually do.

The team still does not know which explanation matters most. Each nest provides only a few milligrams of lining, so some tests ran just once or twice, and all the older nests came from one site.

“The goal is to be able to answer that and then engineer it into something that we can make at scale. I don’t see a future where we have these massive bee farms making all of our plastic products,” Coote said.

If the spacing of the weaker links is the key, scientists could try copying it. They want a useful plastic that can break down in soil after its job is done.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6385. Jackery’s FridgeGuard Brings Basic Automated Backup Power at an Affordable Price

Our tests show that during short blackouts, this automated backup power system gets the job done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not every home power backup solution has to be an expensive and complicated system. Certainly, a portable power station can be affordable, but it usually has to be set up when the power goes out, which isn’t convenient if you’re not at home. What if you could meet in the middle with something affordable but also automated? That’s the aim of a device like Jackery’s FridgeGuard, an automated appliance backup device that costs less than $800.

It’s named FridgeGuard because Jackery, like competitors Bluetti and BioLite (whose products we also reviewed), is banking on the idea that the appliance most people care about powering when the lights go out is the refrigerator. It makes sense; you’ve got the most to lose with spoiled food during an extended blackout. But in truth, you can use this type of backup with any alternating-current-powered device, whether that is a fish tank, automatic pet feeder, garage freezer, or even essential medical equipment. And since this is designed to be always-on, you don’t have to think about it very much once you set it up.

Out of the box, the Jackery FridgeGuard is smaller and lighter than the competition. It’s a few inches shorter than those from Bluetti and BioLite, and only weighs 23 pounds—the others weigh more than 40 pounds. That makes the task of placing this out of the way, either mounted on a cabinet or sitting flat on top of a cabinet, a bit easier. It also has two airflow vents that you can remove to clean or replace filters, which is a nice feature to have in a kitchen, where air particles can be heavier from cooking.

Cutting down on the size keeps the price point lower, but this comes at another cost. At 1,024 watt-hours of battery capacity, FridgeGuard can’t run a refrigerator for as long as the competition, and with only 800 watts of output (roughly half the amount or more of the others), you can’t run as many things from it. There’s also only one outlet, as opposed to two, so if you want to power more than one thing, you’ll need to attach a power strip.

Of course, this may not matter to people who really are only concerned about keeping their refrigerator running. I tested this out on my own full-size French-door, bottom-freezer model, and I was able to run it for 11 hours. That’s enough time for most people experiencing a blackout after a severe storm. If you find that’s not enough, you can always add the FridgeGuard battery pack and double that capacity to 2,048 watt-hours.

There are some other hidden cost-cutting measures, too. Jackery includes attachable feet if you want to stand it vertically, but wall mounts are optional ($29), and if you want to recharge it using a portable solar panel, you’ll need to purchase a proprietary adapter that costs $89. Competitors include wall mounts, and solar inputs are built into their units.

Despite some cost cutting with its hardware, FridgeGuard doesn’t skimp on smart features within the app. If you're away from home, you get notifications when the power goes out and when the FridgeGuard is starting to get low on power. If you live in a region with variable utility rates, you can set it to only recharge from grid power when the rates are at their lowest (your electric company can tell you when that is).

Conversely, you can also use it to save a bit of money by using a time-of-use (TOU) mode that powers the fridge from the battery during high-rate hours and grid power only during the low-rate hours. It would take many months of testing to see how much money you could really save using this mode, but the potential is there.

Some may worry about daily discharge and recharge, but FridgeGuard runs on a lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery that offers up to 6,000 recharge cycles, which is 16 years if you were to do it every day. In the end, TOU mode may be worth it.

If all you want is automated backup power for your refrigerator (or another essential appliance or device) for a few hours, Jackery’s FridgeGuard is the simplest and most economical way to go. It’s easy to set up and the epitome of instant automation. If you frequently experience blackouts longer than 12 hours, spending a bit more on a system from Bluetti or BioLite may suit your needs better, but if not, Jackery has built a good product for you.

#6384. When rain returns after a drought, groundwater reserves don’t always get caught up before the next drought

Most groundwater refills faster than it drains in a drought, but in about a quarter of places, the next drought hits before recovery ends.

When a drought breaks, the rain returns first, then the soil moisture, the plants and the rivers. Groundwater usually comes last, and in some places the next drought arrives before it has caught up.

A new global analysis suggests that, in most places, groundwater refills faster than it drains during a drought. But across about a quarter of the places studied, water levels tended to slip back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That matters because groundwater supplies roughly 35 percent of all the fresh water people withdraw, and it’s the reserve many communities rely on when rivers run low.

Hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth led the work with three colleagues at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. Their results come from a computer model rather than direct measurements.

It estimates how deep you’d have to dig to reach water, a level called the water table, month by month from 1960 to 2019.

This model divides the world’s land into squares about 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) across. It was developed at Utrecht’s Department of Physical Geography, and it tracks both the rain that soaks into soil and the water people pump out of it.

Checked against real wells, the model gave useful estimates at about 80 percent of wells shallower than about 200 feet (60 meters). For deeper wells, the figure was about 70 percent.

For every square and every calendar month, the team worked out how deep the water table usually was and how much that depth normally varied.

A drought started when the groundwater dropped so far below its usual level for that time of year that only about 16 percent of months would qualify. It ended when the water rose back above that line.

Droughts lasting two months or less were left out, because monthly data can’t capture them reliably. For the rest, the team measured how fast the water fell, how fast it rose again, and what it did in the six months afterward.

Climate did more than anything else to set the pace of recovery. Places where a lot of rain soaks into the ground, such as the Amazon and Southeast Asia, recovered quickly. Their droughts also tended to be shorter and more frequent.

Dry regions recovered slowly. The slow places included Australia, the Middle East and Central Asia, southern Africa, southern South America and the U.S. Midwest.

During drought recovery, the groundwater at a typical location rose about 0.7 inches (1.8 centimeters) a month. In the fastest places it climbed as much as about 3 feet (1 meter) a month.

Those raw speeds partly reflect how much a water table swings in an ordinary year. So the team also compared each place with its own normal range, and the split between wet and dry regions became sharper.

Average speed told only part of the story. Two places could recover at the same average rate and still behave very differently during a drought.

Hauswirth hadn’t expected recovery to vary so much within a single region. In an interview with Earth.com, she said, “I was surprised to see that the groundwater recovery pattern was not necessarily homogeneous within a region and could vary quite a bit locally.”

To capture those differences, the team sorted every location by how its droughts unfolded. About 57 percent were resilient: on average, the water came back faster than it had dropped. Another 26 percent were unstable, slipping back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That makes the unstable group the second largest. The researchers described its behavior as even more critical than that of the vulnerable group, where the water fell quickly and climbed back slowly.

The unstable group covered about 15 percent of places, and only around 2 percent were stable, with the fall and the rise at about the same speed.

Unstable places weren’t clustered in one part of the world, and they weren’t limited to heavily pumped areas. Their droughts were shorter, milder and more frequent than in any other group, often with little time to refill in between.

Terrain set the vulnerable places apart. In every region the team examined up close, they turned up at higher elevations, where the ground stores less water and the water table swings more widely.

In Europe, some may be linked to limestone country, where water drains through cracks and caves.

The close-ups included California, Spain, India and the North China Plain, all places known for heavy groundwater use. In Spain, the vulnerable and unstable spots shared similar pumping patterns. In California, pumping appeared to affect more of the categories.

Sorting places this way, Hauswirth said, made it clear that local features “are an important part of the drivers and should not be underestimated.”

For water managers in vulnerable regions, her advice starts with knowing where the water comes from. Where possible, she said, they should map how much of local demand and supply is covered by groundwater.

That “could help us better understand when groundwater resources are overexploited,” she told Earth.com, and when a wet spell could help restore levels, possibly by cutting back on pumping.

The authors name their own blind spots. They filtered out places where water tables have fallen steadily for decades, often from heavy pumping, because a long decline makes single droughts hard to pick out. Those places may be underrepresented in the results.

Every number here is also a model’s estimate. This model performed well against real wells, but global groundwater models have both overestimated and underestimated water levels in the past.

And because the team averaged 60 years together, the results can’t show whether recovery is speeding up or slowing down.

“I want to dive deeper into how these recovery patterns have changed over time, as the current work has mainly focused on the spatial pattern,” Hauswirth said.

Next, the team wants to pair the four categories with projections of a warmer climate. That could show which places are at risk of shifting from resilient toward vulnerable or unstable.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Water.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how frequently did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6382. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in new destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

And the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!)

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy issues).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing new cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!
