#6325. 12 Airline Booking Traps That Could Cost You Money in 2026

Airline websites are not necessarily badly designed, even though they often feel that way. In many cases, the booking process is doing exactly what it was designed to do: get you focused on the lowest advertised fare before revealing the cost of everything else.

You start with a flight that looks like it costs $400. By the time you add a carry-on bag, choose a seat, and work through the final checkout screens, the total is suddenly $650.

After more than 18 years of travel to over 130 countries, we still catch ourselves slowing down to double-check airline bookings. The difference now is that we know where the expensive mistakes are usually hiding. We also use flight-search and tracking tools to compare routes and monitor changes. See our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

The lowest price on the first screen is rarely enough information to tell you which flight is actually cheapest. You need to compare the complete journey, including baggage, seats, fare restrictions, connections, operating airlines, and the risk involved if something goes wrong.

To avoid costly airline booking mistakes, compare the total price of the journey rather than the advertised base fare. Check the conditions of the exact fare, baggage allowances, operating airline, cabin on every segment, connection times, and whether the flights are issued on one protected ticket.Before paying, compare the flight as a round trip, two one-way tickets, and a multi-city itinerary. Before leaving home, verify your passport, visas or travel authorizations, transit requirements, check-in deadline, and gate-closing time.

These airline booking traps—also common flight-booking mistakes—can turn an apparently cheap ticket into the most expensive option.

One of the first mistakes travellers make is comparing flights by airline logo.

You see the airline you normally use, remember the points sitting in your account, and stop comparing. But loyalty should not convince you to pay hundreds of dollars more for a worse schedule, a more restrictive ticket, or a fare that excludes everything you need.

Airline points can still be valuable, especially when you are close to earning useful status or have benefits such as complimentary baggage. But loyalty should be one part of the calculation, not the starting point.

The days of automatically paying more because “this is our airline” are over. Loyalty should follow value, not the other way around.

Basic Economy can be a perfectly reasonable fare. The trap is buying it without understanding what has been removed.

It may work well when you are taking a short flight, travelling with only a small personal item, do not care where you sit, and are confident your plans will not change.

The problem is that airline websites normally display the lowest available fare first. Once you are in booking mode, it is easy to select that number and move forward without reading the restrictions.

You may save $40 on the ticket and then spend $85 adding the carry-on bag you needed from the beginning.

Before booking Basic Economy, price the next fare category. A Standard Economy ticket may cost more initially but include a carry-on bag, checked luggage, seat selection, or greater flexibility.

Also consider whether seat selection genuinely matters. Travellers with children, mobility considerations, medical needs, or a strong need for an aisle or window seat should include that cost when comparing fares.

Do not buy the lowest number. Buy the fare that includes what you actually need.

Airlines do not necessarily sell every Economy Class seat at the same price. Seats are divided into fare classes or pricing tiers, often called fare buckets.

When the cheapest tier sells out, the price can jump even when the aircraft still has many empty seats.

That is one reason a flight might appear at $480 in the morning and $620 later that day. It does not always mean the plane suddenly filled up. It may mean the least expensive fare class is no longer available.

When you see a noticeable price increase, do not assume you must either pay it immediately or lose the trip.

A competitor may now be cheaper. In other cases, the next fare level may include baggage, seat selection, or flexibility that makes it better value than the stripped-down ticket you were originally considering. A fare jump is a signal to widen the search, not automatically accept the new price.

For the tools we use to compare dates, airports, and fare changes, see our guide to the best travel apps for finding flights.

The standard airline search box encourages travellers to enter a departure city, destination, outbound date, and return date.

That does not mean a traditional round trip is always the cheapest or most efficient way to book.

Before purchasing an expensive international itinerary, compare it three ways:

An open-jaw ticket means flying into one city and returning home from another.

For example, if you are travelling through Europe, you might fly into Paris and return from Rome. Even if the airfare is similar to a return ticket from Paris, you could avoid paying for a train or flight back to your starting point. You may also save a hotel night and an entire day of backtracking.

Different airlines can also be used in each direction. One carrier may offer the best outbound flight, while another has a much better return schedule.

When comparing separate tickets, check baggage fees, fare restrictions, connection risks, and cancellation policies. The goal is not to find the cleverest itinerary. It is to determine which option gives you the best total trip.

With a codeshare flight, the airline selling the ticket may not be the airline flying the plane.

You might purchase the journey through one airline’s website and then arrive at the airport to discover that a partner carrier operates the flight.

Before buying, look for the words “operated by” in the flight details.

Then check the itinerary on both airline websites. Confirm the aircraft, seat map, baggage allowance, terminal, and check-in instructions.

After booking, make sure you have the operating carrier’s reservation number. The confirmation number issued by the airline selling the ticket may not work on the partner airline’s website.

Codeshares are not automatically bad. They can provide more destinations and useful connections. The problem is that they create a handoff between companies, and that handoff can become confusing when you need assistance.

As we have learned, one of the most expensive sentences in travel can be: “You need to contact the other airline.”

Mixed-cabin fares are one of the easiest airline traps to miss.

The search result may display a large Premium Economy or Business Class label, making it appear that the entire journey is in the upgraded cabin.

Then you expand the flight details and discover that the 40-minute connection is in Premium Economy while the eight-hour overnight flight is in regular Economy.

We have come close to booking this type of itinerary several times.

Before paying, check the cabin listed beside every individual segment. Make sure the premium seat is on the flight where you will actually benefit from it.

Do not assume one premium segment provides premium benefits throughout the trip.

Screenshot the cabin shown for each flight and confirm that it appears correctly in the final reservation. A mixed-cabin fare is only a deal when the upgraded cabin is on the part of the journey that matters.

There is rarely one simple baggage policy that applies to every passenger flying with an airline.

Do not check only the airline’s general baggage page. Open the conditions attached to the specific fare and route you are considering.

This is especially important when connecting from a transatlantic flight to a smaller airline or low-cost carrier within Europe. A bag accepted on the first flight may be too large, too heavy, or not included on the next one.

A bag fitting inside the overhead compartment does not automatically mean it meets the airline’s rules. Wheels, handles, and outside pockets are normally included when the bag is measured.

Price your luggage before buying the flight. A ticket that appears $30 cheaper can quickly become more expensive once the necessary baggage is added.

Paying for bags online in advance is also frequently less expensive than waiting until the airport, although the difference varies by airline.

Finally, weigh your suitcase at home using a real scale. Picking it up and declaring that it “feels about 20 kilos” is not a reliable baggage strategy.

Once you know your allowance, follow our two-minute checked-bag routine before handing your suitcase over at the airport.

A self-transfer may be the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Some search and booking sites combine two separate tickets and display them as one journey. Look for warnings such as:

The critical detail is that the airlines may not recognize the flights as one protected itinerary.

If the first flight is delayed and you miss the second one, the second airline may consider you a no-show. You could lose the remaining flights on that reservation and be forced to purchase a new last-minute ticket.

The first airline may not be responsible for helping because it transported you to the destination shown on its ticket.

Leaving the international transit area can also trigger entry or transit requirements that would not apply during a normal airside connection.

Self-transfers can work when you have a long buffer, carry-on luggage, an airport you understand, and enough flexibility to absorb a disruption.

We would not use one when connecting to a cruise, wedding, organized tour, or once-daily long-haul flight.

Always compare the self-transfer price with a protected itinerary. The higher fare may not simply be buying convenience. It may be buying the airline’s responsibility to get you to your final destination.

Airlines can sell a connection that technically meets the airport’s minimum requirements.

That does not necessarily mean it is comfortable, sensible, or suitable for you.

A 45-minute connection at a large international airport might involve:

If a connection makes you nervous while sitting at home, it will not feel better when you are waiting for the aircraft door to open. Choose connection time based on the consequences of missing the next flight.

A long layover can be inconvenient. A missed connection can cost a full day or derail the entire trip.

We use third-party flight sites for research. They are useful for comparing airlines, dates, and routing options.

Buying through one is a separate decision.

A third-party fare may be genuinely cheaper, but make sure you are comparing the same product. It could involve:

The biggest issue normally appears when the schedule changes or the flight is cancelled.

The airline may tell you to contact the company that issued the ticket. The booking company may then tell you that only the airline can resolve the flight.

Before buying, find the itinerary through the search site and compare it directly with the airline. When the price difference is small, booking with the airline may be worth it for easier communication during disruptions.

Also check the payment currency. Some booking sites offer to convert the total into your home currency. This feels convenient but may include a less favourable exchange rate.

When your credit card does not charge a foreign transaction fee, paying in the original currency may be less expensive. Compare the final converted amount and check your card’s fees rather than choosing a currency based on familiarity.

Some of the most expensive travel problems do not happen during booking. They happen at the airport after your hotel, tour, rental car, or cruise has already been paid for.

A valid passport may not be enough to enter your destination or transit through a connecting country.

Depending on your nationality, route, and destination, you may need:

A passport can be valid on your departure date and still fail to meet the destination’s entry requirements. Complicated connections are also a good reason to review our international travel safety tips before departure.

Names matter too. The name on your airline ticket should match your passport and any visa or travel authorization. Do not assume that a nickname or commonly used name will be accepted.

Before an international trip, take five minutes to verify:

Canadian travellers should verify current destination-specific requirements using official government travel advisories and the relevant embassy or immigration authority, since entry and transit rules can change.

Five minutes at home can save the entire trip at the airport. For our complete pre-departure routine, read our travel safety checklist for 2026.

Departure time is when the aircraft is scheduled to leave. It is not the time you should arrive at the gate.

Boarding begins earlier, and the gate closes before departure. The exact cutoff depends on the airport, airline, route, and destination.

Once the gate is closed, seeing the aircraft through the terminal window will not save your seat.

If you miss the flight, the cost may extend far beyond a replacement ticket. You might also lose:

Build your airport schedule backward from the airline’s check-in, baggage-drop, boarding, and gate-closing deadlines.

Check current security conditions using the airport’s official app or website, but do not treat an estimated wait time as a guarantee. Add time for airport parking, shuttle transportation, baggage drop, security, passport control, terminal changes, and finding the gate.

It is better to have extra time near the gate than to spend the start of your trip running through an airport while your name is being called over the loudspeaker. Arriving early does not help much if your carry-on slows you down at screening. Read our airport security tips and common mistakes before packing.

Before confirming a flight, we recommend checking the entire itinerary one final time.

The best defence against airline booking traps is not a secret search setting or complicated flight hack. It is slowing down long enough to compare the complete journey.

All 12 of these traps work best when travellers are rushing.

We see a low fare, get excited about the trip, and want to finish before the number changes. The booking process then reveals the bags, seats, restrictions, connections, and other costs after we have already become emotionally committed to the flight.

The cheapest flight is not necessarily the one with the lowest number on the first screen. It is the flight that gets you to your destination without surprise charges, unrealistic connections, or an expensive problem at the airport.

After more than 18 years of travelling, experience has not made us immune to booking mistakes. It has simply taught us when to stop, reopen the details, and check everything one more time.

Take five minutes before pressing confirm. Those five minutes could save hundreds of dollars—or save the entire trip.

#6324. This Swanky Service Lets Commercial Fliers Skip the Airport Entirely—And It's Now Available in Dallas and Miami

As my plane touched down in Dallas, I could already make out my chauffeur waiting on the apron, the jet-black SUV glimmering in the Texas sun. It wasn’t long before my luggage was whisked away and we were driving across the airfield, past rows of planes waiting at their gates—so close that I could read their tail numbers. Our destination? A new private terminal operated by the company PS, which offers a curious promise to commercial fliers: Travel with us, and you will never step foot in the airport.

The shared “Salon” area at the PS Dallas Terminal, included in the entry-level pricing. Access to private suites cost an additional fee based on membership status.

Ten minutes later, my driver dropped me off at PS’s sleek new 12,200-square-foot private terminal at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), where I was greeted by caviar and Champagne and escorted to my own private suite. Between the goodie-filled drawers, marble sinks, and the rainfall shower, I could have spent my whole time in the bathroom, where I had my pick of Le Labo products, plush towels, and comfy robes. It wasn’t like any airport lounge I had ever been to, rivaling even first class. And yet, it's still a fraction of the cost of flying private.

Champagne and caviar at the PS private suite.

PS first launched at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in 2017, then called “The Private Suite.” As the name implies, all PS terminals have their own private, line-free TSA security screenings and dedicated Customs and Immigration checkpoints separate from the crowds. While this has earned the brand a reputation of being a “celebrity terminal," PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter says public figures actually make up "a very, very small portion" of the customer base. The real clientele are premium business travelers, families, and travelers going for celebratory splurges, she says.

"If you fly from LA to New York and back in first class, these days, that's around $4,000. If you do that private, that's probably $100,000,” Porter explains. “The gap is so big, and there are many people that want to bridge that."

For the last decade, PS has continued to expand. After renaming itself to PS in 2020, it opened a terminal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) in 2023. The PS terminal at DFW opened on June 1 and was quickly followed by another PS location at Miami International Airport (MIA) later that month. This October, I flew between the two new terminals to get a better idea of how the exclusive service works behind the scenes—and who it’s actually for.

Each private suite has a bathroom complete with Le Labo products, plush towels, and robes.

In Porter’s view, departing is the most stressful part of air travel. "That's when you're asking, 'Where am I going? What time is my plane? Where's my gate?'" she says. Arrivals or transfers can be just as confusing for many travelers: going through immigration and customs, dealing with heavy bags, finding the right taxi stand or connecting to the right terminal for the next flight. The point of PS is to make both legs of the airport journey as seamless as possible.

After I was welcomed at the PS facility at Dallas-Fort Worth and spent a night in the city, I experienced the departure product en route to Miami. I once again rolled up in a chauffeured car to the PS terminal, where caviar was (naturally) waiting for me. The Dallas terminal occupies a gated facility adjacent to Corporate Aviation at DFW and was designed by interior designer Jean Liu to feel residential, like a luxury hotel.

The 40-foot bar in “The Salon” at the Dallas PS terminal.

I spent much of my pre-flight time in the public lounge area dubbed “the Salon,” which had floor-to-ceiling windows looking out over the tarmac. This area hosts a stunning 40-foot bar, taking inspiration from an old-fashioned Southern saloon. Once I settled in, I ordered breakfast (in Dallas, PS executive chef Matt Roman's blue cornbread is a must), and then worked and read a magazine. My boarding pass came with a sheet telling me when to be ready to board, though the PS staff guides make sure you are always where you need to be regardless.

Behind the scenes, the Control Room tracks all flights, delays, arrivals, and departures. From there, PS coordinates with the airline, TSA, and Customs and Border Protection, and stays in direct contact with the flight crews, which is how they’ll know your flight is delayed before the passengers at the gate do.

When it was time for me to board, I went through security right inside the PS terminal. It's a real TSA checkpoint, because PS is the only company in the United States with a private partnership with both TSA and CBP. Guests go through one at a time, and if you check a bag, PS checks it in with the airline for you. Once again, a car drove me to my plane, and I walked up a set of steps outside the jet bridge, through a door, and straight to my seat.

The open-air courtyard at the Miami PS terminal, located in the historic Pan Am headquarters.

By the time I got to Miami, I knew the PS drill. A sign with my name on it waited at the jet bridge, and from the plane it was a 15-minute drive to the original Pan Am headquarters.

At 34,000 square feet, the PS terminal in Miami is nearly three times the size of the one in Dallas—and the design could not be more different. That’s because the Miami terminal is a loving restoration: the building once housed both Pan Am's former headquarters and its stewardess college, where flight attendants trained in the 1960s. In March 2026, the buildings were added to the National Register of Historic Places as part of the “Pan American Airways Historic District," making the terminal a stunning architectural gem.

Pan Am’s Miami headquarters first opened in 1964, sat empty for 15 years, and was slated for demolition before PS restored it. The restoration shows off the New Formalist style (the bold, geometric designs of Miami's postwar resort boom), with an exterior wrapped in a patterned concrete screen and a repeating trapezoid design that reappears in the planters and door handles. The original insignias and gold paneling are still there, and going up the stairs, the Pan Am logo is engraved over and over into the stone wall.

The Miami PS terminal is filled with playful vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers.

Within the terminal, each PS suite has a different vibe (mine was pink), complete with nods to the beach and vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers. The courtyard is open-air, with a decorative pool tiled by Miami artist Nina Surel in Art Deco pastels that's lined with pink-and-white striped loungers and fringed umbrellas. This time, my Private Suite opened onto a balcony overlooking the courtyard. Inside was the same selection of amenities as in Dallas, plus a fresh food menu that was fitting for glitzy Miami: sashimi with cilantro dust, the classic caviar and Champagne, and—for good measure—a cubano. I enjoyed a chair massage, one of the spa's 30-minute treatments (including reflexology, manicures, hair and beard trims, and full-body massages). As much as I would have liked to linger, when it was time to go I took a sandwich to-go for my next flight, and left in PS style: Another car. Another plane.

Of course, none of this comes cheap. PS operates on a tiered membership system: The entry-level Salon Membership costs $1,250 annually, puts access to the Salon at $995 per person, and allows a member to book a Private Suite (accommodating up to four travelers) for $4,950. The top-tier All Access Membership is priced at $4,850 per year, and lowers access rates to the Salon to $895 per person, and Private Suite rates to $3,650. Without a membership, entry to the Salon costs $1,295 per person, and a Private Suite booking costs $4,950. Notably, because the Salon has an age requirement (21 and over, there’s alcohol), parties traveling with those underage are required to book a Private Suite. Pets are welcome in all PS private terminals, and all PS reservations must be made at least 24 hours ahead of travelers’ departure times.

Access to the private suites starts at $4,950 for members, with room for four travelers.

How should you decide if it's a worthwhile purchase for your trip? Porter is honest about which travelers should skip the whole thing: “If you're on your own, with no checked bags, going on an hour flight for the weekend, then the airport is just fine,” she says. "It makes the most sense for long flights and complicated routings; and parties with a lot of checked bags, kids, and older parents who could use the assistance.”

Because the concept blends private and commercial aviation in a way that hasn't been done before, Porter believes it's hard for travelers to fully understand the value of PS—until they've experienced it themselves. "It's just complete peace of mind," she tells me in Dallas. “That's what we're selling.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6323. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#6322. Tracing Wild Horse Nine's Route Through Chile—From Santiago to Rapa Nui

Within a few minutes of arriving at archaeological site Ahu Tongariki in Rapa Nui, where 15 gargantuan moai statues stand with their backs to the sea, my guide Gina’s phone lights up with the words “Tsunami Alert.” I ask her if this is a relatively normal occurrence on the island. “No… Although there was one [tsunami] in 1960 that washed several of these away towards the hill,” she says, gesturing towards the large sacred monolithic heads carved from volcanic stone, the Pacific Ocean sitting vast and blue behind them. The alert was later lifted, but I still felt a sense of impending doom as I posed for a photo in front of the moai.

Martin McDonagh's new film, starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, follows two CIA agents through Chile.

Flirting with one’s own mortality at the edge of the world sits right at the heart of Wild Horse Nine, a new film written and directed by Martin McDonagh and filmed partially on Rapa Nui. Starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, the dark comedy charts the journey of two CIA agents in Chile as they travel from their station in Santiago to the Polynesian island for a week-long vacation. Their trip also happens to be just before the country’s 1973 military coup, which would oust socialist president Salvador Allende and install dictator General Augusto Pinochet—an event that, for those at all familiar with the history of American foreign policy in Latin America, these two agents have clearly meddled in as operatives. I’d come to Chile to follow in the film's wake—to trace the real-life locations and history behind the silver-screen fiction.

The film’s characters Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) form the kind of acerbic buddy duo that’s become associated with McDonagh films like In Bruges. The older, brasher Chris, now in the waning years of his spy career, considers their trip to Rapa Nui his final act following a terminal cancer diagnosis, bullishly demanding to see “the big heads” in reference to the moai. Lee, meanwhile, functions as exasperated colleague, grieving friend, and increasingly, minder, as his mentor’s memory begins to slip, sometimes returning loudly in moments of unguarded truth—or perhaps deathbed confessions. (One such example: a monologue where he cheerily reminisces about other elected governments he’d helped overthrow on the job.)

Chris and Lee are an uncurious pair of travelers, bristling at polite requests to educate themselves about Rapa Nui's Indigenous culture, and showing little interest in taking its history seriously. (“Why are you here if you’re just going to make fun of the place?” a fellow tourist asks Chris.) They play the part of ugly American tourists astutely—and yet, it’s largely through their eyes that we see both a 1970's Santiago and Rapa Nui on the screen.

Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) travel from Santiago to Rapa Nui once character Chris receives a teminal diagnosis.

The rising interest in traveling to film locations is why tour operator Abercrombie & Kent has launched a 9-day itinerary, which allows guests to chase Wild Horse Nine's trail. I traveled to Chile to road-test the new offering. And like the characters of Carlisle and Chesterfield, I begin my trip in Santiago.

Unlike in the movie, the city is experiencing an unseasonable amount of rain on the morning I arrive. The Andes, which usually loom imposingly over the skyline, are concealed behind thick clouds, and the Mapocho River, which cuts through the city like an artery, is close to bursting its banks. But the 19th-century architecture of bohemian Barrio Lastarria is much more familiar. I’m met outside my hotel by my guide Lisette Matamala, who will spend the next couple of days introducing me to the fraught political history that serves as the backbone of Wild Horse Nine’s suspenseful plot.

The rain is lashing down, but we forge ahead on foot to nearby Plaza de la Constitución, and stand under comically sized umbrellas to have a look at La Moneda Palace. The seat of the Chilean president, this palace was bombed during the coup, resulting in one of the most memorable images from that day. In the movie, viewers see the regal structure, still intact, glimpsed through the office window of cranky CIA bureau chief MJ (Steve Buscemi), a key player in orchestrating the chaos. According to production designer Denis Schnegg, who I will speak to later on the phone, the team filmed that scene in an office opposite the palace that really had been used by the CIA during that time: “To stand in that room and look out at the palace, knowing how these people had been orchestrating it from their window, that the whole thing was planned—it's quite chilling.”

Santiago's presidential palace La Moneda in the aftermath of the 1973 coup d'etat led by Commander of the Army General Augusto Pinochet.

The consequences of their work are etched within the Salvador Allende Museum of Solidarity, a contemporary art museum in the historic neighborhood of Barrio República that has lived several lives: First, as an affluent mid-20th-century family home; then a left wing exhibition space founded in 1971 by a group of creative intellectuals; and, later, as a detention center and listening station operated by Pinochet’s Directorate of National Intelligence (DINA). It has since returned to its original form as a museum, resurrected after the return to democracy in 1990.

While not a Wild Horse Nine filming location, it’s an important stop to help place the film within the context of these very real historical events. “This house has a lot of layers of history and meaning,” museum director María José Lemaitre tells me as we walk down a flight of wide, winding wooden stairs. “And also, darkness.” When the art was reinstalled, secrets were uncovered within the bones of the building: transcriptions of tapped phone calls were hidden by DINA in the ceilings, and phone-tapping equipment sat in the basement.

Lemaitre and her colleague, museum curator Caroll Yasky, bring me to see the latter, housed in a dusty, windowless subterranean room. We linger over the handwritten names and phone numbers of families the DINA had spied on—tangible evidence of the horrors enacted by the history driving McDonagh’s plot. “The museum may show the past, but what is important is the future,” says Yasky as we walk back upstairs into the daylight.

The fingerprints of Pinochet’s regime are never far away in Santiago. I spend a pisco sour-filled evening dining with a university professor whose father had been one of the dictator's driver—a role that, he suggests, haunted his father so deeply he had a stroke to forget it. (It's an anecdote I can’t help but thread back to Chris’ struggles with redemption in Wild Horse Nine, which we often see him exploring in misguided attempts to write a memoir that he plans to leave behind following his imminent death.)

Much of Rapa Nui feels—and appears in the film—as though it sits on the edge of the world.

Another afternoon, we visit Villa Grimaldi, a once-notorious detention center on the outskirts of the city that now serves as a memorial. Two of its survivors are Alvaro Ahumada and Ignacio Puelma, smartly dressed and in their early 70s, who meet us under the trees near the entrance for a tour. We pass sobering remnants of the detention center’s structures, but also clusters of fragrant roses, colorful mosaics, and water features. “We didn’t want to have a horror museum,” says Ahumada, who is also the president of the foundation. “Instead, we wanted to wash away what happened here.”

The pair, I realize, would have been around the same age as the character of a young, optimistic left-wing student in the film named Monica, played by Mariana di Girolamo. These two were both members of the student-led Movement of the Revolutionary Left, and at just 19 and 21 at the time, they had been transferred from Villa Grimaldi to the same concentration camp where they connected over music, even forming a band during their imprisonment. “Our bond is very deep,” says Puelma, as a flock of squawking parakeets fly over us. “We were both rockers, so we had a lot to talk about,” adds Ahumada. “Helping each other, and looking after each other, was an act of resistance.”

Their story evokes a poignant scene in Wild Horse Nine, when they later reach Rapa Nui, during which Chris meets up with Monica at a low-lit, moody bar. As the ill-fated folk singer Victor Jara (Aron Hernandez) performs on stage, Chris tells her with disturbing frankness that he is not just a CIA agent, but one who has come down to Chile to “destabilize your democracy,” a direct reference to the United States’ involvement in installing Pinochet.

In one of the film's scenes, young Chileans are confronted by Chris's character, who tells them he has come to Chile to “destabilize your democracy.”

McDonagh’s decision to depict Jara, who was murdered by members of Pinochet's regime, is yet another reminder that beyond the buffoonery of Chris and Lee, lie the stories of real people like Ahumada and Puelma. Some of the film’s cast still feel its impact, too. “Monica [is based on] a real character: Comandante Tamara, a left-wing student and [guerilla leader] who attempted to assassinate Pinochet. And, of course, we know what happened to Victor Jara, the singer who is playing a Violeta Parra song in that bar,” di Girolamo tells me after the trip. “I was born in the first year of democracy, but my parents were students in school in ‘73. [This history] is just something you grow up with, and it's still an open wound for us.”

I arrive in Rapa Nui the same way Chris and Lee do: on vacation, via the one daily flight from Santiago, landing at a thatched airport where ukulele music wafts through the air and chickens toddle around baggage claim. Gina Pakarati, who was born and raised on the island, picks me up outside in her white Suzuki Jimny, and we set off to visit the same moai sites that, in the film, Chris tells Lee he wants to see before he dies. In fact, it’s when they first reach the island that it’s revealed to viewers that Chris has asked Lee to put a gun to his head and end things right here on Rapa Nui.

Wild horses run across the open, lush green plains of Rapa Nui island.

Pakarati, who knows the island like the back of her hand, blasts local Polynesian folk-country band Topatangi as we trace the rugged coastal drive captured in the film, past swathes of electric-green grassland and black volcanic rock. We pause for herds of the same chestnut-brown wild horses McDonagh frequently turns his camera to.

I wind my window down, and the air smells sweet yet woody. There is a surreal, heavenly quality to being here. At one point, Pakarati pulls over and plucks a small guava off a tree, so ripe that she can pull it apart with her hands, for us to eat at the side of the road.

As we drive up towards Ahu Akivi, one of several imposing moai sites on the island, small groups of tourists are milling around, some of whom I recognize. (Given the island’s size, you tend to cross paths with the same visitors fairly quickly.) Just like Chris and Lee, we’ve all come here for the same once-in-a-lifetime experience—albeit without a Super 8 camera and guns in holsters. But finally laying eyes on the moai feels like seeing a myth come to life. Pakarati, who is 43 and comes from a long lineage of Rapa Nui people, explains to me that of all the ceremonial platforms here, this one is particularly special because its seven statues are “looking towards Polynesia, the land where they came from.”

Towering moai made from volcanic stone—which Malkovich's character refers to as “the big heads”—are a living piece of ancient Polynesian history on Rapa Nui.

She recalls playing among the statues as a child (an activity now deterred by a rope) and hearing her grandfather’s stories of helping the visiting archeologist William Mulloy with their restoration in the 1960s. Thanks largely to Mulloy, that period drew more attention to the island and, after the first commercial flight arrived in 1967, ushered in the first real wave of tourism. Though it is a territory of Chile, life on Rapa Nui felt awfully far away from the coup, I'm told. Hotels began opening, more cars appeared on the roads, and in 1993, the first Hollywood film crew arrived. Despite the fact that the subsequent Kevin Costner-produced movie Rapa Nui was a widely criticized box-office flop, Pakarati says, economically everything changed after it, due to how many jobs were created—and she suggests that the spotlight of Wild Horse Nine might prompt another such wave of activity.

That initial Hollywood-driven boom on the island inspired hospitality ventures like still-operating, family-run Iorana Hotel. It’s an eccentric ocean-view property just outside of town that opened in the 1990s but feels frozen in the '70s. So much so that, in Wild Horse Nine, Chris and Lee both stay there, picking fights with unsuspecting tourists and waving their guns around in the rooms. Cars from the era were temporarily shipped over to drive past the property in certain shots, says Schnegg, but when it came to the interiors, which feature floor-to-ceiling wood paneling, tiki-style floral-patterned upholstery, and buttercup-yellow room doors, little was changed. (“The hotel is actually sort of disconnected from [town], which is probably why it's a bit stuck in time,” Schnegg notes.) One addition, however, were the protagonist’s rooms, which were specially built for the film. The owners plan to keep the set and turn it into a tourist attraction. “The last night [of filming] we were set up until 7 a.m. and then had a huge celebration in the morning,” says the owners' daughter, Carolina, as we take a look at the set. “I think this film will be good for the island.”

The family-run Iorana Hotel transports visitors—and viewers—straight to the 1970s.

We watch Chris and Lee ramble around many of the moai sites, but the one that stuns me most in its scale and beauty is the quarry at Rano Raraku, where hundreds of moai protrude at different levels from the hillside of an extinct volcano. Many lie solemnly in situ among the grass, while others now stand, having been hauled up into a standing position by archeologists in the ‘70s. Some are massive, and others unfinished. A view towards the coastline offers a spectacular vantage point of the fifteen statues of Ahu Tongariki, which all look back upon the quarry where they were created.

In Wild Horse Nine, we witness Chris and Lee unravel at this very site in a dramatic final shootout. I, in contrast, sit on a bench with Pakarati, the breeze making the grass shimmer (nowhere else have I been so astounded by the green of the grass), as she explains how these mammoth works were constructed and moved around the island by her ancestors. It may be a thrill to stand where the actors of Wild Horse Nine stood, but there’s much more gravity in knowing that I’m treading the same soil as those who carved the hulking statues before me. These days, Rapa Nui's archaeological sites can only be entered with an authorized guide—and I’m grateful for it as Pakarati shares her stories.

Rapa Nui provides a pensive setting for the film's character's, particularly Chris who knows his days are numbered.

Toward the film's end, Chris, death knocking on his door, describes isolated Rapa Nui as a lonely place. But I find it to be quite the opposite. On my final morning, we wake early and drive back over to Ahu Tongariki to watch the sun rise. The atmosphere is similar to gathering in anticipation of an eclipse. Locals and tourists alike set up camping chairs and drink coffee out of flasks as the sky changes hue: deep purple merging into soft blues, followed by shades of pink, ochre, and yellow bursting from behind the silhouettes of the moai.

Standing in the early dawn light, it’s easy to understand why such an epic natural landscape was used as a burial ground on ancient Rapa Nui—and why McDonagh thought a CIA agent like Chris, dying and trying to seek redemption from his darkened memories, may want to swagger over to such a place before his morally disreputable life comes to an end. Even with his internal struggle, does he have the right to such a bucket list? “When I read the script for the first time, I felt a little guilty about laughing [while they do] these terrible things,” di Girolamo had told me during our conversation. “Yet I’d felt empathy for these agents. I cried.”

The sun fixes itself high above the moai and we all clap. Another new day at the edge of the world.

Wild Rapa Nui is a 5.5-hour flight from Santiago, and feels a world away.

I flew direct from New York City to Santiago, before catching the 5.5-hour flight to Rapa Nui on LATAM Airlines—currently the only commercial flight to get you there. My itinerary was booked through tour operator Abercrombie & Kent, which has crafted an exclusive Wild Horse Nine trip tailored to the movie locations, while also connecting travelers with the real-life Chileans who lived under the Pinochet regime and want to share their stories.

Santiago: I spent three nights at the Singular Hotel, a boutique property in the center of artsy Barrio Lastarria. Rooms are spacious and comfortable, but the real winner here is the buzzy rooftop bar serving excellent pisco sours. It’s also walking distance from La Moneda Palace and the must-visit Chilean Museum of Pre-Columbian Art, which features several artifacts from Rapa Nui.

Rapa Nui: While there is an Explora property further inland, most hotels are clustered in and around the sole town of Hanga Roa, a laid-back, sunny community lined with seafood restaurants, surf shops, and cafes and bars wafting ukulele music. Check into Nayara Hangaroa for oceanfront rooms, a pool set upon volcanic rocks, and a concierge to assist with arranging excursions. Rumor has it that John Malkovich stayed here while filming Wild Horse Nine.

La Moneda Palace: A 15-minute walk from the Singular Hotel, Chile’s presidential palace is worth a pause as you pass through downtown. Buttressed by the Plaza de la Constitución and the Plaza de la Ciudadanía, it’s a largely civic area, but it’s hard not to be stirred by the location knowing, as Schnegg noted, that everything that took place here.

In Wild Horse Nine, the still-operating Municipal Theatre of Santiago is turned into an upper-class restaurant.

Municipal Theatre of Santiago: “For a pivotal scene with Chris and Lee, we turned the opera house into a sort of upper-class restaurant where [you’d imagine] the political elite would meet,” says Schnegg of the Municipal Theatre of Santiago, a beautiful, fully operational theater in the center of the city. Buy tickets for a performance to see its grand 19th-century interiors, or do as I did and request Abercrombie & Kent arrange a tour for a behind-the-scenes glimpse.

Museum of Memory and Human Rights: While not a location in Wild Horse Nine, this museum is an essential stop to confront Chile’s recent history and understand the lasting trauma of the Pinochet dictatorship. “It's an open wound for us because we didn't have justice,” says di Girolamo. “There are still mothers looking for their sons.” Set within a brutalist building near Quinta Normal Park, the museum displays testimonials from survivors, preserved artifacts, memorials to the missing, and government documents from the time—including several declassified CIA documents revealing its role in the 1973 coup.

Iorana Hotel: One of the main locations in Wild Horse Nine, this family-owned property overlooking the ocean is fully in operation and taking bookings. With furniture clad in tiki prints, retro wood paneling, and palm trees swaying outside the windows, it’s also a fun place just to snap a couple of photos. Ask to see the set that still remains—just watch out for the grumpy resident dog, who is best admired from afar.

Anakena Beach is a scenic tourist site on Rapa Nui, and actor Mariana di Girolamo's favorite filming location.

Anakena Beach: “My favorite location in the movie is Anakena Beach,” says di Girolamo of the scene where she and Chris strike up a brief, unlikely friendship at the Rapa Nui tourist spot, where a bar serving piña coladas sits side by side with the Ahu Nau Nau moai. “That beach is so beautiful, but I was also able to go to a very special place nearby that you can only visit with someone local: the Cave of the Virgins [or Ana o Keke] set inside a cliff.”

Ahu Tongariki and Rano Raraku: These two moai sites are within short driving distance of each other (as are most sites on Rapa Nui) and make frequent appearances in the movie. Book a local authorized guide to visit them, or arrange a guided excursion through Nayara Hangaroa. And don’t rush, either: the statues and the landscape look vastly different throughout the day as the light changes. “We were filming there for weeks on end, just living with the sky and the wind and the water and the sounds and the horses,” says Schnegg. “I’d just think, is this real?”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

After a six-year hiatus, American Airlines’ most exclusive lounge offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is back in business.

This week, the carrier reopened Flagship Dining at LAX. That’s American’s a la carte restaurant-style experience, which is available to customers flying in its most premium seats.

It had been closed since 2020 but is now open again after a face-lift.

And it also has a new access policy at LAX — and at the two other American hubs that offer the service.

American now offers Flagship Dining at three of its hubs:

At those airports, you'll find the a la carte dining experience is available within its Flagship Lounge, AA's premium lounge that's open to premium cabin passengers and AAdvantage elites taking long-haul flights.

Instead of grabbing food at the buffet, Flagship Dining offers flyers a sit-down meal with table service — we’re talking a full menu with coursed-out dishes, all complimentary.

In the past, the airline limited access to Flagship Dining to passengers flying in its Flagship First cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER or Airbus A321T aircraft.

But as the carrier gets set to phase out its international-style first-class cabin, access to Flagship Dining is opening up to more passengers.

In September, American began allowing passengers in its Flagship business-class cabins to sit for its exclusive dining experience.

If you’re flying out of DFW, MIA or LAX, you can have a Flagship Dining meal if you are:

That change is especially notable at LAX, because it allows business-class passengers to use Flagship Dining on certain transcontinental flights. To get in, you'll need to have a ticket that's marketed as "Flagship" (domestic first-class tickets won't be enough).

Like with any restaurant or airport lounge, space is limited. You can join the waitlist for a table after arriving at the Flagship Lounge in LA, Dallas and Miami.

American used to offer Flagship Dining at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Today, the carrier instead operates its three premium lounges (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho) in Terminal 8 with partner British Airways.

Meanwhile, its newest Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) features a la carte dining within the main club.

Speaking of American’s “Flagship” product, the end is rapidly approaching for Flagship First.

Nov. 19 will mark the last date AA offers long-haul first-class as a stand-alone product on its 777s.

Those jets are getting refreshed with new interiors, with the airline ditching first-class and adding the highest business-class seat count it's ever offered.

American will phase out Flagship First on transcontinental service in March.

#6320. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6319. Awkwafina Takes Us on a Nostalgic Food-Tour of NYC's Koreatown

“It's so cool that in this city you have SoHo and Times Square but also these enclaves where you can totally belong,” says Nora Lum, the actor and comedian also known as Awkwafina. We're upstairs at the 24-hour Miss Korea, her go-to spot in Manhattan's Koreatown, picking our way over a lavish Korean barbecue spread of assorted banchan and gleaming chargrilled short ribs. “I love this!” she says, before popping a clump of braised burdock into her mouth.

Lum, who is Korean-Chinese American, has just wrapped filming Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, an unscripted Apple TV series that she hosts and executive-produces. A descendant of the family behind the legendary Cantonese American restaurant Lum's, which her great-grandfather ran in Flushing, Queens, from 1953 to 1982, she spends eight episodes gathering cooking tips from the nation's Asian communities, particularly its Chinatowns. She heads to America's oldest Chinatown, in San Francisco, to cook with chef Martin Yan, who, using “insane” knife work, “absolutely destroyed a chicken in 16 seconds”; Texas for a barbecue-fueled road trip with comedian Jimmy O. Yang, making pit stops at Korean-American-owned Eaker Barbecue in Fredericksburg and Thai-American Curry Boys BBQ in San Antonio; and Los Angeles to wait tables at the dim sum joint Golden Dragon. All these experiences lead to her own pop-up revival of Lum's in Manhattan's Little Italy, where she serves beloved staples like orange chicken and barbecue beef to friends and family.

Lum crosses 32nd Street in the heart of New York City’s Koreatown.

At its heart Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is about heritage, community, and small-business immigrant entrepreneurship. “After the pandemic so many mom-and-pop shops were closing and Chinatowns were declining,” says Lum. “The show is about exploring that phenomenon but then also seeing who in my generation is keeping it going.”

Our first lunch stop is Miss Korea, on 32nd Street between Broadway and Fifth Avenue, the stretch where Koreatown first emerged in the late 1970s. Then home to a Korean-language bookstore and a smattering of restaurants, it's since evolved into an around-the-clock entertainment hub for anyone looking to pick up K-pop memorabilia, sing karaoke, and eat everything from Korean corn dogs at Jongro Rice Hotdog to a Michelin-starred tasting menu at Joo Ok. For Lum it's a nostalgic stretch of the city. “I went to MK, Maru, Circle,” she says in reference to nightlife spots frequented by Korean American party kids coming of age in 1990s and 2000s New York. “Oh man, I've been so messy on this one block.”

Patrons fill the tables at the ever-popular BCD Tofu House, which specializes in soondubu.

We cross the street to BCD Tofu House for crispy seafood pancakes, spicy marinated crab slicked with red pepper seasoning, and Lum's favorite: the signature soondubu, a tofu stew bubbling in a clay pot. Since opening in 2008, the Los Angeles export has increasingly drawn long lines—a testament to the growing popularity of Korean food across the US. “Twenty years ago customers were 70 to 80 percent Korean,” general manager Alex Kim tells us. “Now it's a lot more non-Korean.”

Lum notes that, for a long time in the US, immigrants selling their traditional cuisines were often met with gratitude within the culture yet distrust outside of it. Adaptation followed: the invention of chop suey, for example, and wok-fired cooking of non-Chinese vegetables like broccoli. Her great-grandfather experienced this himself with Lum's, and local appreciation for the restaurant's Americanized Chinese classics like egg rolls and shrimp with lobster sauce has remained long after it closed. “I learned to think about it less as my family's attempt at just making money but rather, ‘Hey, this is the cuisine that we ate growing up,’ ” she says. “It's a fascinating story of belonging and acculturation.”

We wander over to Woorijip, a fast-casual institution for snacking and soju drinking to pick up kimbap, and then to food hall Food Gallery 32. “This is where I get the fish!” Lum says of bungeoppang, the fish-shaped pastry introduced to Korea by Japanese colonists in the 1930s and popularized again in the '90s. In Manhattan this is the rare spot to find it.

Freshly made bungeoppang lined up at Food Gallery 32

While filming, Lum prioritized places that are moving the needle forward while still preserving their communities' culture, like Phoenix Palace in Manhattan's Chinatown. The Cantonese American restaurant hosts local elders at affordable rates and buys plates from Wing on Wo & Co., a porcelain shop dating back to 1925. Lum recalls co-owner Cory Ng's father appearing with ingredients sourced from the neighborhood.

“Chinatown is totally a local economy,” she says. But it's also where immigrants can speak their native languages, play mahjong, eat dim sum, and celebrate Lunar New Year. “So when you see Chinatowns decline, it's a bigger problem”—a problem she hopes her show can help resolve.

In San Antonio, bright pink barbecue spot Curry Boys BBQ run by three childhood friends dishes out Southeast Asian–Texan blends like oak-smoked brisket with green curry. “They're combining their own cultures into something that's so authentic to where they're from,” says Lum.

For the show, Lum waited tables at classic banquet hall Golden Dragon in Los Angeles's Chinatown, which, with its traditional dim sum service, has remained a stronghold for 64 years. Step outside, says Lum, and “it looks like a movie set.”

Lum stopped by Oahu's Kō Hana Distillers while visiting Hawaii to learn about the tiki culture that inspired her great-grandfather's drinks menu. Come here for its farm-to-bottle selection using homegrown sugarcane.

In San Francisco, the nation's oldest Chinatown “serves the community in a different way from elsewhere,” says Lum. She also loves the comparatively younger, yet still landmark, Mister Jiu's for its Western take on Cantonese cooking.

The best way to redeem Marriott points is for free nights at Marriott hotels and resorts. However, you can also transfer your points to airline partners.

Marriott Bonvoy Boundless provides a standout suite of perks, including an annual free night award and automatic Silver Elite status, for a $95 annual fee.

I find it especially impressive that a mid-tier hotel card with a modest annual fee offers such lucrative perks, especially the annual free night award. Certain hotels have resort fees.

You don't have to go all in on Marriott to get a lot out of having this $95-annual-fee card in your wallet, and that's what makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless worth considering.

The packs a punch for its reasonable annual fee. Here's what cardholders can expect.

Given TPG's November 2026 valuation of Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, the 35,000-point certificate is worth $263. This is nearly three times the card's $95 annual fee and is a fantastic benefit, especially since you don't have to spend on the card to earn the certificate.

While the Silver Elite status on the card is the first of Marriott's elite status tiers, it does offer a few useful benefits, such as a 10% points bonus on paid stays and priority late checkout.

If you put at least $35,000 of spending on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in a calendar year, you'll earn Gold Elite status. This comes with more perks, such as a 25% points boost and enhanced room upgrade (when available).

For most cardholders, it’s hard to justify putting $35,000 in purchases on the card solely to earn Gold Elite status.

If Gold Elite status is your goal, you may be better off combining the card's 15 complimentary elite night credits with 10 paid nights; this totals 25 elite nights needed for Gold Elite status.

If you're eligible for a business card, you can also pair the 15 elite night credits given by the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless with 15 elite night credits provided by the . These 30 total elite night credits leave you with just 20 nights to earn Platinum Elite.

You can also reach a higher elite status by earning one elite night credit for every $5,000 spent on purchases with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless.

Given TPG's relatively low valuation of Marriott points, I only recommend paying for Marriott stays with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. There are other cards on the market that earn more valuable rewards on dining, gas and groceries.

The best way to redeem your Marriott points is to book free nights at one of the brand's hotels.

Since Marriott uses dynamic award pricing (meaning the number of points needed fluctuates based on demand and availability), you may have to take extra time and effort to strategize for maximum value.

Marriott has an award calendar search function that can help narrow down the best deal for your points. For example, a night at the Moxy NYC Lower East Side in January 2027 could cost as few as 57,000 points per night or as many as 81,000 points per night, depending on when you book.

While we value Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, there are ways to get better value.

For instance, TPG lead writer for loyalty programs Katie Genter previously redeemed 112,000 points for a five-night stay at the Courtyard by Marriott Toronto Vaughan for a music festival. Compared against a cash rate of $1,464, she got an impressive 1.31 cents per point from this redemption.

Also, keep in mind that Marriott offers a fifth-night-free benefit. When you book at least five consecutive nights on points, you'll get the night that's worth the lowest number of points for free. This can help you stretch your points for longer trips.

Marriott points are also transferable to nearly 40 airline partners, most at a 3:1 ratio. These include some hard-to-earn currencies, such as Air China PhoenixMiles and Frontier Airlines.

However, unless you have a specific airline redemption in mind and need to top off your balance, transferring is unlikely to be the best use of your points.
