#6316. Best Things to Do in Hamilton, Ontario

A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something new therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

Hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

The house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a big museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how important the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

The Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:

Webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

Important Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

Spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

The Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

Hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

Hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

The Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a big part of the city’s story.

ThGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

The Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

Hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

This is the kind of event that shows how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Plan your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

The Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most important artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

Hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre company and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

You can find fresh produce, cheese, meat, baked goods, prepared foods, coffee, and international food stalls, plus it is a great lunch stop, especially if you are visiting the Art Gallery of Hamilton or exploring downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t just shop. Plan to eat here. It is one of the easiest ways to sample Hamilton’s food scene in one place.

Born & Raised is one of the best restaurants to pair with a visit to James Street North, as it is located right in the Art Crawl district, it is surrounded by galleries, shops, cafes, and the creative energy that makes this part of Hamilton so fun.

The restaurant was created by chef Vittorio Colacitti and focuses on bold flavours, Italian-inspired dishes, pizza, and a lively neighbourhood atmosphere. It is a great choice for dinner after Art Crawl or a night out downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are visiting during James Street Art Crawl, make a reservation if possible because the street gets busy, and this is exactly the kind of place you’ll want to settle into after walking the galleries.

King William Street has become one of Hamilton’s best dining areas, with restaurants, patios, and cocktail spots packed into a walkable downtown strip especially if you want a more polished dinner, this is a good area to explore.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: King William is a great choice if you want to turn a Hamilton day trip into an evening out.

Hamilton is a great family day trip because many attractions are easy to combine. therefore good family-friendly stops include:

The key with kids is not to overpack the day. Pick one museum, one outdoor stop, and one easy food stop.

Hamilton can be a budget-friendly day trip if you plan it well.

Always check parking and reservation requirements before visiting waterfalls or conservation areas.

Yes, Hamilton is worth visiting because it combines waterfalls, hiking trails, museums, waterfront parks, restaurants, art galleries, and local culture in one easy day trip or weekend getaway. It has the outdoor appeal of the Niagara Escarpment, the history of an old industrial city, and the food and arts scene of a place that has reinvented itself without losing its character.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it is close enough for a full-day visit but different enough to feel like a real change of scenery. You can tour Dundurn Castle, hike to waterfalls, walk the waterfront, visit the Art Gallery of Hamilton, and end the day with dinner on James Street North.

Hamilton is best known for its industrial history, waterfalls, hiking trails, the Niagara Escarpment, arts scene, food scene, and waterfront. It is still called “Steeltown,” but today it is just as well known for outdoor adventure, creative neighbourhoods, and one of Ontario’s most underrated city breaks.

Spring, summer, and fall are the best times to visit Hamilton for waterfalls, hiking, gardens, patios, festivals, and James Street Art Crawl. Fall is especially beautiful in the Dundas Valley, while winter is better for museums, restaurants, theatre, the Royal Botanical Gardens, and indoor attractions.

A car is useful in Hamilton, especially if you want to visit waterfalls, conservation areas, Dundas, Stoney Creek, the Royal Botanical Gardens, or attractions outside downtown. Once you are downtown, areas like James Street North, King William Street, the farmers’ market, and the Art Gallery of Hamilton are much easier to explore on foot.

#6315. Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?

At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year.

Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world.

"The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.”

An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives.

This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise.

The first Dubai Fitness Challenge took place in 2017

Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building.

Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps.

The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city.

It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary.

Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends.

The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day.

The Dubai Ride closes the city's busiest highway for one morning each year

Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.”

For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.”

Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.”

He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.”

For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day.

Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year.

Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.”

But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.”

This year’s Dubai Fitness Challenge runs under the theme What’s Your 30x30?

The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants.

Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.”

He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.”

The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers.

Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.”

He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.”

Residents and visitors alike are invited to discover new ways to move, connect and build healthy habits that last beyond the challenge's 30 days

Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.”

He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance.

Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior.

Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary.

According to experts, Dubai's mix of international residents has made wellness more mainstream

For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free.

Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.”

Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.”

Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up.

Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year.

Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the FutureWhen: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m.How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women.

Where: DIFC Gate BuildingWhen: Sunday, November 29, sunriseHow to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop.

Where: Kite Beach, JumeirahWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run.

Where: Zabeel Park, Gate 2When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball.

Where: Al Warqa’a ParkWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

#6314. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

This is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines quickly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

The waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole plan.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

This is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and big nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

No car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and big adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

Bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

This is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

Canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

Stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

For nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

Earlier this year, I was in the middle of a United Airlines status challenge, and I saw an offer for a new credit card with a nice welcome offer that I couldn't resist. I hadn't really played too deeply in the United ecosystem and didn't have any of Chase's United-branded credit cards.

Anyway, I was excited when I was able to open the (see rates and fees).

Of course, I quickly earned the generous 90,000-mile and 3,000 PQP welcome bonus after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening and adding an authorized user (no longer available), but I was just as excited to learn I had many perks that came with the card, which I've continued to enjoy this year.

Currently, new cardholders can earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs: earn 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Here is what comes with the card, which pleasantly surprised me after I got it.

One thing I didn't realize when I signed up for the card was that cardholders get a $200 United travel credit. That came in handy when I needed to book a recent flight to Montana to see my father.

I used the card's $200 annual United TravelBank cash to offset the $488 round-trip ticket cost for my flight from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Bozeman International Airport (BZN). So that trip cost me just $288. Score.

The Quest card also comes with an up to $150 JSX flight credit each anniversary year, up to $180 in Instacart credits each calendar year (through Dec. 31, 2027), and up to $80 ($40 each) in rental car credits each anniversary year for your first and second Avis or Budget rental when you book through cars.united.com. I have used the ride-hailing statement credits a few times. You get up to $100 in ride-hailing statement credits with this card (up to $8 monthly from January through November and up to $12 in December; yearly activation required). So far this year, I've used it five times, saving $40.

Finally, there's also a $120 Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus credit every four years.

The Quest card comes with some pretty good mileage multipliers. You get 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights and 4 miles per dollar spent on other eligible United purchases (like onboard food). Note that your mileage earning on Basic Economy and base option tickets may differ from the Quest's standard 10 total miles per dollar spent rate.

The card also comes with 1,000 bonus Premier qualifying points (PQPs) each year that can give you a head start on earning United elite status. I was mostly interested in the generous welcome bonus when I opened the United Quest Card, but I've been pleasantly surprised by how much additional value I've gotten from it. #6312. 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, cedar barrel sauna, pool and ping-pong tables, arcade games, boot warmers

If you’re an avid East Coast skier, you’re likely no stranger to Killington’s buzzy ski resort, home to over 200 ski trails of terrain for any level shredder. This five-bedroom cabin makes a great launchpad for those staying in the area. The amenity-filled gem sits only four minutes away from Killington Resort, and comes with a game room, cedar barrel sauna, and mountain views for days. Use the boot warmers in the closet before hitting the mountain, then leave all your gear in the ski shed for storage once you’ve returned. In the evenings, fire up some food on the patio grill then cozy up around the wood-burning fireplace.

Where to ski: Killington Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: Killington Skyeship Base Lodge, The Lookout Tavern, Killington Village, Gifford Woods State Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, mountain views, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

I’m adding this Vermont gem to my ski bucket list for a dozen different reasons, starting with the fact that the mountain access is second to none: This spruced-up, slopeside penthouse apartment sits steps from the ski lifts, less than just a five-minute walk to Stowe Mountain Resort’s six-passenger Over Easy Gondola. It’s also a 15-minute drive to one of my favorite mountains, Smugglers’ Notch, where the vibes are always high and the terrain is suitable for all kinds of skiers.

Back at “home,” this modern mountain aesthetic will refresh you after a long day on the slopes. A picture-perfect gas fireplace hangs in front of floor-to-ceiling windows that provide mountain views for days. Tasteful pops of color complete the dining space, comfy blankets line the couch, and the small-but-mighty kitchen has all the appliances you might need for cooking dinner.

Where to ski: Stowe Mountain Resort or Smugglers’ NotchThings to do nearby: Stowe Village, Matterhorn, Cliff House Restaurant, Gondola Skyride (to Mount Mansfield’s peak), The Club at Spruce Peak

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, wraparound deck, dining area with grill, mountain views, wood-burning fireplace

Perched 60 feet above New York’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, with a ski (or hiking) trail just across the street, this rental is ideal for a fun-filled New York ski trip not far from the city. In true log cabin fashion, guests can admire the vaulted ceiling made of cedarwood beams, indoor fireplace, and mountain-facing sliding doors which open to a wraparound deck with a firepit. There are odes to nature everywhere, from framed landscape paintings to horns and antlers as wall decor.

The home’s slopeside location is the real draw: As one previous guest wrote in an Airbnb review, “you’ll feel like you’ll have your own backdoor to Hunter Mountain.” While it’s not a true ski-in/ski-out property, the home sits a quick drive or walk away from the Hunter North area, where you can gear up and take off.

Where to ski: Hunter Mountain Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Tannersville, Hunter Mountain Brewery, Ze Burger Wine Bar, Fellow Mountain Cafe

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedroom, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: California king bed, laundry facilities, wood-burning fireplace, patio with private hot tub

This extra-luxurious abode has the look and feel of an upscale hotel—à la The Cloudveil—but it’s actually a private townhouse at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort with three bedrooms that sleep up to seven. While the prime location may be one of the biggest selling points, the decor and design make it even more enticing: The living room, for example, has classic Jackson Hole touches (note the antler chandelier and cozy fireplace), balanced out by light linens and airy textures. You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

Where to ski: Jackson Hole Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: JH Sports (for gear rentals), Teton Village, Moose Creek Quad Chair, Mangy Moose Jackson Hole

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, wood-burning sauna, gas grill, indoor fireplace, kid-friendly amenities, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

Where to ski: Breckenridge Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Hoosier Pass, Peaceful Valley Lodge, Downtown Breckenridge, Boreas Mountain, Quandary Peak, BreckConnect Gondola

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Fully equipped kitchen, mountain views, hot tub, firepit, central location

This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, Montana, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. And Big Sky Resort sits at the top of many Montana itineraries for good reason—especially come wintertime. Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. For one, each of the two bedrooms feature king beds with mattress warmers to keep you cozy during winter nights. Take advantage of the big patio space for stargazing, relaxing in the hot tub, and cooking up some s’mores before heading inside for a movie night. The house can technically host up to eight guests, but it’s more ideal for families or smaller groups. Aside from the two bedrooms, the living room offers one sofa bed and two bunk beds.

Where to ski: Big Sky ResortThings to do nearby: Lone Mountain Ranch, Gallatin Peak, Big Sky Mountain Village, Fan Mountain, Beehive Peak, Madison Base (at Big Sky Resort)

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski out access, hot tub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

When it comes to access to Utah’s renowned slopes and cool ski towns, you can’t get much better than this four-bedroom luxury penthouse. At the base of Park City Mountain, this condo boasts ski-in/ski-out access directly from the mountain's Silver Star lift. Spacious living areas, a chef’s kitchen, a hot tub, and a balcony overlooking the golf course and icy lakes create a refined on-mountain experience. The penthouse’s proximity to both ski runs and downtown makes for a seamless mix—not to mention you’ll be just a 10-minute drive to Deer Valley Resort, accessible from the condo via a free ski shuttle. With bunk beds for families and plenty of lounge areas for après-ski downtime, this Park City gem accommodates groups seeking easy access to slopes in style.

Where to ski: Park City Mountain; Deer Valley ResortThings to do nearby: Kimball Art Center, Old Town Main Street, Creekside Park, Iron Mountain Trailhead, Thaynes Canyon

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, firepit, fully equipped kitchen, game area, in-unit washer and dryer

New Mexico ski trips mean a real change of scenery, and this year there’s an extra reason to have this underrated mountain range on your radar. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. (It’s a great one for beginners, featuring the renowned Heading Home 3.2-mile green run that traverses all the way from the summit to the base.)

This home is only around 100 yards away from that exact ski run, with slope access right out the door. Inside, there’s a ton of space to sprawl out and indulge in simple creature comforts: soaking in the hot tub, roasting marshmallows around the firepit on the expansive deck, and playing board games (or one of the vintage arcade games inside the den).

Where to ski: Angel Fire Resort; Taos Ski ValleyThings to do nearby: Oeste Vista Trail, Summit Haus, Cabin at Southwest Flyer Lift, Liberation Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound deck, sauna, firepit, unique design, opt-in grocery delivery, Koyo massage chair

Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

Where to ski: Mammoth Mountain Ski AreaThings to do nearby: Twin Lakes Vista, Mammoth Creek Park, Sherwin Lakes Trailhead, Mammoth Brewing Company, Canyon Lodge, Whitmore Hot Springs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside and central location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

Where to ski: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort; Aspen Snowmass Ski Resort; Aspen Highlands Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Where to ski: Big Sky Ski ResortThings to do nearby Lone Mountain Ranch, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center, Gondola Mid Station, Montana Jack, Beehive Basin Trailhead

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

#6311. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.
