#6294. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6293. The Best Way to Eat Swiss Fondue? Floating on Lake Brienz

I could say that I was surprised to find myself and my family floating along in a red Zodiac on the deepest lake in Switzerland, eating cheese fondue and sipping white wine as the sun set. But really, it was all by design. When I designated myself as chief planner for an autumnal family trip to the Alpine nation with my adult children and their partners, I searched for an activity that would knock their socks off. I found it in Interlaken, with a floating fondue experience. Yes, you read that right.

I love Switzerland, and have visited the land where the hills are alive with the sound of cowbells more than 30 times in my life. And while I’ve done many amazing things in and around the Swiss Alps—skiing, hiking, trottinetting, whittling my own Swiss cow from a block of wood—I knew getting my Gen Z crew excited about family time involved finding something a little more unconventional.

We were going to be staying in the Bernese Oberland, a picture-postcard region with legendary sites like Grindelwald, the Jungfrau and Eiger mountains, and Interlaken. Everyone was up for hiking and taking cable cars to waterfalls; paragliding was sadly vetoed. But a unique culinary experience would surely work, I thought—the way to their hearts is through their stomachs.

Luckily, I had heard about a Cheese Fondue Float experience offered by a company called Outdoor Switzerland a few years ago. Back then, it was raclette—toasted cheese scraped onto boiled potatoes—that served as the dish du jour. But fondue, Switzerland’s national dish, is much more well-known, so the company savvily swapped raclette trays for caquelons (ceramic fondue pots). I found the experience listing on Get Your Guide, and reviews praised the change, highlighting the delicious cheese and wine and the gregarious fondue fun. I confirmed a private booking for the six of us a month before we left home, and kept my fingers crossed for good weather.

I needn’t have worried—my prayers were answered with glorious temperatures and bluebird skies on the day of the tour, a leisurely Sunday in September. A five-minute bus ride from downtown Interlaken brought us to the small village of Bonigen, the launch site located on scenic Lake Brienz. After shaking hands with our guide, a tall, friendly Dutchman named Hild, we donned life jackets, listened to the mandatory safety briefing, and stepped into the boat, alternating sides to keep the weight even. Once comfortably settled around the pretty red-and-white-checkered tablecloth, which was already topped with plates, cups, and two fondue pots, Hild slowly rowed us onto the lake.

An overhead shot of the pretty tablescape and gorgeous lake

Lake Brienz is the deepest lake in the country, and it’s surely one of the most scenic too. Moving out from the shore, we encountered spectacular views of towering mountains, their peaks mirrored in the impossibly blue water. I poured the prepared cheese fondue into the heated fondue pots, and the mixture began bubbling, filling the air with a sharp aroma as it warmed into readiness.

The fondue float experience includes white wine (one 500-ml bottle per person), as well as water and hot tea. We took turns pouring wine into our copper cups as my eldest son took command of the Bluetooth speaker, setting a lively mood with traditional Alpine tunes played on accordions and hackbretts (a kind of dulcimer), mixed with the occasional yodel ditty. At one point, our float’s music and laughter brought friendly waves from passengers on a passing cruise boat, along with toots from the ship’s horn. We whooped and waved in return.

Once the cheese was steaming hot, we dipped and swished bread cubes into the melted goodness, savoring the delicious alchemy of bread and cheese alongside celebratory toasts in honor of our family adventure. As the cheese disappeared, the fondue pot heated the remains into what the Swiss call “la réligieuse”—toasted cheese bits that are scraped from the bottom of the pot. We fought playfully over dibs on the last delicious morsels—trust me, they’re good to the last perfectly browned crumb.

Raising a glass to a unique family adventure

The entire experience lasted about an hour and a half, and during that time, the six of us managed to drink all six wine bottles on board. None of us are big drinkers, but the beauty of the surroundings inspired the good times to flow, and, well, so did the wine.

Photos and videos captured our cheesy adventure, but the memory of enjoying such a unique culinary and cultural experience with my favorite people in the world will be forever burned into my mind. You can have a fondue anywhere, but while floating in one of the most iconic locations in one of the most beautiful countries on earth? Even my discerning Gen Z travel companions agreed: “That’s extra.”

The Cheese Fondue Float experience on Lake Brienz in Interlaken is available to book on the Outdoor Switzerland website, as well as on GetYourGuide and Viator. It is offered between September and April, weather permitting. If booking in the colder months, bundle up with coats, beanies, and gloves, as you’ll be out on the water for up to an hour and a half. Private charters are available for groups up to eight people; kids eight years and up are welcome. More of a dessert person? Outdoor Switzerland also offers a Swiss Chocolate Fondue experience. Get cozy under blankets, sip hot tea, and dip marshmallows and fruit into creamy melted Swiss chocolate while a qualified guide rows you merrily along the beautiful Brienzersee.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6292. Hilton Is Growing Faster Than Marriott, Hyatt And IHG

Hilton opened 182 hotels and 27,000 rooms in the Q3 2026, which works out to 23,000 net additional rooms and net unit growth of 6% from a year prior, according to its earnings release. Net income was $536MM, up from $421MM, and adjusted EBITDA was $1.058bn. Management and franchise fee revenue rose 9.5% which is the company’s core business model.

Comparing that to the other three big loyalty hotel companies, Marriott added roughly 20,000 net rooms and grew 4.6%. IHG reported net system growth of 4.9% after opening 12,900 rooms across 92 hotels. Hyatt posted net rooms growth of 3.8% over the trailing 12 months. The companies define growth a little differently, but Hilton leads on every version I can find, and it did so while adding more net rooms in a quarter than Marriott, the larger of the two companies.

More rooms does not necessarily mean higher earnings. Hyatt’s comparable system-wide RevPAR rose 7.2%, Marriott’s rose 6.5% worldwide and 7.4% in the US and Canada, while Hilton’s rose 5.8%, and IHG’s rose just 5.3%. Hilton ranks third of four on that list which starts to eat into its net rooms added lead. Hyatt’s caveat is its all-inclusive business, where Net Package RevPAR fell 2.5%, which matters because every big hotel brand wants your all-inclusive money right now. This, for me, probably deserves its own post if the drops continue into the fourth quarter compared with YoY.

Net profit confirms the rate growth relative to both peers and net rooms is more tied to RevPAR than absolute growth. Marriott earned $794MM in the quarter and $1.52bn in adjusted EBITDA, well ahead of Hilton. Hyatt’s net income was $58MM, or $122MM adjusted, which is considerably less but HYatt is far smaller (and underperforms.) I wrote last week that Royal Caribbean out-earned Hilton’s whole 2025 in a quarter, and the hotel sector is a reminder that growth and earnings are different races.

Marriott’s development pipeline hit a record of more than 634,000 rooms across over 4,200 properties, with 44% of those rooms under construction. Hilton’s pipeline is 543,100 rooms across 3,869 hotels in 135 countries, with nearly half under construction and more than half outside the United States. IHG’s pipeline is 353,000 rooms, up 3.2% and equal to 33% of its current system. Hyatt’s is about 158,000 rooms, up 12.1%.

Marriott has the biggest pipeline in absolute terms, Hyatt’s is growing fastest of the three that disclosed growth, and Hilton grew 5%. Conversions matter here too. Marriott said conversions (existing independent hotels or those being reflagged) made up over a third of signings and over 40% of openings in the first nine months, and IHG says development splits roughly evenly between new builds and conversions. Hilton opened its first Select by Hilton hotels this quarter, one of several newer brands it is leaning on to fill that pipeline.

As someone whose agency sells hotel rooms, both of these numbers are important but for different reasons. My clients and I prefer to see the rate creep slow or stop (rate regression might be a dream) with more stays. But more properties to choose from is good news too and increases competition.

For travelers, the bigger question is what all this growth does to loyalty programs especially when comparing Hilton vs Marriott. Marriott Bonvoy and Hilton Honors each span well over a million rooms, and their luxury brands include Waldorf Astoria, Conrad, St. Regis, Ritz-Carlton and JW Marriott. But with so many of the new rooms being conversions and limited-service hotels where elite status buys less, that can reduce the shine of the programs. Lounge access and complimentary breakfast (a daily food and beverage credit at most U.S. Hilton hotels) are what business travelers chase but lounges are almost gone completely, and those perks are thinner at a select-service property. Hilton offers elites a fifth night free on standard reward stays and waives resort fees on free nights, and Hilton points pile up quickly through its brand credit cards with American Express. Long term, more hotels should mean more places to redeem, not just more places to earn. But the question also becomes how important those advantages are, and with both Bonvoy’s accelerated status earning, and Hilton’s Diamond via credit card option, the true value of those benefits continue to diminish.

Hilton returned $879MM to shareholders in the quarter, $2.9bn so far this year, and projects about $3.5 billion for 2026. It also moved its stock listing to Nasdaq on November 5, 2026 under the same HLT ticker. IHG has completed $707MM of a $950MM buyback and expects to return over $1.2bn in 2026. Hyatt projects $375MM to $425MM in capital returns. Hotels are on a tear over the last couple of years and Hilton’s growth in room count demonstrates confidence in the market for the future.

Hilton is winning the room race and not the rate race, and Marriott is winning the profit race. I expect Hilton to hold the unit growth lead through 2027, but Marriott’s larger pipeline will make that lead uncomfortable. Hyatt will continue winning on rate while sitting out the growth sprint barring another acquisition which it has been drawn to as of late, which is exactly how a luxury-leaning brand should behave. Still, it’s impressive to see Hilton with such strong numbers for growing the brand.

I think Hyatt needs to make some acquisitions – Omni, Viceroy, Loews – would all make nice additions

I’ve stayed in w Hilton garden inn and had lack of heating issues in both. No more

Over the last few years, I do feel, specifically in the U.S., that Hilton’s race is just bigger and more for rooms; room quality is holding but slightly diminishing – across the board, from service to room quality is less impressive than my stays at Hyatt…maybe it’s like Starbucks – there’s one everywhere, but I feel they are slightly overpriced and quality is fine, but nothing all that impressive, at least in the U.S. I don’t feel like I get great value from Honors either, with Hamptons in major U.S. cities, easily going for 50-60K a night. So basically, Hilton or Marriott is your giant everywhere choice; then there are preferred accommodation providers when the choice exists.

I would put revenue ahead of property portfolio growth. That said, I’ll hand it to Hilton. They have acquired several niche hotel brands, whether it’d Graduate or Scandic.

Hyatt is like the 50-year-old lady who still think she’s the hot 20-something. They are chasing everything and not getting anything right. Meanwhile, they are neglecting Grand Hyatt and Hyatt Regency, which, at least in North America and Europe, nobody seems to want to build and develop these days. Then there’s Hyatt Place, which is an absolute disaster of a brand. You have some brand-new or newly-renovated Hyatt Place properties that are as nice (minus the lack of a real restaurant) as a Hyatt Regency. Then you have awful Hyatt Places that are complete dumps.

That brings us to Marriott. I think Marriott has hit its ceiling, which explains why the corporate leadership has went after low-end hotels/motels converted to City Express, etc. Is there any market that can support a Courtyard, Marriott, Sheraton, Renaissance, or Westin that doesn’t already have one? Marriott also faces a problem in that it has a large number of 1970s and 1980s properties that are coming up on 50 years of age. They are at the point in time where they need to be gutted and renovated floor-to-ceiling or demolished and replaced. Marriott also has to cut corporate staff because most of its revenue is now generated through franchising and licensing fees, not hotel management contracts. It doesn’t need as much corporate staff when you’re only a booking platform.

#6291. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6290. The Wonder—and Weirdness—of Exploring a National Park in the Dark

I’ve spent the majority of my life doing outdoor activities: camping, hiking, biking, kayaking, you name it. It’s intrinsically part of who I am, something that defines my siblings and I so deeply it feels like it’s braided into our DNA.

Perhaps that’s because, when I was just two-and-a-half years old, my parents took my siblings and me on a two-month-long road trip from New York to Arizona, hitting dozens of state and national parks on the way. We still talk about that adventure, lovingly referred to as the Out West Trip. It was the first time I visited Utah’s national parks, known as the Mighty 5: Zion, Arches, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Bryce Canyon.

Once night falls in Utah's national parks, most travelers head back to their campfires or motor lodges—except for those willing to brave the dark and explore their nocturnal side.

A lot has changed since I first visited. Now, millions of visitors head to Southern Utah every year, flocking to these five well-known national parks in addition to the whopping 46 state parks across the whole of Utah. Even in the staggeringly hot and dry summer season, these protected areas teem with tourists from all over the world—Zion alone reported over 1.4 million visitors in June, July, and August of 2026, while Arches reported over 445,000 in the same season.

Once night falls in the Utah desert, though, the temperatures cool off, most tourists head back to their campsites and motor lodges, and the stars shine through that clear desert sky. All of the Mighty 5 are certified dark sky parks—Utah, in fact, boasts the highest concentration of certified International Dark Sky Places in the world. So maybe it's no surprise that, in recent years, these destinations have embraced night-centric recreation, showcasing a lesser-known version of themselves for those willing to brave the dark.

In Capitol Reef National Park, the The Temple of the Sun summit stands against a sky full of stars.

It's why, nearly 30 years after my first Utah park trip, I decided to return—this time, experiencing Southern Utah’s state and national parks once the sun set. I’m a night owl, but I also wanted to revive that sense of wonder I felt so long ago when I first visited. I knew the parks by day, but by night? They were brand new to me. And so, in late September, my friend Sarra and I plotted a week-long road trip linking four national parks and three state parks in Utah. Our goal was to take it easy during the daylight hours with a gentle hike or two, and store up our energy for a nocturnal expedition come sundown. We wanted to get to know Utah’s parks in a way that too few do.

It’s 9 p.m. when we walk into Capitol Reef National Park with hiking guides Samuel and Suzanne Francis, the married owners of Western Whiptails Adventures. The sun has set by a couple hours; my friend and I rely on flashlights, while our guides trust themselves in the dark. As we begin on the trail, I’m struck by the silence surrounding us, serene in a way I’ve experienced only in the redwoods, where the massive trees cradle you against human noise; by day, the stone of Utah’s parks almost reverberates with the many overlapping voices of the crowd. Now, there is no sound left to bounce.

The view of the Hickman Bridge in Capitol Reef National Park at midnight.

Our goal is to hike to Hickman Bridge, a natural sandstone arch—completely in the dark. It’s a 1.8-mile round-trip that begins with an initial climb on switchbacks, flattens out in the middle, and then resumes a narrower uphill path with a bit of a scramble required to reach the view. It’s a hike that should take about 1.5 hours in daylight. Sam says he and Suz have led hundreds of guided tours throughout the park and surrounding public lands, but nothing quite like this. “Capitol Reef’s landscape takes on an entirely different character at night,” he says.

I feel the ground under my sneakers shift from hard-packed dirt to softer sand as we set out, and the herbal scent of pinon and Utah juniper trees tickles my nose. We’re surrounded by dust and desert, but the area feels alive with the chirping of bugs and rustling of leaves.

Suz leads us to little-known petroglyphs, then points out a site where the Fremont people once stored corn. Sarra and I shine our flashlights and look on in admiration. It’s a respite in the adrenaline-pumping stretch of the hike—we have gained a couple hundred feet of elevation, and I am imagining the drop-offs that I’m quite sure lie beyond the tiny circle of my flashlight. My grip gets tighter and I begin to sweat through my layers, realizing that the dark can't quiet my fear of heights. Suz is up ahead, climbing like it’s second nature: “If you turn your flashlights off, your eyes will adjust,” she says, turning back. I laugh, knowing there's no way I can get myself to follow her advice.

The nearly full moon directly over the sandstone summit in Capitol Reef National Park

A hard-to-find petroglyph site in Capitol Reef National Park

“Many animals in Capitol Reef are nocturnal or crepuscular, especially during warmer months,” Sam says, listing off the species we share the night with as we plod on. “Bats, kangaroo rats, desert cottontails, foxes, desert bighorn sheep, mule deer, or even the rare ringtail.”

Once we reach flatter ground, I concede to turn off my light, blinking to let my eyes adjust. I realize the nearly full moon above is blindingly bright—and yet we can still make out hundreds of glittering stars sharing the sky. “The darkness really offers a unique connection to the landscape,” says Sam. I can't help but agree.

And then we finally catch sight of the stone bridge, bathed in moonlight and backlit by stars, appearing especially mammoth in the low light. We sit beneath it, the silence wrapped around us, the space above looking unimaginably infinite. “I’ve seen this bridge plenty of times during the day,” says Suz, agreeing with me, “but at night, it's even better.”

The starry sky shines over Dead Horse Point State Park, where after-dark activities include scorpion spotting and stargazing.

While Capitol Reef's night hike was nothing short of thrilling, another type of excitement awaits us at Dead Horse State Park. The park is known for its dramatic red-rock canyon vistas and hiking trails that cross them—and yet the evening programming is just as robust, with scorpion searching, stargazing, sunset walks, and astronomy talks all included in the $20 entrance fee. Unlike Capitol Reef, where we were possibly the only visitors on the grounds that night (despite it being open 24 hours), Dead Horse is known for its nocturnal programming (much of which begins around 8 p.m., and runs until the park closes at 10). According to Ally O'Rullian, public information officer at Utah State Parks, Dead Horse Point naturalist programs have “likely included dark sky viewings” since as early as the mid 1970s, and this new slate of activities was added to the regular calendar in 2015 as part of its application for International Dark Sky status. We are far from the only ones out tonight—it feels as though this is how the Dead Horse is meant to be appreciated.

A group of travelers gather around a state ranger as they prepare for a scorpion search

We've opted to go scorpion searching, which is exactly as wacky as it sounds. Scorpions are biofluorescent, meaning they emit a visible bluish glow under UV lights. And so we gather at the Visitor Center, where ranger Jimmy Burch is handing out special flashlights. This is one of the most popular activities at the park, Burch says, and perhaps unsurprisingly, the one with the greatest youth turnout. We do feel like kids, as our group of a dozen or so of all ages start down a gentle, meandering path, shining our torches on brush and rocks to see if we can find anything hiding among them. Shine a UV light directly on a bush with a scorpion in it, Burch says, and it would be nearly impossible to overlook the glowing body within. “If you hear hissing, step away,” he cautions, as we sweep the area. Burch assures us that no one has ever been stung on one of these walks.

We are nearing the end of “scorpion season” in late September, as the weather is getting too cold for the critters to wander freely. In winter, scorpions enter a low-activity state and hide in dark, quiet locations, like underground burrows, conserving their energy against the cold. I wonder if that means we won't see much—but then, after just a few minutes, a boy in my group begins to call out, “Scorpion, scorpion, scorpion!” Burch heads over, congratulatory as he crouches down a few inches away from the tiny, glowing arachnid. The rest of us follow, taking turns leaning closer to take in its luminous body, just a few inches long. It turns out that scorpions are perfectly happy to hang out under the UV light, surrounded by a large group of people taking photos. It doesn't move a single muscle as we pap it in awe.

Setting up kayaks at the edge of the Sand Hollow State Park reservoir, just as the moon begins to rise

Jaw-dropping colors appear in the sky over Sand Hollow State Park and its reservoir.

Ready for something a bit calmer, we make the early morning drive to our final destination: Hurricane, Utah—about 25 miles away from Zion National Park, and home to the lesser-known Sand Hollow. Initially, we had plans to do nocturnal canyoneering in Zion, but when the weather turned, it gave us permission to settle into a slower place.

For the past two years, Sand Hollow State Park—known for its large reservoir set against red-rock cliffs—has been offering a monthly full-moon paddle in the warmer months, to complement the hiking and biking trails that families enjoy year-round.

The paddle is only available from April through September (depending on the weather) and starts at moonrise—which is just after 7 p.m. for us, when our group meets ranger Carlie Mallow on the shore of the reservoir. Just on the other side of sunset, the sky still has tinges of light to it, and we can hear the gentle chatter of dozens of other people who are still swimming, fishing, and hanging out on the water's edge as we pull our kayaks into the water. The park is open until 10 p.m., and those accompanied by a ranger can stay even later. I feel as though I'm at an after-hours summer camp, as I notice the people on piers, jumping in the water, and sitting at picnic tables nearby.

Two kayaks at the edge of Sand Hollow State Park reservoir at the end of the moonlit paddle

The night is relatively warm, as we make the gentle paddle out. We take pauses to float and listen to history; Mallow points at an island in the middle of the water: "a family of raccoons lives there", she tells us.

We let our kayaks rest when we near the isle, collecting among the rippling water to watch the moon continue its rise. I hear the water brushing against my kayak, and realize my eyes are now more used to navigating these wild spaces in the absence of the sun.

Our group is substantial. Sometimes there will 30 kayaks or paddleboards on the water at a time, Mallow says. “The moonlit paddle is pretty popular,” Mallow tells us from her own kayak, as we circle the island. "We hope programs like these both spark adventure and curiosity in visitors, and encourage neighbors to fall in love with their backyard.” As we navigate the water, we come across night fishers and a swimmer (“people train for the Ironman here,” says Mallow). I wonder if the scuba divers who were on the shore when we pushed off were entering or exiting. Before this trip, my imagination couldn't have fathomed so many ways to experience these lands after sunset.

As parks get increasingly crowded, I have to wonder if nighttime adventures will become a part of my regular routine. There are always new ways to discover America’s national and state park system—and now, I know that darkness can make even the most familiar places feel like a whole new world. Once you get past the fear of it—the dark, the height, the critters—you are free to soak up the feeling of being so small against the endless night sky, amazed by all the life that continues even once the sun has gone down.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6289. My Abysmal Enterprise Car Rental Experience In Omaha

Attending to a personal matter in Omaha with little notice, I booked a flight, hotel, and car rental. The miracle of points and miles is the ability to make anything happen when you really need it to without significant expense or inconvenience and I recommend to anyone that asks me about the loyalty space to leave a reserve to of 2.5x standard rates for an emergency trip home.

The flight was unremarkable (and priced about at that range, unfortunately), the hotel was a remodeled but otherwise unremarkable Hampton Inn, well located for my visit. But my typical rental car provider, National (owned by ERAC) was unavailable at the airport. I have some status with Avis and Hertz due to credit cards and reciprocal status but wanted to try the Drive Alliance angle for Enterprise companies. However, this required a nearby city location and not an airport rental. Honestly, it wasn’t that big of a deal to grab a Lyft to the downtown location at 23rd & Harney, and because of a credit, the ride only set me back $6.97 before tip.

Upon arrival, I was informed that my preferred car type was unavailable. For my trip a few vehicle types were offered, the cheapest being a mystery vehicle, but I opted for 2-4 levels above that for a Standard car and paid more for it. Not only was I told that the car I paid more for was not available, but that they only had minivans and there were zero other choices.

“Car choices aren’t guaranteed when booking within 24 hours.” There’s a little more context due, I know that car types are never guaranteed, but typically there’s more than just one type left.

“I don’t see that on my confirmation, can you show it to me?” She couldn’t, of course, then stated that “St. Louis”, ERAC headquarters, isn’t connected to their inventory. This opens a host of other questions. I searched the website, then I tried Google, then I enlisted AI and none of those options showed me specific adjustments described by the branch attendant stated by ERAC specific to the 24-hour booking period. I reached out to the brand on October 20th, it has yet to respond.

I had a choice to make, either take what they have or move on. As I was not at the airport and couldn’t just walk to another counter, I accepted my fate and moved to the garage.

The most unsavory part about the Enterprise experience as it differs from other brands is the endless damage evaluation. Walking around with an iPad, the attendant points out a knick here, a scratch there – the perfect moment to take out the insurance or pay with a card that includes the Collision Damage Waiver just to avoid participation.

I can’t say for certain that the vehicle was used to move pounds of marijuana across state lines – I couldn’t say that at all. But I could say for certain that it smelled so deeply of weed that I doubt any amount of cleaning could be effective.

“This one smells like weed.” I said, shutting the door.

“I’ll have to take your word for it.” She replied and moved on.

Really? Would you have noticed if I said it smelled as though a den of skunks had made their home in the stow-and-go or would you have to take my word for it? I don’t want to show up to family smelling like backstage at Coachella.

We moved on to the vehicle next to it, a California tag with 51,000 miles and a quarter tank of gas. She started the walk around again, noting that the chip in the windshield could spider but I wouldn’t be responsible if the windshield needed to be replaced upon my return. Cool. How about not giving me a vehicle where I might have a spiderwebbed safety issue?

I tossed my luggage inside, and addressed her one more time.

I had to address the fuel level, as I might not make it to my first stop without the low fuel light illuminating.

“A quarter tank?” I was borderline ready to leave but knew that I didn’t have time to start this all over somewhere else.

“Those two guys in the wash bay sitting down on their phones – do they work here?”

“Yes.” She said it to me unironically without connecting the challenge of the cleanliness, or the useless fuel level and how both of those service challenges might have been solved (in the case of the skunky van, maybe not) by the staff being asked to do their jobs.

They aren’t understaffed, they are unbothered, indifferent, and at a minimum unwilling to ask them to perform their duties, or more likely, incapable of actual management. It’s a crazy position to take with Enterprise’s excellent corporate structure and the fact that they give you the tools to be your own boss.

I guess some things are just better in the movies.

In the words of our 43rd US President, “Fool me once, shame on – shame on you. Fool me – you can’t get fooled again.” It was simpler times when that sort of turn of phrase failure was the height of presidential gaffes.

I don’t care that National’s ownership is the same (ERAC), I will continue to rent from them as long as their model remains the same and continues to deliver. But from Enterprise? Never, ever again. Maybe a “neighborhood location” has different rules, but the staff at the Downtown Omaha location exhibited a total lack of interest in my experience or their own jobs. Corporate didn’t respond to my survey nor to my request for comment. And while I would agree that I’m not Cooper Anderson reaching out to them, readers in the past have asked if the brand has a comment. They did not.

I shouldn’t have to drive around in a dented safety concern reeking of weed while I get gas immediately after departing the parking lot and somehow try to perfectly return with a quarter tank or pay $7/gallon. It’s disrespectful to your clients but it appears the great corporate structure at Enterprise may have given this branch the tools to be their own boss, and they were even less interested in doing that than I am in renting from any Enterprise location anywhere.

Besides renting from them in the first place, my greatest regret was that I didn’t get to try my credit card’s Collision Damage Waiver on for size, just in case I needed it.

I have had terrible experiences with Enterprise in the past – being stranded with a disabled vehicle that could have been prevented by adequate maintenance, spurious cleaning charges, etc., I was forced to use Enterprise due to being at remote locations recently and was very pleased with their service. Sorry you were not as lucky.

I had a bad experience with Enterprise many years ago and stopped using them. A couple of years ago I booked with them when National was too expensive and had a good experience, and I have mostly booked with Enterprise ever since. All my recent experiences have been good. However, I have been booking almost exclusively at large or medium sized airports, so that could be the difference. They almost always have skip the counter and except at the largest airports they often share cars with National and Alamo anyway.

For best results, in an off airport location, try to use a car dealership. Perhaps one that has a relationship with friends or other local contacts. There you will find a few newer rentals in great condition that are not of skunk smell. These are not advertised but kept for the company. Cannot say they would honor t & c but at least you get a better choice.

You rented from Enterprise (at a non-airport) location. What could go wrong? Well, you learned what could go wrong.

From my experience, I’m not sure Enterprise is the problem. You wrote “maybe a neighborhood location has different rules” and I don’t think it’s different rules but perhaps different standards. And to be clear, this is the case for every rental car brand where I go to a neighborhood location – I used to do this often when I didn’t have a car, and I know that it is very different than the airport experience. Point by point… – Gas tank: more likely to be less than full, but that close to empty is particularly bad. In many neighborhood locations it is literally one person working the place. Still you need enough gas to drive it off the lot. – Cleanliness: Unacceptable. That sucks and reflects poorly on the brand. – Damage/Inspection: They always do the walkaround, and there’s almost always some damage they note. Many of mine had divots in the windshield or rear windshield and a couple door dings. Combined with there being one employee this process often means renting a car takes 20-30 minutes per person, which is another issue. – 24 hour rule: I don’t know of anywhere this is written but it is absolutely true at multiple brands that those booked within 24 hours are basically considered walk-ups in terms of availability. In fact there are usually printed signs when I go to the location saying as much. I rented from an Avis in a Portland suburb in the summer and multiple printed signs and a single unhappy employee greeted at least two people who had made reservations in the last day, showed up at 8am opening, and were turned away wholesale with no cars available on a random Thursday. I’m glad this story confirmed my assumption that it had to do with connection to real time inventory at corporate locations, as many neighborhood ones are franchises.

I do not disagree that this is a terrible experience, I’m just saying this is par for the course. I’ve rented at Enterprise, Hertz, and Avis neighborhood locations all with near-identical experiences, in San Diego, Portland, and San Francisco, for what it’s worth. Usually the neighborhood locations *inside* actual car dealerships (like a full-service Nissan dealer) are much better than the standalone or hotel-attached ones in the same city and have fewer of these problems, but they also tend to be open more limited hours.

Alex is right. Never use off-airport locations if you can avoid it. Most do not have good standards, and you are lucky if they have any decent car resembling the one you reserved available. If you have to, you might have slightly better luck at Hertz or Avis.

Sorry that you did have a bad experience with Enterprise I did have a very positive expriences (3) with them at a local office in Tysons corner

The car was clean, full tank, and all persons i dealt with were friendly and very efficient

“Thanks for the F shack – love Dirty Mike and the boys.”

Enterprise at least leaves you a jar of old mustard!

When I first started traveling regularly for work around 2012 and 2013, I used Enterprise. My first two employers had corporate contracts with the company.

I always had problems with Enterprise, mostly with branches taking reservations and then having no car available. Not just the particular car I had booked, but any car at all. It became such an issue that my second employer canceled its contract with Enterprise in 2014, the same year I left.

In late 2014 or early 2015, Delta and Hertz struck a deal that gave Delta Diamond medallions top-tier Hertz President’s Circle status. It worked great for a few years. Then Hertz went downhill during and afrter the pandemic and, in my opinion, has never recovered. I blindly stuck with Hertz for 10 years.

I will say with Hertz that it paid to get to know a manager at a branch you frequent. For example, around 2018, I was going to Honolulu for work once or twice a month. I did something like 18 trips in a 12-month period. I became “friends” with a supervisor or manager at the Honolulu airport branch. He always pre-blocked me into a Jeep Wrangler without me having to book one. That was great.

Then in 2020, I relocated for work on an 11.5-month contract. I arrived in early January. I made a booking for the whole year. Then the pandemic hit. Hertz wanted to sell my car. I’d get a new car every 3-4 weeks, when Hertz required me to come into the office for a vehicle inspection. They usually took the car and gave me something new. The manager always made sure they had something decent for me even though Hertz was selling virtually its entire fleet.

I tried Avis in 2024 and 2025. They matched me to their top tier, and, for whatever reason, I kept that status for a year and a half. President’s Club or Chairman’s Club. Something like that. I received a couple of decent upgrades without asking, but the service was awful.

Twice, an airport branch failed to close out my rental contract after I returned the car. Another branch refused to let me take a car because its system showed I still had an open rental at another location from more than a year earlier. It was a complete mess, and I could never get anyone at Avis to resolve it.

The final straw came when I prepaid for an Avis rental through the Delta Air Lines portal. The branch then charged me again, so I paid twice. Avis refused to issue a refund. I disputed the duplicate charge with Chase Visa, but Chase sided with Avis even though I supplied the documentation. I lost $700 and stopped renting from Avis.

In late 2025, I decided to give Enterprise another chance. Since then, I’ve rented from them about 25 times, totaling roughly 70 rental days in the United States, Canada, the UK, France, and Germany.

Customer service is generally very good at the branch level. Sometimes, employees are a little over the top in trying to please you. I’ve had locations knock $75 off the bill for relatively minor issues, even when I insisted no compensation was necessary.

The problem, just as in 2012 and 2013, is that many branches continue to accept bookings when they have no vehicles available. This happened to me at an Enterprise location in Zurich. Thankfully, Sixt had a car with an automatic transmission within my budget.

Enterprise also regularly gives me older vehicles or cars with higher mileage. I’ve paid for premium, vehicle-specific rentals, such as a Suburban or Jeep Wrangler, and received vehicles with 55,000 miles on them. Even the worst cars I rented from Hertz never had more than 20,000 or 25,000 miles on the odometer.

My other big issue with Enterprise is the lack of a choose-your-own-car aisle like Hertz offers. I have Enterprise Gold status, its second-highest tier, but I often have to wait in line to go through the charade with a staff member who then escorts me to the parking lot and finds me a car. I probably waste 10 to 15 minutes on this with every rental. I understand that Enterprise emphasizes personal interactions as part of its approach to customer service, but it’s just too much.

I also never get upgrades unless I ask. Ever. Sometimes I’ll ask and get a “sure, no problem,” but nothing is ever offered proactively.

The weed issue is more and more prevalent. I have had both Hertz and Avis vehicles in Louisiana given to me reeking of Snoop Dogg or Willie Nelson concerts and had to change. Recently they had no other cars so I was a stuck driving with windows down hoping to not be pulled over and lose my government clearance, because I am sure the local cops would buy the “it was already in the rental” story. I djd have the agent make a note before I left in ase something came up. I had an Uber once that reeked as I was going to an airport for an international flight (all I need is some drug to hit a d delay me at the border because of it). Just do it at home at home people!

Our Viking guide, Karim Zohny, is leading us through one of the best-preserved ancient temples in all of Egypt, the Temple of Hathor, explaining the famously colorful reliefs that line its massive sandstone pillars, walls and ceilings.

Located along the Nile near the Egyptian city of Qena, it is, as Zohny notes, unusual in its motifs, which include intricate celestial maps and giant images of the Egyptian queen Cleopatra and her son Caesarion.

That our small group of two dozen passengers from the Viking river ship Viking Osiris is even here is also relatively unusual.

Most vessels that sail the Nile don’t come this far north. Instead, they stick to the 130-mile stretch of river that runs between the more southerly cities of Luxor and Aswan.

It's just one of several things that make Viking's 11-night Egypt tours, in my opinion at least (after years of traveling in Egypt), among the best choices for exploring the country's splendors.

Pairing a seven-night Nile sailing with four nights of land-based travel, Viking’s “Pharaohs and Pyramids” trips offer some of the most comprehensive, in-depth touring that you will find in Egypt. They also offer a Nile river ship experience that has few rivals, thanks to Viking’s recent rollout of an all-new series of Nile vessels that is setting a new bar for the region.

In addition, as I have seen on more than one Viking trip in Egypt, the trips offer a particularly seamless and mostly all-inclusive experience, with just about every element — from lodging and meals to expert-led guided tours and special access to iconic sites — included in the fare.

Aimed at the same sort of history-loving travelers who get excited about visiting the ancient ruins of Greece and Italy, Viking’s Egypt trips — like many tours of the country — focus heavily on what some consider the greatest civilization of all time: ancient Egypt.

Indeed, almost from the moment we land in Cairo to begin the tour, which begins with a three-night stay at the upscale Fairmont Nile City Hotel, we are thrust more than 4,500 years back in time to one of the oldest and greatest eras of ancient Egypt: The Old Kingdom.

Also known as the Age of the Pyramids, this was the period that saw the construction of monumental structures such as the 4,700-year-old Step Pyramid of Djoser, which we visit on our first full day of touring.

Located at the edge of the desert just outside Cairo, in an area known as Saqqara, it was, as Zohny explains, not only the first pyramid built in Egypt but also by far the largest stone structure built by humans up to that time.

In that respect, its construction was one of the great milestones of history.

It's a history we experience viscerally as we frog-walk down a low-sloping tunnel into another nearby pyramid built for the pharaoh Teti. After nearly a hundred feet, we emerge into a three-room tomb covered in ancient hieroglyphics, among the oldest funerary texts ever found in an Egyptian tomb.

The next day, Zohny, an expert “Egyptologist” who will be our guide for the entire trip, brings us to the even bigger (and more famous) Pyramids of Giza and the nearby Great Sphinx, which also are just outside of Cairo.

Built about a century after the Step Pyramid of Djoser, the Giza pyramids mark the peak of pyramid building in Egypt and are truly a sight to behold.

In between visiting these massive structures, we are treated to a full morning of exploring the new Grand Egyptian Museum, where we marvel at the gilded treasures recovered from the pharaoh Tutankhamun's tomb just a century ago. We also visit Cairo's alabaster-clad Mosque of Muhammad Ali.

It is a whirlwind two days that prepare us for the equally stunning sites from the more recent New Kingdom, Ptolemaic and Roman periods of ancient Egypt that we will see while sailing the Nile on Viking Osiris.

But first, we must get to the ship. Like most of the vessels that sail the Nile, Viking Osiris is based in Luxor, hundreds of miles south of Cairo — the center of ancient Egypt, which began around 4,100 years ago (when it was called Thebes).

After checking out of the Fairmont, we fly as a group to Luxor on a charter flight.

To sail the Nile on Viking Osiris or one of its many sister vessels (at last count, there were eight on the river) is to be on something akin to a greatest hits tour of nearly 2,000 years of iconic Egyptian structures.

Luxor, Qena, Kom Ombo, Edfu. On the ship's weeklong itineraries, these Nile river destinations famous for ancient sites come one after the other, each offering something spectacular that you probably remember from your second-grade history class.

In Luxor, it is the massive Temple of Karnak, with its colossal sandstone columns arranged in neat rows (if you’ve seen the James Bond vs. Jaws chase scene in the 1977 film “The Spy Who Loved Me,” you know what I’m talking about).

In Qena, it is the impressive Temple of Hathor, which is part of an even bigger archeological site known as the Dendera Temple Complex.

In Kom Ombo, it is the equally impressive temple of the same name, built during the Greco-Roman period and featuring reliefs of the Roman emperors Tiberius and Domitian.

Then there’s Edfu, home to the long-buried-in-sand Temple of Horus. Lost to time until a French archeologist began digging it out 166 years ago, it is almost completely intact, with its hypostyle halls and inner sanctuary looking much as they did 2,000 years ago.

Some of these destinations that the ship visits are gateways to multiple world-class sites. In addition to the Temple of Karnak (where Viking ships have an exclusive dock location), Luxor is our base for an outing to the nearby pharaonic burial grounds, the Valley of the Kings, a highlight of any Egypt tour.

In our case, the visit includes the opportunity to descend into five of the more than 60 tombs found in the valley so far — two more than is typical for many Egypt tours.

Viking has paid extra to get us access to perhaps the most famous tomb of them all, that of the pharaoh Tutankhamun (King Tut, as we called him when I was a boy), who remains inside the tomb in mummified form, as well as the spectacular (and normally expensive to visit) tomb of Seti I.

During our stay in Luxor, we also wandered through the Temple of Luxor and the terraced Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut — the latter a masterpiece of ancient architecture.

Some passengers also soar skyward in a hot air balloon (one of the few extra-charge excursions during the trip) for views of the Mortuary Temple, Valley of the Kings and other area sites from the air.

While exploring the remnants of ancient Egypt is a big part of the trip, it’s not the only focus. As we sail the Nile, we also get a taste of everyday life on the river.

Some of my favorite moments of the voyage come as we steam through the many rural stretches of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, where the riverbanks often are lined with date palms, reeds, wild grasses and, in some areas, lush agricultural crops.

It is a scene evoking the Nile of ancient times.

At times, I spot farmers working in small fields of bananas or sugarcane, or tending to cows grazing along the waterfront.

We regularly pass fishermen in small boats slapping the water with oars to scare the fish into nets — a traditional technique.

It is, notably, a narrow band of abundance. In some places, the fertile area fed by the life-giving waters of the Nile stretches just a few hundred feet inland, in other places maybe a mile or two, before the landscape abruptly transforms into harsh desert that stretches for hundreds of miles.

It’s one of the things that makes Egypt so fascinating. It is a country that essentially unfolds along one very long, very narrow ribbon of green in a sea of desert.

Or, as the Greek historian Herodotus famously wrote, Egypt is the gift of the Nile.

You can read about this in books, of course. But it's something you only truly understand when you see it up close from the deck of a passing vessel.

One of the big allurements of Viking sailings on the Nile is their laid-back pace.

Many Egypt tour itineraries include only three or four nights of cruising between Luxor and Aswan to see the major sites, or even fewer, resulting in a frenetic touring schedule. There is a lot to pack into just a few days.

Viking is one of just a small number of Egypt tour companies that slow the Nile-cruising portion of the trip by spreading it over a seven-night span. This allows for not only a more in-depth experience but also a more relaxed one — the latter of which has particular appeal to the mostly older travelers who are Viking's core market.

Many of Viking's customers are retirees who have the time for longer trips and also prefer to "explore the world in comfort," as Viking likes to say.

On several days of the sailing, notably, we only tour ancient sites for a few hours in the morning and spend the afternoon relaxing on board as the vessel sails the river.

During this time, Zohny and two other onboard Egyptologists lecture on topics such as medicine in ancient Egypt and Egyptian hieroglyphics. There are lessons in Egyptian cooking and basic Arabic. There's afternoon tea.

But there’s also plenty of time to just kick back on the sun deck.

The extra days also allow time for visits to ancient sites that most tours don’t include and for experiencing more on land than just ancient sites.

In addition to stopping at lesser-visited Qena to see the Temple of Hathor, for instance, we spend a morning docked in the often overlooked Nile town of Esna to see not just its lovely if small Roman-era Temple of Khnum but to shop in one of its small markets for local textiles.

For many of us, the shopping time allows us to haggle for Egyptian galabeyas — a traditional, loose-fitting robe worn by men and women across Egypt — for another major moment of the cruise, that night’s Taste of Egypt & Galabeya Evening. Passengers are encouraged to wear local dress, as the crew does, too, for a special dinner of all-local cuisine, and local music and entertainment.

In Aswan, which is as far south as river ships on these itineraries can go, we spend two days experiencing a wide variety of activities that range from touring the dedicated-to-Isis Temple of Philae and sailing in a traditional wind-powered felucca to visiting one of the local villages that are home to Nubians — a distinct ethnic group that has been living in the region for thousands of years.

We also visit the mighty 56-year-old Aswan High Dam, a marvel of construction that blocks river ships from going farther south on the Nile.

As noted above, Viking Osiris is part of a new series of Viking vessels on the Nile that, in my opinion, are the best-designed on the river.

Upscale and intimate, with just 41 cabins and suites apiece, these vessels feature the same elegant, clean-lined Scandinavian-influenced décor that can be found on Viking ships around the world and lots of high-end touches.

Public areas on each vessel include a stylish restaurant overseen by a European chef, a casual deck-top eatery with indoor and outdoor seating, and a cozy lounge and bar — all offering commanding views.

A key element of the design is the wide expanses of clear glass that serve as the outward-facing walls of nearly every public room. This essentially turns the entire ship into a window onto the stunning, colorful scenery that is scrolling by.

In essence, the light-greenish water of the Nile, the rich green papyrus and tall bamboo-like grasses along its banks, and the tan desert cliffs in the distance become the "art" and focal points of the ship's spaces.

That the glass is clear is notable for the Nile, where many vessels are wrapped in dark or metallic glass to reflect the often-intense heat of the sun — glass that, alas, often makes these ships feel closed off to the splendors of the river. Viking went to great lengths to keep the view clear by sourcing a more expensive type of glass that blocks heat without appearing tinted from the inside — a seemingly small detail that makes all the difference.

Other public spaces on each ship include a swanky sun deck with rows of plush lounge chairs for sunning and lovely shaded seating areas. At the very back of the top deck is a narrow pool.

Even the smallest cabins on the ships are generous in size, measuring 232 square feet. And they are filled with luxury elements such as high-end linens and pillows on the beds, heated bathroom floors and roomy wardrobes with wooden hangers.

My cabin — one of eight suites measuring 409 square feet or more — was among the most luxurious that I have seen on a Nile ship. Modern and residential in feel, it featured a large living room with a seating area and desk for working, an adjacent bedroom with a walk-in closet and bathroom, and an outdoor balcony with seating for two. The latter is something you don't always see on Nile ships.

Still, perhaps the most upscale touch of the vessel is the service level that it offers. A crew of 48 people is on hand to serve at most 82 passengers (the ship's maximum capacity with every cabin full — on my sailing, there were just 72), so there's never a lack of staff to cater to your every whim.

I saw this high service level firsthand quite a few times on board, whether it be from the waiter in the restaurant who, unprompted, prepared my traveling companion a special soothing tea with ginger, lime and honey after she mentioned she was feeling a little queasy, to the bartender in the lounge who not only remembered my favorite cocktail but started mixing it before I even had to ask.

In addition, Zohny, our Egyptologist, was the most knowledgeable and engaging Egypt guide that I have encountered during 25 years of visiting the country.

As is typical for higher-end tours of Egypt, Viking's trips in the region aren't inexpensive.

Sold as a combined land-and-cruise tour package, the 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" journeys start at $6,999 per person, based on double occupancy (about $14,000 for a couple sharing a room). And such starting fares are specifically for packages that include an entry-level "standard" cabin without a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip.

For a package that includes a cabin with a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip, you'll find starting rates of around $7,499 per person (about $15,000 per couple). Packages that include a stay in a larger suite cost closer to $25,000 per couple or more, depending on the departure date.

In general, you'll also pay more at all cabin levels for departures from late December through early April, when cooler temperatures in Egypt make touring more pleasant.

That said, such fares are highly all-inclusive. Not only are your ship and hotel rooms included in the price, but most of your meals (along with wine, beer and soft drinks with lunch and dinner while on the ship). You also get extensive guided tours to all the main sites every day of your trip. The latter is a significant value, given the cost and logistical headaches of booking tours in Egypt on your own.

Indeed, a notable part of what you're paying for on a Viking trip to Egypt is access to extremely knowledgeable Egypt experts (known as Egyptologists) who travel with you and explain the many ancient temples, tombs and other historic sites you're seeing.

In addition, the fares include the interior flights in Egypt that will get you between Cairo and Luxor for the cruise portion of the trip, as well as airport transfers when you book international flights through Viking.

Some higher-level cabins also come with complimentary laundry service and a premium beverage package. Little things like shipboard WiFi are also included for all.

Viking's 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" tours offer one of the most comprehensive and seamless ways to explore Egypt. The trips pair a well-paced, seven-night Nile sailing aboard an exceptionally designed new ship with a multi-night land stay in Cairo, together allowing visits to many of Egypt's most iconic attractions, including the Pyramids of Giza and the Valley of the Kings.

While fares are on the higher side among Egypt tours, the extensive all-inclusive nature of the trips — accommodations, most meals, extensive touring with an expert Egyptologist and internal flights are among the inclusions — means they offer a lot of value for the money. And perhaps most importantly, they make touring Egypt easy.

#6287. Allegiant Says MAX 7 Seat Cost ‘Loses Pace’

Allegiant prefers the economics of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 over the smaller MAX 7 as its plans for premium seating change how it evaluates the two aircraft.

The MAX 7 originally accounted for the majority of Allegiant’s Boeing commitment. In January 2022, the airline announced an order for 50 aircraft, split between 30 MAX 7s and 20 high-density MAX 8-200s, with options for another 50 jets.

The agreement, signed in December 2021, was Allegiant’s first direct Boeing order and marked a shift for a carrier that had largely built its business around buying used aircraft. At the time of the announcement, Allegiant operated 108 Airbus A319s and A320s.

Boeing said the new jets would reduce fuel consumption by about 20% compared with the older Airbus aircraft.

Speaking during the carrier’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Neal said the MAX 7 initially offered an attractive balance between the cost of operating each flight and the cost per seat.

“When we did the order, we really liked the MAX 7 because we were looking at both the MAX 8 and MAX 7 at very high density,” Neal said. “And so you’ve got a really nice trip cost seat cost mix with the MAX 7.”

That calculation has changed as Allegiant expands its extra-legroom Allegiant Extra product and prepares to introduce Allegiant First.

“But over time, as you’ve seen us roll out incremental premium offerings at the moment through Allegiant Extra and eventually with Allegiant First, the seat cost just sort of loses pace with the MAX 8,” Neal said. “And so we prefer the cost economics of the MAX 8 at this point.”

Allegiant began shifting its order toward the larger variant in September 2023. An amended agreement retained the 50 firm aircraft but increased the number of MAX 8-200s, reduced the number of MAX 7s and expanded the option pool to 80 aircraft.

The MAX 7 faced years of certification delays, including work to redesign its engine anti-ice system. The FAA approved the variant on Aug. 3, after requiring changes to that system, flight-control software, and cockpit alerts.

The ultra-low-cost carrier added to its MAX 8 commitments last month, exercising six options for delivery in 2028. That brought its firm Boeing order to 56 aircraft, including 22 delivered through Oct. 23, with 74 options remaining.

#6286. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.
