#6271. Brit Arrested After Flight Attendant Finds Hidden Camera In Airplane Bathroom, Now Faces Voyeurism And Cover-Up Charges

A flight attendant discovered a hidden camera while using the lavatory on a Scoot flight from Japan to Singapore. A British passenger now faces charges of voyeurism and obstructing justice, with police alleging that he remotely activated the camera and later tried to erase evidence after realizing it had been found.

Hugh Lutley, a 52-year-old British national, was charged on November 5, 2026, following an incident aboard Scoot flight TR821 from Osaka (KIX) to Singapore (SIN) on October 7.

He faces one charge each of voyeurism and obstruction of justice. It appears Lutley intends to plead guilty, was offered bail of S$10,000, and has a pretrial conference scheduled for November 17 (which of course is not a conviction or a sentence).

The Singapore Police Force’s account describes an alleged attempt to record people inside an aircraft toilet. Police say the passenger concealed a camera in the lavatory, left, and activated its recording function through an application on his phone.

A cabin crew member subsequently used the lavatory and discovered the device. She removed it and immediately alerted a colleague. The passenger allegedly returned to retrieve the camera, found it missing, and deleted the application and related photographs from his phone in an attempt to avoid detection.

Police detained him when the flight arrived at Singapore Changi Airport and seized his phone and the camera.

Those are statutory maximums, but the alleged attempt to destroy evidence exposes him to a charge carrying a substantially longer maximum prison term than the underlying voyeurism charge.

I am thankful the flight attendant found the device and reported it. Discovering something like that while using the restroom must be deeply unsettling.

The published accounts do not establish how many people, if any, were recorded before the camera was discovered…the alleged installation and remote operation are disturbing enough.

Is this world so twisted that passengers must become amateur surveillance experts every time they use an airplane bathroom? If you notice an unfamiliar device or something suspicious, alert the crew promptly…yeah, I guess you should look around before you drop your drawers.

A British passenger faces criminal charges after a flight attendant found a hidden camera in a Scoot lavatory. Police allege he remotely operated it and then deleted material from his phone after discovering the camera had been removed.

#6270. How to Spend a Rainy Day in New York City

A rainy day in New York City is no new phenomenon, but that doesn’t make its occurrence any less disappointing. According to reporting from News 12, Central Park only reported nine completely dry weekends out of the past 40 weekends of 2026, putting a real—forgive me—damper on park hangs and beach days. In case you count yourself among the masses with foiled plans, we at Condé Nast Traveler have you covered. Our editors have weathered their fair share of cold and dreary days in the city and learned to love the rain. After all, it’s the best excuse to dry off by the crackling fireplace of a plush hotel lobby, or conversely, to take a dip into the steaming Russian Turkish baths to cure the sinking cold. Instead of willing the clouds to part, bear your galoshes and head to our editors’ favorite things to do in New York City on a rainy day.

That travel editors love a hotel lobby is about as unsurprising as a dad joke, but there’s nothing like a mini staycation to salvage a lost weekend. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is partial to The Hotel Chelsea. The neighborhood institution has moved far past its roach-ridden days when Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe were Just Kids, and the experience of their lobby is the apotheosis of that evolution. There’s a lot of modern polish, sure, but all the charming verdigris has been kept intact. There’s the art from the hotel’s most (in)famous guests splashed over the walls, the wrought iron chandeliers bathing the space in romantic lighting, and the aforementioned fireplace tying a bow around the mood. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that the hotel’s Lobby Bar is just right next door. If Chelsea feels like a slog to commute to, there are plenty of great options scattered across the map, from the Ace Hotel Brooklyn which has plenty of public workspaces, or Times Square’s Algonquin Hotel, which saw the genesis of The New Yorker just 100 years ago.

The easiest remedy for rainy day restlessness is to stretch your legs at one of the city’s finest museums, though even the impressive 2.2 million-square-foot expanse of the Met becomes easily dwarfed when you’re crammed in by a surge of fellow museum-goers who had the exact same idea. Instead, spend your day exploring NYC’s smaller scholarly corners. Editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez heads to East Williamsburg art organization Amant whenever she feels like she’s cooped inside her apartment, watching the hours just slip away. To start, there’s no need to worry about ponying up big ticket prices as entry is always free. “Peruse the titles at Kis Café and Bookstore, then head to gallery spaces 932 Grand and 315 Maujer; across the street, you’ll find multimedia installations in Géza,” says Alvarez, “The exhibit Sentient Earth currently spans all three galleries, bringing together 28 artists to examine the ways we’ve impacted the planet (and what—if it gained sentience—its response to us might be). Do explore Amant's event programming of screenings and panels, which you can find here.” Other small but mighty options include the Financial District’s public poetry library Poets House, which overlooks the Hudson and Bushwick’s Bone Museum, which also houses resident tuxedo cat Bone Jovi.

Film critic Anthony Lane once posited, “as a rough rule, cinema can be sundered into two halves: six-o’clock films and nine-o’clock films,” and a rainy day is certainly the occasion for the six-o’clock variety and all its ritual: rallying a group to go with, booking the early dinner reservation, whiling away at a nearby bar after to unpack what you’ve just seen. Commerce director Madison Flager likes the Lincoln Center AMC, home to the largest IMAX screen in the country, clocking in at 75.6 feet tall by 101 feet wide, which is roughly the size of a 10-story building. News editor Hannah Towey, on the other hand, dodges the rain at the Metrograph, a boutique two-screen theater keeping the spirit of Prohibition-era New York alive and well. Whichever way you lean, you can always count on NYC’s trusty movie theaters to show you something new.

The less-than-stellar weather shouldn’t keep you from embarking on a treasure hunt, and doing your due diligence enclosed inside one of the city’s coolest vintage stores is a surefire way to uncover a few gems. Alvarez recommends the Flatiron District’s Surrender Dorothy, where the racks are piled with the well-loved and pristine, collector’s items and forgotten blasts from the past, avant-garde art pieces, and buy-it-for-life workwear. It’s dopamine dressing at its best. You could also try your luck at one of the city’s larger franchises like Beacon’s Closet, or, if you’re willing to face the elements, dive into a flea market.

One of the best spots to people-watch in the city, come rain or shine, is the baths. And having a place to hide from the chill and unforgiving precipitation is a welcome bonus. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima touts the East Village’s Russian Turkish Baths as the perfect place to drop by. Melt away whatever’s ailing you in the 215 °F Russian Sauna, and if you need any help doing so, get the platza oak leaf ritual where spa employees forcefully smack your pores open with bushels of oak leaves in the sauna. If you’re looking for something a little more communal, Flager likes to warm up at Othership, which sets itself apart with its guided wellness experiences that combine breath work, aromatherapy, visualizations, somatic movement, live music, and group “shares.”

Nothing brings a bar together like its pool table, but if you’ve spent more time watching the queue of quarters waiting for your turn than the game itself, head to a dedicated pool hall instead, where there’s a better chance of scoring a table all your own and watching the real pros practice their hand. Union Square’s Amsterdam Billiards has been a staple ever since I came to the city five years ago. The 11,000-square-foot hall decked with its array of Brunswick tables might seem intimidating at first, but take it from a real amateur: they may be serious about their snooker here, but they’re not snobby. Pool aside, patrons keep occupied with the hall’s other offerings like table tennis, beer pong, and darts. If you’re serious about upping your game, you can even book one-hour lessons with their in-house pros.

Jazz is one of the country’s greatest art forms, and New York is the genre’s most inspiring muse and resourceful studio. The city cemented its status in the 1920s Harlem Renaissance when legendary venues like the Cotton Club and Small’s Paradise put Duke Ellington, Fats Waller, and Billie Holiday in the national consciousness. Jazz in the city has traveled beyond its uptown crucible, and there’s great clubs peppered throughout the boroughs. Some of our favorites include Ornithology Jazz Club, which also has a killer vegan menu; Funny Bar, which comes from the same team as Baby’s All Right; and Greenwich Village’s Smalls Jazz Club, which keeps things true to form and no-frills.

New York’s historic theatre scene is far from confined to Broadway’s flashing lights. Some of the most exciting, intimate, and interactive productions in the city are playing Off-Broadway. Big names like Andrew Lloyd Webber have found a second wind in shows like Masquerade, a roving retelling of Phantom of the Opera, and fresh concepts like Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody are attracting their own audiences with their lower budget, DIY charm. Shows like these are a trove of talent, and odds are you can find one where you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg for entry at venues like La MaMa or Signature Theatre.

Associate social media manager Bridget Knowles swears by the people's princess of a dive bar as a haven from the harsh weather: “Interjecting here with what I’m sure we’re all thinking. I mean, sheesh. This is unspoken. A great dive bar is an oasis in New York City on a rainy day: a grunge mecca, a throw-some-hours-away swan song. My kind of place. A healthy dose of grime on an already lyrically imposing, moody day is great for the soul. Even if you’re off the Miller High Life (ah, it hurt to type, but pun intended) one of the greatest pastimes in life, according to me, is to simply load up touch tunes and shoot at a table a bit. Make some friends, watch something insane playing on a corner TV. You know, commiserate. Get your hands on some of the best in the city here.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6269. “You Can Have My Middle Seat!” Frontier Passenger Swipes Another Man’s Aisle Seat To Sit With His Wife, Crew Does Nothing

A Frontier Airlines passenger reportedly found another man sitting in his assigned aisle seat because that man wanted to sit beside his wife. The proposed solution? The displaced passenger could take a middle seat two rows behind him. According to a witness, a flight attendant became involved but did not resolve the situation, and the passenger ultimately gave up. If that account is accurate, the airline failed him and owes him more than an apology.

The seating dispute occurred aboard Frontier flight 1550 from Atlanta (ATL) to Jacksonville (JAX).

According to the witness, a passenger arrived at seat 28C and found another man occupying it beside his wife. When he pointed out the assignment, the seated passenger reportedly responded:

“Well, I wanted to sit next to my wife. You can have my middle seat (30E).”

The witness says a flight attendant heard what had happened, but the man remained in the aisle seat. The displaced passenger eventually accepted 30E, saying:

The original Reddit post has since been deleted, though the discussion remains. This is an unverified witness account on reddit…it might be all malarkey…but at worst it makes for an interesting theoretical discussion.

I have no objection to asking another passenger to switch seats. Sometimes couples end up separated despite trying to arrange seats together. But there is a proper way to ask. Start in your assigned seat, explain the situation, and accept the answer. Offering a comparable or better seat certainly helps and is something I view as a starting point.

Taking someone’s aisle seat before he arrives, then informing him that he can have your middle seat instead, turns a request into a confrontation: wanting to sit beside your spouse does not give you authority to make that decision for him.

Why not ask the person beside your assigned middle seat whether they would like to move forward and take your wife’s seat? That would at least give someone a genuine choice while leaving the unwilling passenger out of it.

But the broader problem is the alleged response by Frontier flight attendants. Especially on Frontier, which has totally unbundled fares and has made seat selection a major part of the booking process. The practice of charging for seat selection makes indifference to these disputes even harder to defend. Still, I’m suspicious because even on Frontier I find it difficult to fathom that the crew could reasonably leave the rightful occupant to negotiate for it.

I recognize that airlines sometimes must move passengers for operational or safety reasons. But that is quite different than allowing one traveler’s preference to override another’s confirmed seat assignment merely because he sat down first. If the witness’s account captures the full exchange, the straightforward response would have been to check the boarding passes and ask the man to return to his seat or be ejected from the flight. The crew could then explore a voluntary swap if someone wanted to help.

It is easy to read this story and declare that you would never surrender your seat.

I would have calmly asked the flight attendant to confirm my assignment and help me sit there. If that went nowhere, I would have asked whether another crew member or a gate agent could assist. And yes, I would have filmed it all.

But I also understand the exhaustion behind “I just want to get home.” Sometimes a passenger has already endured enough that a middle seat seems preferable to another argument.

That does not make him foolish and certainly does not establish that the swap was fair.

Frontier (or any carrier) should not create a situation in which the most persistent passenger gets what he wants while the more accommodating one absorbs the inconvenience. That rewards precisely the behavior crews should be discouraging.

This account comes from a witness, and the original post is no longer available. We should leave room for details that may be missing and be open to the possibility that this story is a fabrication.

But the principle is simple and it’s still worth repeating: you may ask someone to switch seats so you can sit with your spouse. You may not decide that his aisle seat is yours and that he should accept your middle seat instead.

When that happens, the crew should help resolve it. Airlines cannot spend the booking process telling us how valuable seat assignments are, then treat those assignments as optional once we board.

Among major hotel loyalty programs, Marriott Bonvoy offers some of the most attainable lifetime elite status tiers. I already have lifetime Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and will secure lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years.

If you're wondering if it's within reach for you, here's what you should know about Marriott lifetime status.

Marriott Bonvoy lets its members earn three tiers of lifetime elite status as follows:

Marriott also historically let members earn lifetime Titanium Elite status, but the program stopped offering it Dec. 31, 2018. Additionally, keep in mind that some Marriott brands don't offer a full qualifying night per eligible night stayed; for example, City Express, Four Points Flex and Protea Hotels award half an elite night credit per qualifying night, while StudioRes doesn't award any elite night credits.

The years of elite status don't need to be consecutive, and years spent at higher elite tiers count toward the requirements for lower lifetime tiers. Marriott status you get as a credit card perk counts toward the calculation of years in a specific elite status tier.

In addition to elite night credits earned from qualifying stays (which include qualifying award stays), elite night credits from credit cards and the five elite night credits you can select as an Annual Choice Benefit also count toward lifetime status.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Members with lifetime Marriott elite status enjoy the same benefits as members who earn these statuses annually, including waived points expiration. Plus, upon earning lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll also get a complimentary gift and access to a webpage that looks back at your lifetime journey.

However, lifetime Platinum Elite status doesn't automatically qualify you for Annual Choice Benefits. You'll still need to earn 50 or 75 elite night credits in a calendar year to unlock these benefits.

And while lifetime members get the perks of the status they've earned, there's no guarantee that Marriott won't change the benefits of a particular status tier. So, if you earn lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll get the current benefits of Platinum Elite instead of the benefits available at the time you secured lifetime status.

Marriott has made it easy to check your lifetime status progress. Go to the Marriott website, log in to your account, click your name in the upper-right corner and select "Overview." Then, click "Nights this year" on the left side of the page.

On the right side of the panel, you'll see your lifetime statistics.

This panel shows your lifetime nights, lifetime years with each status and how far you are from earning the next lifetime status tier.

Earning lifetime Marriott elite status can be relatively easy if you frequently stay with Marriott Bonvoy, hold a Marriott credit card that provides elite status and elite night credits, or both.

I'm looking forward to securing lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years. Although Marriott could change the benefits associated with each status tier, I'm excited about eventually enjoying Platinum Elite perks without requalifying each year.

#6267. 9 All-Inclusive Resorts in Cancún That Go Way Beyond an Open Bar

I first arrived in Cancún, Mexico, more than 20 years ago. I had big hair, pencil-thin eyebrows, and limited expectations for an all-inclusive vacation: A swim-up bar serving frozen margaritas was about all I needed. Since then, my priorities have shifted, and thankfully, Cancún’s all-inclusive resorts have grown up alongside me.

After two decades of return visits made easier by an abundance of nonstop US flights, I’ve become more discerning about what deserves a place in that up-front price. I’ve also discovered that Cancún’s enduring spring break reputation tells an incomplete story about what's on offer. Choose the right resort, and you can have a butler draw your evening bath, a private pool overlooking the Caribbean, and à la carte restaurants you’ll look forward to all afternoon, whether you prefer the Hotel Zone’s long sweep of white sand, the relative quiet of Playa Mujeres, or a boat ride out to Isla Mujeres.

The frozen margaritas are still here. But now, there’s much more worth checking in for. Read on for the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún worth planning a vacation around.

Mexican art gives this Playa Mujeres resort its personality. Rubén Soto’s concrete mural depicts native wildlife amid geometric patterns, while suites carry the aesthetic through warm woods and marble rather than tropical clichés. At Atelier, which welcomes ages 16+, you might have lunch overlooking the water at El Suspiro, then enjoy a pre-dinner mezcal cocktail at Bar de la Calle. Back in your suite, a rolling minibar holds wine and gourmet snacks, and room service answers around the clock. Most dining and premium spirits are included, though María Dolores by Edgar Núñez warrants a separate reservation—and budget—for its contemporary Mexican menu. Book an Inspira suite, and a butler can arrange your dinner reservations while you spend the afternoon at the rooftop infinity pool.

At Le Blanc, the pampering begins before you’ve unpacked—and your butler can handle that, too. Once you’re settled, the day’s agenda might amount to a poolside cocktail, a soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy pools, and deciding what to wear to dinner. This adults-only Hotel Zone retreat pairs pale interiors and Caribbean frontage with an unusually generous all-inclusive package: À la carte dining, premium drinks, 24-hour room service, and access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit are all included. Dinner might mean a French tasting menu at the esteemed Lumière or Italian cooking at Blanc Italia. Massages cost extra, but the daily chance to steam, soak, and unwind in the spa does not.

Two beaches are better than one, especially when they come with a lighthouse and Caribbean views in nearly every direction. Perched on the tip of Punta Cancún, Hyatt Ziva makes the most of its peninsula setting, with room for both family playtime and grown-up downtime. Little ones can race down waterslides and splash beneath fountains, while teenagers claim their own turf over billiards and foosball in the teens' lounge. For those whose idea of vacation involves neither, Turquoize (a tower within the resort) offers an adults-only escape with ocean-facing suites, butlers just a WhatsApp message away, and a rooftop infinity pool blissfully removed from the splash zone.

Behind Paradisus’s five glass-topped pyramids, one of Cancún’s most recognizable silhouettes, vines cascade through a soaring atrium, fountains burble below, and newly redesigned rooms turn beds toward Caribbean sunrises or Nichupté Lagoon sunsets. A 2026 renovation refreshed this Cancún landmark without sacrificing its theatrical streak. Days might involve salsa lessons, pickleball, or children gleefully getting drenched beneath splash-park tipping buckets. Included meals feature freshly pressed tortillas at Taqueria Blue Agave and ceviche at Agua Marina, and bars pour Patrón and Grey Goose without a surcharge. For a quieter stay, The Reserve upgrade tier adds an adults-only pool, restaurant, and concierge service.

Here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Not all Cancún resorts are sprawling tropical compounds. At Secrets The Vine, a sleek adults-only tower brings a more cosmopolitan beach experience, with teak furnishings, Italian porcelain floors, and balconies suspended over that improbable Caribbean blue. As the name suggests, afternoons and evenings are devoted to the grape. Sommelier-led tastings gather guests around a handcrafted wooden table at the Vine Bar; evenings bring Mexican and international pours, and between glasses, a white-sand beach and three infinity pools tempt you outside. While many wines and premium spirits are included, special bottles from the cellar carry additional charges but are well worth it.

Dinner without one eye on a restless toddler is a luxury Finest Playa Mujeres has thought to provide. At Imagine Lounge, staff look after potty-trained children ages three and older for up to 90 minutes while parents eat nearby. The practical details are equally reassuring: homemade baby purées, bottle warmers, and family suites with a separate bedroom for the children. Meals, drinks, and 24-hour room service are included, so parents can order dinner after the little ones are asleep. One Spa even offers treatments for younger guests, though those appointments cost extra.

At Almare’s swim-up bar, the rum is blended with coconut or mango; at Botanik, the coffee is Mexican and locally roasted. Those touches give this 109-room, adults-only retreat on Isla Mujeres a sense of place. Get better acquainted through a tikin xic cooking experience devoted to the island’s signature fish dish, or take a kayak out from the beach—all complimentary. There’s a pool by the shore and an infinity pool on the rooftop, where dinner at Seasalt comes with Caribbean views and Mexican-European cooking. The resort also arranges guided visits to Punta Sur’s temple ruins for a fee, where you’ll hear stories of the Maya goddess Ixchel.

Excellence Playa Mujeres is a place to spread out—even the entry-level suites are upwards of 800 square feet, with whirlpool tubs and furnished terraces. Book a rooftop suite, and you can spend the afternoon between your plunge pool and daybed, with lunch delivered whenever you’re ready. Venture downstairs, though, and there's so much more: winding pools lead past swim-up terraces, beach waiters keep the margaritas coming, and dinner could mean Indian curries at Basmati or a lingering French meal at Chez Isabelle. Club suites at this adults-only Playa Mujeres retreat add private pools and beach areas and one Miilé Spa hydrotherapy session per person, per stay.

What is the best all-inclusive resort in Cancún?

For an adult-only stay, Le Blanc Spa Resort Cancún gets my vote. Butler service and French tasting menus make it feel suitably indulgent, and the rate includes access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit. With children, I’d choose Finest Playa Mujeres, where separate kids' bedrooms and supervised care during mealtimes give parents a holiday too.

Is it worth getting an all-inclusive package in Cancún?

Yes, especially if you plan to spend most of your vacation at the resort. At the right property, your rate covers dinners you actually look forward to, premium drinks, and activities you’d otherwise pay for separately. If you plan to spend each day exploring and eating around town, a traditional hotel may make more sense. Before booking your all-inclusive, be sure to check the exclusions—you might find you'll have to pay extra for spa treatments, special bottles of wine, and some restaurant experiences.

What’s the cheapest month to go to Cancún?

September is generally one of the cheapest months for Cancún hotels, after summer vacation crowds leave. The trade-off is wetter weather and the possibility of tropical storms during hurricane season. For a better balance of price and weather, consider late October through the week before Thanksgiving.

#6266. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

#6265. What Travelers Should Know About the Galápagos Floods—and the Ongoing Impact of El Ñino

On October 30 and 31, 2026, torrential rainfall on the Galápagos's Santa Cruz island caused waterways to overflow, flooding neighborhoods, damaging homes, and disrupting essential infrastructure. The local government declared an emergency, with over 2,000 people affected by the damage. This places the Galápagos among several beloved tourism destinations that are already grappling with the effects of El Ñino.

The news has also left many travelers wondering: Is it safe to travel to the Galápagos right now? And how should those with upcoming cruises and hotel stays proceed?

Rodrigo Jácome, who runs La K-leta Guest House and a small coffee farm on Santa Cruz, which is the archipelago's main inhabited island and a central hub for tourism, says the flooding has not damaged key tourism infrastructure—though it devastated other local livelihoods. “The flooding affected residential neighborhoods that are not particularly close to the main hotel areas,” says Jácome, who lost most of his coffee harvest in the rains. For those with upcoming travel, and locals who rely on travelers to make a living, however, “tourism operations resumed within days.”

Authorities have reopened most visitor sites in the Galápagos National Park, and transportation has resumed, though conditions remain subject to change. Below, we report on all of the impacted areas across the Galápagos, which tours may be rerouted, and how to stay up on the news as future weather develops, according to those on the ground. Plus, local tour operators share advice on planning accordingly for trips in the months ahead.

Santa Cruz is where you'll find many hotels, restaurants, tour operators, and transportation connections, and the area that experienced the most significant damage. Santa Cruz serves as a major base for day trips and cruises to other islands. Most visitors arriving by air fly in via neighboring Baltra, where the airport is located.

Puerto Ayora, the island's main town, and the highland parish of Bellavista, were among the affected areas. Floodwaters damaged homes and roads, disrupted water and electricity services, and forced families to evacuate. The flooding also affected transportation infrastructure connecting Santa Cruz to Baltra Airport, the main gateway for visitors arriving by air to Santa Cruz. The road reopened on November 5 and reconstruction work is being carried out in parallel, allowing travelers to continue arriving to the island as planned.

Although the emergency was concentrated in Santa Cruz, other islands also experienced heavy rainfall and localized flooding. Whitman Cox, a Galápagos National Park naturalist guide based in San Cristóbal, which is known for its sea lion colonies, volcanic landscapes, and popular snorkeling and diving sites, says there was no such damage in San Cristobal, but access to some of the beaches around the island has been restricted as weather conditions change.

Travelers should therefore check conditions for all destinations on their itinerary, across the archipelago, rather than assuming all islands have been affected equally. Constant communication with tour guides, your hotel, or cruise line is the best way to get up-to-date information.

While the Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened, the Los Humedales sector in Isabela (above) remains closed.

As of November 9, flights to Baltra and San Cristóbal were operating on their regular schedules, according to local reporting. Tourism activities have also continued, although some visitor sites remain temporarily closed.

The Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened areas following safety assessments: As of November 9, Playa El Garrapatero in Santa Cruz was accessible again, while popular visitor sites Las Grietas, El Chato, and El Puntudo remained restricted. In San Cristóbal, La Lobería and Punta Carola had reopened, while surfing spots Puerto Chino and Playa Baquerizo remained closed. The Los Humedales sector in Isabela also remained closed. From November 9-18, Tortuga Bay, a beach in Santa Cruz, will be closed as a preventative measure due to tide changes.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office updated its Ecuador travel advisory on November 1 to include the flooding on Santa Cruz. It advises travelers to follow local authorities' instructions, avoid flooded areas, and confirm travel arrangements with airlines and tour operators.

Cox emphasizes that travelers shouldn't panic—El Niño is a natural weather cycle. “People can still come. We shouldn't frighten them," says Cox. His main guidance is to be patient. “They may encounter transportation difficulties between certain points, which could take additional time.” He adds that the park has done its best in the interest of safety by closing the above sites as a precautionary measure.

The flooding comes as Ecuador experiences an El Niño event, a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures across the equatorial Pacific, which can alter atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. In Ecuador, El Niño is often associated with heavier rainfall, particularly along the coast and in the Galápagos. However, its effects vary by region and over time.

According to the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI), the El Niño event remained active and was strengthening for the upcoming months with weather reports suggesting that heavy rainfall may last until February 2027.

The potential implications for travelers include heavy rain, temporary road closures, changes to boat excursions, and restricted access to natural visitor sites. Weather conditions can also affect marine activities and inter-island transportation.

However, this is not the first time El Niño has impacted the islands, and tour guides understand how to prepare. “It is a cyclical part of nature that we have seen every 10-15 years,” says Charles Wittmer, president of the Association of Boat Operators in the Galápagos, ADATUR. “Nature is unpredictable and if anything, this is a chance to see the adaptations of animals to changing weather conditions,” he says. “Remember: this is a natural laboratory of evolution.” On the wildlife front, Wittmer mentions that Galápagos penguins and cormorants adapt to warming ocean waters. And there's a plus: These shifts in marine ecosystem activity may increase the variety of species spotted while snorkeling.

If you have an upcoming trip, local tourism specialists recommend staying informed and remaining flexible. It’s best to ask about excursion alternatives when booking a tour in the islands, should weather create the need to pivot.

Before departure, confirm your flights and accommodation directly with your airline and tour operator. Ask whether your planned excursions are operating as anticipated and whether alternative activities are available if certain visitor sites are closed. Ask your tour guide for updates daily.

It's also a good idea to purchase travel insurance that covers weather-related disruptions, medical emergencies, and unexpected accommodation or transportation expenses. Travelers can monitor official updates from INAMHI and the Galápagos National Park social media and from their website with forecasts, and plan smart by allowing extra flexibility in travel connections and excursions. Remember to also pack lightweight rain protection and waterproof bags for electronics and important documents.

Like Cox, Wittmer emphasizes that nature is out of our control. “People should bring clothing and be ready for heavier rainfall and be flexible in their expectations.”

Though travelers come to the Galápagos for the nature, local guides are the greatest resource in appreciating this place—and navigating it in uncertain times.

Whether staying in local communities, visiting for a few hours on cruise excursions, or simply passing through in transit, travelers contribute to the livelihoods of local businesses and workers, many of whom are also dealing with the consequences of the flooding, simply by visiting. As Jácome puts it, “Tourism is needed now more than ever to help rebuild the communities that lost everything.”

Consider booking locally owned accommodation, hiring licensed local guides, eating at independent restaurants, and purchasing goods from small businesses.

As always, travelers should also be mindful that affected neighborhoods are not tourist attractions. Avoid visiting damaged homes or taking photographs of residents dealing with the aftermath of the flooding without their permission.

If you are traveling to Galápagos right now, consider packing water purification tablets, basic first-aid supplies, and hygiene kits to done to affected families (your guide or hotel can assist with routing these to the right place). You can also check with local emergency centers or your tour operator upon arrival to donate pet food or clean clothes directly to the most impacted neighborhoods.

If you want to contribute to recovery efforts from afar, several organizations and initiatives have mobilized support:

Fundación Charles Darwin: The foundation is part of an emergency fundraising initiative, with proceeds directed to the Santa Cruz emergency response committee (COE) to support urgent community needs.

San Francisco de Quito University: The University has established a SOS Galapagos fund, collecting donations on their campus in Quito. They also have a donations link.

Fundación Torraja: This local organization is administering a Community Kitchen and providing meals and donations directly to families who lost their belongings in the floods.

#6264. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Through 11:59PM ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is tiered, as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses. With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

If you’ve been frustrated by soaring airfare, now may be your best chance to book flights without the sticker shock.

American Airlines just launched one of its biggest AAdvantage award sales of the year. And you'll want to act quickly: It’s only scheduled to be live for 72 hours.

American has put more than 1 million main cabin seats on sale for the winter months.

If holiday fares were out of your budget this year, this could be a chance to redeem miles for a long weekend getaway in the Caribbean in January — or to hit the ski slopes over President’s Day weekend in February.

American’s winter AAdvantage award sale covers flights from Jan. 11 through Feb. 28, 2027.

The deals are slated to run through 12:59 a.m. EST on Nov. 12.

These aren’t the cheapest AAdvantage award redemptions we’ve ever seen (a similar award sale last year offered award prices even lower than this year’s).

And some of these redemptions are in the range of what I typically look for in the quieter winter months.

The good news here is that these cheaper award prices are widely available. And that’s significant in a year where fares (and award prices) have surged.

As an AAdvantage member myself, I'd feel pretty good about booking at any of these price points.

You won’t find these discounted award prices on every flight, date or route. Instead, American simply says it’s discounting more than 1 million main cabin seats across its network.

Fortunately, there aren't blackout dates — which means you don't need to fly at 10 p.m. on a Tuesday to take advantage of this deal. There are options on Fridays, Sundays, peak long weekend travel days and during other popular times.

These deals apply to economy bookings; American is not offering up these discounts on premium economy, first class or business class.

However, these cheaper award redemptions could be a way to get a spot on the plane and then watch for a targeted upgraded offer to a premium seat.

You can find domestic bookings within the 48 contiguous U.S. states for as low as 8,000 miles one-way.

That includes longer transcontinental flights.

For instance, here’s a January flight from Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

There are also short-haul international redemptions to warm-weather island destinations at that rate, too — like this February flight from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) to Turks and Caicos.

As a Raleigh-based flyer, I could book this Martin Luther King, Jr. weekend flight from North Carolina to Zurich, Switzerland, for 22,500 miles one-way.

There are a ton of AAdvantage redemptions to Europe at that price point, with options for both nonstop and connecting itineraries, depending on your final destination.

I also found pretty open award availability for 25,000 miles one-way.

Here are some examples: LAX to Tokyo’s Haneda Airport (HND), and another to Sydney, Australia.

Passengers in Chicagoland are the biggest winners.

American's award sale includes discounted AAdvantage redemptions starting even lower than the rest of the country, at 7,000 miles one-way.

These AAdvantage deals for the winter months aren’t the cheapest award discounts American has ever offered. But they’re pretty solid — and widely available — for the upcoming winter months.

And for consumers plagued by high prices this year, that could be reason enough to lock in a winter getaway.

Just be sure to book by Wednesday night to take advantage of these deals.

#6262. Introduction: An Orient Express Adventure Via Africa

Welcome to my next trip report series, covering a trip that I recently wrapped up, which will include reviews of flights and a cruise. This will be a relatively short series, since the trip didn’t last that long, and had a specific purpose. However, as usual, I tried to take an unconventional routing to get to and from the destination, so I could review new experiences.

You can expect reviews of Air Algerie and Royal Air Maroc business class, as well as a review of Orient Express Sailing Yachts, which is Orient Express’ new cruising venture. In this post I’d like to share a basic outline of the trip, and then I’ll have individual review installments in the near future.

The primary reason for this trip was simple, and it was to take a cruise with Orient Express Sailing Yachts. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry, and in particular, the increasing number of new lines associated with existing luxury hospitality brands.

Prior to this year, I hadn’t taken a cruise with any cruise line since I was a child, so I’ve been curious to check this all out. At the beginning of the year, I reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, which was surprisingly lovely, and a very nice reintroduction to cruising.

Then over the summer, I reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which was definitely upmarket, but had some growing pains.

The newest entrant into this market is Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and arguably it takes luxury cruising to a new level, so you can expect a full review of the experience. Full disclosure — Ford was invited on the sailing (so traveled as a guest of Orient Express) and I tagged along. I’ll still review the experience objectively, of course, but I’ll say upfront that Orient Express simply nailed it, and this matched the feedback Ford has received from clients who have sailed with the company.

Anyway, we sailed with Orient Express Sailing Yachts on a four night journey that started in Marseille, France, and ended in Malaga, Spain, so we needed to position to and from there.

I’m of course always looking for an interesting airline angle when I travel long haul, since my goal is always to try as many new airline products as possible. So rather than flying to Marseille and from Malaga on the “typical” airlines (Air France, British Airways, Lufthansa, etc.), I tried to see if I could instead check some airlines off my list that I’ve been wanting to try. I accomplished that, and below is what my routing looked like.

While I sent Ford direct, I booked a four segment routing for myself, spread across three different tickets.

I had heard a lot about Air Algerie over the years (and not in a good way!), so I decided I finally had to give the carrier a try. Air Algerie typically has very high business class fares, despite the carrier’s lackluster product.

However, I found one decent fare on the carrier’s only route from North America, from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, that doesn’t start where I’d like to start, and it doesn’t end where I’d like to end, but that has never stopped me if the price is right. 😉

This included a flight in Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class across the Atlantic, and then a connecting flight in Avion Express’ Airbus A320neo business class for the short hop in Africa (this was a wet leased flight operated on behalf of Air Algerie). So I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day) 10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

From there, I of course had to get from Tunis to Marseille (MRS), so I had booked Tunisair’s A320 business class for $270, with the following schedule:

10/04 TU902 Tunis to Marseille departing 1:05PM arriving 3:40PM

Unfortunately I ended up being downgraded shortly before departure due to an aircraft swap. That’s because the flight was swapped to a wet leased Fly2Sky Airbus A320, and I guess they don’t offer business class on those planes. I’m still waiting on any sort of a refund.

Suffice it to say that the outbound wasn’t that smooth, between Air Algerie just royally sucking, and Tunisair downgrading me. I’m happy I had the experience, though!

I should also mention that I had to position to Montreal, so I did that in Air Canada Rouge economy, and flew the following for 11,500 avianca lifemiles plus $54 in taxes & fees:

10/04 AC1651 Miami to Montreal departing 7:55AM arriving 11:28AM

The return portion of our trip was a little more straightforward. Our priority was to get home the same day as our cruise arrived, since we wanted to minimize time away from our kids, and had a family event the next day. So we booked the one routing that would best get us home the same day, which was on Royal Air Maroc, from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA), with the first flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class, and the second flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class.

I booked one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM 10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

On this trip, we just had a single hotel night ahead of our cruise in Marseille (in order to build in a buffer), and we decided to stay at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. I booked this using an IHG free night award, and it cost 60,000 points before applying the award, so I just had to redeem the difference in points.

I had intended to review the hotel, but I have to apologize, it just didn’t end up working out (since I pride myself in thoroughly reviewing hotels). To be honest, I was dead tired from the journey over, and then we had some drama to deal with back at home most of the afternoon. Then the next morning I prioritized sleeping in, as I was just getting over a cold, rather than getting up at 5AM so I could photograph all parts of the hotel.

So I’m sorry about that. My conclusion is that the hotel has a central location, and from the outside you’d think it’s super charming, but the interior feels mismatched and rather uninspiring and generic.

We had an absolutely amazing time cruising with Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and I was blown away by the experience. What I was less impressed by was my flights to and from Europe, which I routed via Africa in both directions. Air Algerie was downright terrible, while Royal Air Maroc was just unnecessarily bad.

#6261. 9 NYC Christmas Markets for Food, Fun, and Getting All Your Gift Shopping Done

New York City is electric any time of year, but few months on the calendar are as magical as the final two. In the run up to Christmas in New York, the Big Apple transforms into a holiday winter wonderland: think twinkling lights on street posts, elaborate department store window displays, and marquee theater events like New York City Ballet’s The Nutcracker or the Radio City Rockettes. It’s also probably the best time of the year to shop, thanks to a flurry of NYC Christmas markets that set up everywhere from Bryant Park to Grand Central Terminal.

But with so many to choose from, and locations all over the boroughs, how do you know which one is best for you to visit? That’s where we come in. Not only are we yearly visitors to all the annual markets, we’ve already done the research to scout the best newcomers to the field for 2026. Below, find our New Yorker-vetted NYC Christmas markets worth a holiday visit, from favorite and famed ones like Union Square’s, to newer events like Eater Under Wraps and Field + Supply.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

The rink at Bryant Park is tied only with Wollman in Central Park for the title of most famous in the city, and it's part of the Winter Village that runs here every year.

Location: Bryant Park, New York, NY 10018

Why we love it: There’s something for everyone at the massive Bank of America Winter Village at Bryant Park in the heart of Midtown. Gift givers will love The Holiday Shops by Urbanspace, a European-style market made up of “jewel box” kiosks filled with 180-plus vendors stocking everything from cozy winter hats to artisanal ornaments, while outdoor food stands at The Lodge provide plenty of fuel like s’mores and sausages for your shopping escapades. The Winter Village is also home to one of the city’s most famed ice rinks, which is free to use (though skate rental fees apply if you don’t bring your own).

The Grand Central Holiday Fair is celebrating its 21st year within the iconic terminal's shuttle passage.

Location: Vanderbilt Hall, Grand Central Terminal, 89 E. 42nd Street, New York, NY 10017

Why we love it: If you’re not exactly a fan of the cold weather, we have good news: New York City is also home to a handful of fantastic indoor holiday markets. The longest-running is the Grand Central Holiday Fair inside the city’s transportation crown jewel, Grand Central Terminal. The train station’s annual Holiday Fair inside Vanderbilt Hall features over thirty small businesses selling handmade gifts, plus an Uncommon Goods pop-up and an outpost of the Grand Central Gift Shop for all the train lovers on your list. And speaking of trains: after you’re done shopping, stick around the Terminal to watch the famed Holiday Train Show, featuring model trains trundling along decorated tracks that feature NYC landmarks and even the North Pole.

Union Square Holiday Market remains the gold standard classic for most New Yorkers, with 185 vendors spiraling out in a seemingly endless array of booths.

Location: Union Square, New York, NY 10003

Why we love it: If you say “holiday market” to a New Yorker, chances are they’ll direct you to the bustling Union Square Holiday Market. With nearly 200 vendors spread across concentric half-circles of booths, we’re not exaggerating when we say you can find the perfect present for everyone on your list at this sprawling pop-up. Some buzzy vendors to look out for this year? The MB Edit for vintage accessories and silk scarves, Hudson Valley Seed Company for organic bulbs and seeds, and make sure to save time to explore the many food purveyors for snacks, like Fan-Fan Donuts from James Beard Award nominee Fany Gerson. Pro tip: As the city’s most famous market, it can get quite crowded on nights and weekends, so try to opt for daytime weekday visits if possible.

Location: 100 W. 77th Street, New York, NY 10024

Dates: Every Sunday from November 29 until December 30

Why we love it: While many of New York’s most famed holiday markets have the polish so closely associated with the city, one of the reasons Grand Holiday Bazaar is beloved is that it feels like a proper neighborhood event. Held every Sunday in a combo indoor-outdoor space on the Upper West Side, the Bazaar hosts over 150 independent, rotating local vendors who sell everything from handmade holiday decor to vintage accessories to skincare. Plus, 100 percent of the event’s profits are donated to four local public schools that serve over 2,000 kids.

FAD Market Holiday Pop-Up will set up shop in the lobby of Empire Stores in Dumbo, also home to Time Out Market.

Location: Empire Stores, 55 Water Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Dumbo) and St. Paul, 190 Court Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Cobble Hill)

Dates: November 30 – December 20 (Dumbo) and December 5–6, 12–13, and 19–20 (Cobble Hill)

Why we love it: FAD (which stands for Fashion, Art, Design) will host double the markets this year, in two separate locations in Brooklyn. Dumbo, which will run continuously from November 30th until December 20th inside Empire Stores, will have a rotating selection of jewelry makers, ceramicists, and small-batch food purveyors, with about 35 vendors on weekends and 14 during the week. Cobble Hill’s pop-up, meanwhile, will run over three weekends in December at St. Paul church, with a brand-new crew of 70-plus makers selling giftables like apparel, home decor, and skincare.

Turkish jewelry, fondue baguettes, and artisan soaps are on offer at Columbus Circle's Central Park-adjacent Christmas market.

Location: Columbus Circle, New York, NY, 10019

Why we love it: Situated at one of the prettiest corners of Manhattan—smack between Columbus Circle and Central Park—this market would be worth the trip even if the vendors were hawking only touristy souvenirs. Luckily though, the selection here is carefully curated, with makers this year ranging from Seyahan’s Turkish-inspired jewelry to Fairy Greens Lavender Farm’s fragrant collection of candles, soaps, and body oils made with the dreamy plant. There’s also plenty to snack on: don’t miss first-time vendor Fondue Baguette selling—you guessed it—baguettes filled with cheese.

Location: Herald Square, New York, NY 10001

Field + Supply, one of upstate New York's premier makers' markets, has landed in the city for the first time this year with a weekend pop-up in the Starrett-Lehigh Building.

Location: Starrett-Lehigh Building, 601 W. 26th Street, New York, NY 10001

Why we love it: One of upstate New York’s premier makers’ markets returns to the city this year, much to the delight of anyone looking for chic home goods, artisanal jewelry, and much more. There will be 140-plus vendors at the two-day Field + Supply event in Chelsea, with products ranging from ceramics to textiles to specialty foods. And even if you’re shopped out, there’s plenty else to lure you, including a visit from Santa himself and retro tintype portraits.

Location: Iron23, 29 W. 23rd Street, New York, NY 10010

Why we love it: The ultimate one-stop-shop for foodies, Eater Under Wraps, returns for a one-day-only market this year in Chelsea. Brands like Pepsi, Reese’s, and Kahlúa will host activations, along with food and drink samples from local spots like Shania's Max Bet and Nishaan, and, naturally, a robust, curated selection of gifts chosen by Eater’s own editors.

#6259. The 7 Airlines Flying Airbus A321XLRs On Both Short & Long-Haul Routes

In evolutionary biology, conversation is often focused on 'the' thing features evolved for. For example, bird wings evolved for flying. In reality, birds will use them for whatever they can. Penguins use them for swimming, while chickens use them for changing direction while running and shading their chicks.

Aircraft are somewhat similar. They may be optimized for a specific mission, but that doesn't mean they will be used for those missions by the airline all the time. In Vietnam, VietJet sometimes flies its widebody A330s on ultra-short domestic routes from Ho Chi Minh City to Nha Trang half empty. VietJet apparently does this because the time slot is available in the A330's international schedule.

The Airbus A321XLR is optimized for longer, but thinner routes. On shorter routes, its increased weight from its extra tanks and strengthened landing gear imposes a penalty. Even so, some airlines will operate them on short routes, partly because they are available. Let's examine some of the airlines using the XLR on both short and longer-haul routes.

Aer Lingus is the flag carrier of Ireland and has a fleet of six Airbus A321XLRs. These are configured with 16 business class seats and 168 economy class seats for a total of 184 seats. This is identical to its complementary fleet of eight A321LRs. In July 2026, Aer Lingus flew more than 300 flights longer than 3,100 miles (5,000 kilometers) and more than 200 routes shorter than 1,250 miles (2,000 kilometers) with its XLRs.

Those shorter routes are European hops when the aircraft are not flying their longer transatlantic trips. An example of a long Aer Lingus XLR flight is Dublin to Nashville, which comes with a scheduled flight time of nine hours and 20 minutes. Meanwhile, during the first week of November, the XLR (registered EI-XLU) has flown hops such as Dublin to London (48 minutes) and Dublin to Barcelona (one hour and 50 minutes).

Flightradar24 shows EI-XLU's longer recent flights include Nashville (Tennessee), Cleveland (Ohio), Toronto (Canada), Indianapolis (Indiana), and New York. Being located at the far western edge of Europe, Aer Lingus has the advantage of being able to reach more destinations in the US with the XLR. The XLR is an excellent aircraft for thinner transatlantic missions, but it is also ok to use on short hops, accepting a modest penalty.

Iberia was the launch customer for the Airbus A321XLR in late 2024, and today it operates a fleet of seven examples with an eighth on order. These are configured with 14 business class seats and 168 economy seats, totaling 182 seats. Spain (excluding Russia) leads Europe with the most domestic flights, driven by the need to connect the mainland with the Canary Islands and Balearic Islands.

From its base in Madrid, Iberia flies its A321XLRs to transatlantic destinations in the United States such as Boston, Newark, Washington DC, and Canada's Toronto. Having a more Spanish and Latin focus than carriers like the UK or Ireland, it also flies them to the Dominican Republic (Santo Domingo) and Puerto Rico (San Juan) in the Caribbean (both Spanish-speaking).

In South America, its XLRs fly as far as Recife and Fortaleza in Brazil. Recent flight tracking data for the XLR registered EC-OOJ reveals it is mostly flying longer transatlantic routes. However, it has also flown European hops to Zurich and Paris (both one hour and 30 minutes) as well as Venice (two hours).

Qantas will have one of the highest passenger capacities onboard its Airbus A321XLRs.

Air Canada is one of the XLR's newest operators, with the national Canadian airline flying the aircraft since June. Now the airline has a growing fleet of five to six in service. Air Canada's official website says it has six in inventory, while Planespotters.net still records five delivered, of which one is currently grounded. That aircraft is brand new and working up.

Regardless, Air Canada is in the process of building up one of the world's largest XLR fleets, with around 24 of its 30-strong order still to be delivered. Air Canada is using the aircraft on a range of longer routes, including transatlantic flights to Europe. C-GXLR was the first XLR delivered to Air Canada. In recent weeks, its longest flight was Toronto to Copenhagen (up to eight hours),

Other longer routes include Montreal to Toulouse (about seven hours), as well as Montreal to Lisbon, Montreal to Porto, and other European destinations. It is also used extensively on medium (three- to five-hour) flights to various destinations in the United States and western Canada such as Los Angeles and Calgary. Ultra short hops include Ottawa to Toronto (39 minutes) and Montreal to Toronto (53 minutes).

Qantas is another of the leading Airbus A321XLR customers, with a total of 48 on order or delivered. The Flying Kangaroo is currently taking delivery of its XLRs, with seven now in inventory. These are ideally suited to some Pacific routes where the range is vast, but the routes are thin. The fact that Qantas ordered 20 more XLRs in August 2025 suggests it has many Asia-Pacific routes in mind.

However, few have been announced. The XLR registered VH-OGA was the first delivered to Qantas in April 2025. Confusingly, its flight history over the last month shows it has only been used on domestic routes. The shortest route is the one-hour flight between Sydney and Melbourne, while the longest flight is the domestic transcontinental flight from Sydney to Perth, which is less than five hours.

Qantas is introducing the type progressively and assigning it to domestic trunk routes before expanding internationally. Upcoming international routes include Perth to India (expected), Adelaide to Singapore, and Brisbane to Manila. While Qantas has not announced all of its upcoming Pacific routes, interesting destinations include Fiji, Samoa, the Cook Islands, and Tahiti.

American Airlines now has 11 of its 40 XLRs ordered in inventory. As with European carriers, American is assigning these to transatlantic routes. They also have the range to reach many leisure and thinner destinations in the Caribbean, Central America, and South America.

The first XLR American took delivery of is N300NY. Its most recent flight history is dominated by transcontinental routes flying from Boston or New York to Los Angeles or San Francisco, taking around five hours. It is also flying transatlantic routes from New York to Barcelona (up to eight hours) and New York to Edinburgh (up to six hours).

Largest publicly reported A321XLR customers

While short hops appear less common in American's fleet, there are some. One XLR (N301NY) has flown hops like Boston to Philadelphia (one hour). As with other airlines, the American XLR fleet is working up and is yet to take on many of its intended routes. South America is identified as a future market with potential American routes including Miami to Porto Alegre, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, and others.

The Airbus321XLR will change the mid-sized market and allow new destinations for airlines.

United Airlines is another major airline busy inducting its new XLR fleet and gearing up for transatlantic and other routes. It has recently suggested that the XLR lacks the range to serve some deeper European routes, such as those to Greece. This is somewhat confusing, as it is well within the advertised range and other airlines fly comparable distances.

United has not provided a detailed breakdown of its calculations, including payload, required margins, routing, etc., to understand the assertion. It has just received the first three of its 50-strong order, leaving 47 remaining on the order book. These are now starting to replace its aging fleet of 757-200s.

With the first delivered in May, United's XLR remains a fleet in its infancy. Flight records show they have yet to fly longer transatlantic routes to Western Europe, although they are coming. Mostly, the flights have been transcontinental, around four to five hours. One short hop in the record is San Diego to Denver, a flight time of less than two hours.

IndiGo is the leading low-cost carrier of India and is one of the world's fastest-rising carriers. It boasts a fleet of 425 aircraft in service and has 881 more on order. While delivered, that will make it one of the largest airlines in the world in the 2030s. The airline's fleet is overwhelmingly A320 family narrowbodies, although it has 60 A350 widebodies on order.

IndiGo has 175 A321neos in service plus four new XLRs. It has the largest order for the XLR, totalling 69 examples. This is made up of the 40 original firm orders publicly confirmed by IndiGo and 29 additional aircraft reflected in industry fleet databases. Once again, the fleet is in its infancy and is working up.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

With that being said, IndiGo seems much faster at deploying them on its longer-haul routes than other airlines. Flight history for VT-NLA shows it has been flying between Delhi and Athens (over eight hours), Mumbai and Istanbul (over seven hours), Mumbai and Amsterdam (up to nine hours and 30 minutes). One example of a short hop is the two-hour route between Delhi and Mumbai.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

UA will be starting their XLR flights to Dublin and Amsterdam from Washington from December 1.
